explanations.A: As the power is increased to enter a constant-rate climb in straight flight, the primary pitch instrument is the attitude indicator until the vertical speed indicator stabilizes at the desired rate of climb (then the vertical speed indicator becomes primary). The primary bank instrument is the heading indicator. The primary power instrument is the manifold pressure gauge or tachometer.
explanations.B: because the vertical speed indicator is the primary pitch instrument once the constant-rate climb is established. Also, the manifold pressure gauge, not the airspeed indicator, is primary for power.
explanations.C: because the heading indicator, not the attitude indicator, is primary for bank in straight flight.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 145.) What is the correct sequence for recovery from the unusual attitude indicated?

answers.A: Reduce power, increase back elevator pressure, and level the wings.
answers.B: Reduce power, level the wings, bring pitch attitude to level flight.
answers.C: Level the wings, raise the nose of the aircraft to level flight attitude, and obtain desired airspeed.

explanations.A: because the wings should be level before you increase back pressure to decrease the load factor during leveling off.
explanations.B: In Fig. 145, a nose-low attitude is indicated by a negative vertical speed indicator, high airspeed (i.e., near Vne), and the airplane below the horizon on the attitude indicator. For nose-low unusual attitudes, the correct sequence for recovery is to reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of altitude; level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder pressure to straight flight by referring to the turn coordinator; and raise the nose to level flight attitude by smooth back elevator pressure. b
explanations.C: because the power should be reduced first.

questions.question: While recovering from an unusual flight attitude without the aid of the attitude indicator, approximate level pitch attitude is reached when the

answers.A: airspeed and altimeter stop their movement and the VSI reverses its trend.
answers.B: airspeed arrives at cruising speed, the altimeter reverses its trend, and the vertical speed stops its movement.
answers.C: altimeter and vertical speed reverse their trend and the airspeed stops its movement.

explanations.A: As the rate of movement of the altimeter and airspeed indicator needles decreases, the attitude is approaching level flight. When the needles stop and reverse direction, the aircraft is passing through level flight.
explanations.B: because the vertical speed indicator will be lagging, i.e., showing a decrease in vertical movement when vertical movement has stopped.
explanations.C: because the rate is only slowing and has not stabilized when the altimeter reverses its trend; i.e., it must stop to indicate level flight.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 147.) Which is the correct sequence for recovery from the unusual attitude indicated?

answers.A: Level wings, add power, lower nose, descend to original attitude, and heading.
answers.B: Add power, lower nose, level wings, return to original attitude and heading.
answers.C: Stop turn by raising right wing and add power at the same time, lower the nose, and return to original attitude and heading.

explanations.A: because you should both add power and lower the nose before you level the wings.
explanations.B: In Fig. 147, a nose-high attitude is indicated by the increasing altitude, the rate-of-climb indication ‘on the vertical speed indicator, and the decreasing airspeed. The correct sequence for recovery is to add power, apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder pressure to straight flight, and return to original altitude and heading. «| b>
explanations.C: because you should both add power and lower the nose before you level the wings.

questions.question: if an airplane is in an unusual flight attitude and the attitude indicator has exceeded its limits, which instruments should be relied on to determine pitch attitude before starting recovery?

answers.A: Turn indicator and VSI.
answers.B: Airspeed and altimeter.
answers.C: VSI and airspeed to detect approaching VSI or VMO.

explanations.A: because the turn indicator indicates nothing about pitch attitude.
explanations.B: If the attitude indicator is inoperative, a nose-low or nose-high attitude can be determined by the airspeed and altimeter. In a nose-high attitude, airspeed is decreasing and altimeter is increasing, and vice versa for nose-low attitudes.
explanations.C: because the altimeter, not the VSI, is the primary pitch instrument. Note the FAA answer selection has VSI and VMO, which should be Vs; and Vo, respectively.

questions.question: Which is the correct sequence for recovery from a spiraling, nose-low, increasing airspeed, unusual flight attitude?

answers.A: Increase pitch attitude, reduce power, and level wings.
answers.B: Reduce power, correct the bank attitude, and raise the nose toa level attitude.
answers.C: Reduce power, raise the nose to level attitude, and correct the bank attitude.

explanations.A: because the power should be decreased first, then the wings leveled.
explanations.B: For nose-low unusual attitudes, one should reduce the power, level the wings, and then increase the pitch to raise the nose to a level attitude.
explanations.C: because the wings should be leveled before the nose is raised to minimize the load factor.

questions.question: During recoveries from unusual attitudes, level flight is attained the instant

answers.A: the horizon bar on the attitude indicator is exactly overlapped with the miniature airplane.
answers.B: a zero rate of climb is indicated on the VSI.
answers.C: the altimeter and airspeed needles stop prior to reversing their direction of movement.

explanations.A: because the attitude indicator has a tendency to precess during an unusual attitude and may not be Teliable.
explanations.B: because there is a lag or delay in the vertical speed indicator. It cannot be relied on for determining the instant level flight is attained.
explanations.C: In unusual attitudes, you can determine the attainment of level flight (not vertical movement) when the altimeter and airspeed needles stop prior to reversing their direction of movement.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 146.) Identify the system that has failed and determine a corrective action to return the airplane to straight-and-level flight.

answers.A: Static/pitot system is blocked; lower the nose and level the wings to levelfight attitude by use of attitude indicator.
answers.B: Vacuum system has failed; reduce power, roll left to level wings, and pitchup to reduce airspeed.
answers.C: Electrical system has failed; reduce power, roll left to level wings, and raise the nose to reduce airspeed.

explanations.A: In Fig. 146, the airplane is in a right turn as indicated by the attitude indicator, the heading indicator, and the turn coordinator; thus the vacuum and electrical instruments are consistent with each other. Since the attitude indicator indicates
explanations.B: because the attitude indicator and heading indicator are consistent with the turn coordinator.
explanations.C: because the turn coordinator, which is normally electric, is consistent with the attitude indicator, which is normally a vacuum system instrument.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 148.) What is the flight attitude? One system which transmits information to the instruments has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to left.
answers.B: Climbing tum to right.
answers.C: Level turn to left.

explanations.A: because the turn is to the right, not the left.
explanations.B: Fig. 148 illustrates a climbing turn to the right. Note that the attitude indicator shows a climbing turn to the right, the heading indicator shows a turn to the right, and both the altimeter and vertical speed indicator indicate a climb. The turn coordinator shows no turn and is malfunctioning.
explanations.C: because the attitude indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator all indicate a climb, and the turn is to the right, not left.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 149.) What is the flight attitude? One system which transmits information to the instruments has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Level turn to the right.
answers.B: Level tur to the left.
answers.C: Straight-and-level flight.

explanations.A: because the vacuum system (i.e., the attitude and heading indicators) is inoperative, and the airplane is in straight flight, not a right turn.
explanations.B: because the vacuum system (i.e., the attitude and heading indicators) is inoperative, and the airplane is in straight flight, not a left turn.
explanations.C: In Fig. 149, the vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and turn coordinator all indicate straight-and-level flight. The heading indicator indicates a turn to the south from west, which is a tu to the left. The attitude indicator indicates a turn to the right; i.e., the attitude indicator and heading indicator are in conflict. Thus, the vacuum system must be malfunctioning, and the airplane must be in straight-and-level flight.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 150.) What is the flight attitude? One instrument has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to the right.
answers.B: Climbing turn to the left.
answers.C: Descending turn to the right.

explanations.A: In Fig. 150, the airplane is in a climb as evidenced by the vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and airspeed indicator. The heading indicator indicates a turn from west to north, which is a turn to the right. The turn coordinator also indicates a turn to the right. Thus, the airplane is in a climbing turn to the right. The attitude indicator is the instrument that is malfunctioning since it indicates a level turn to the left.
explanations.B: because the attitude indicator is inoperative; thus, the airplane is turning to the right, not left.
explanations.C: because the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator all show that the airplane is climbing, not descending.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 151.) What is the flight attitude? One instrument has malfunctioned.

answers.A: Climbing turn to the right.
answers.B: Level turn to the right.
answers.C: Level turn to the left.

explanations.A: because flight is level, not climbing, according to the vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and attitude indicator.
explanations.B: The vertical speed indicator, altimeter, and attitude indicator indicate level flight. The turn coordinator, attitude indicator, and heading indicator indicate a turn to the right. Accordingly, there is a level turn to the right, and the airspeed should not be near the stall speed. Thus, the ram air inlet and the drain hole of the pitot tube are clogged. The airspeed indicator will react the same way as an altimeter, if the static port is open, by showing a decrease in airspeed as altitude decreases and an increase in speed as altitude increases. Pile |
explanations.C: because the turn is to the right, not left.

questions.question: If you fly into severe turbulence, which flight condition should you attempt to maintain?

answers.A: Constant airspeed (Va).
answers.B: Level flight attitude.
answers.C: Constant altitude and constant airspeed.

explanations.A: because you want to maintain an airspeed at or below Va, but in severe turbulence, there will be large variations in airspeed, and you will not be able to keep it constant.
explanations.B: In severe turbulence, you should attempt to maintain a level flight attitude. You will not be able to maintain a constant altitude and/or airspeed, but you should fly at or below design maneuvering speed (Va) and attempt to maintain a level flight attitude.
explanations.C: because, in severe turbulence, you will not be able to maintain a constant altitude and/or constant airspeed.

questions.question: If severe turbulence is encountered during your IFR flight, the airplane should be slowed to the design maneuvering speed because the

answers.A: maneuverability of the airplane will be increased.
answers.B: amount of excess load that can be imposed on the wing will be decreased.
answers.C: airplane will stall at a lower angle of attack, giving an increased margin of safety.

explanations.A: because you should slow the airspeed to reduce excessive loads, not because the airplane will be more maneuverable at a slow airspeed.
explanations.B: Flight at or below the design maneuvering speed (Va) means that the airplane will stall before excess loads can be imposed on the wings.
explanations.C: because an airplane will always stall when the critical angle of attack is exceeded.

questions.question: When a climb or descent through an inversion or wind-shear zone is being performed, the pilot should be alert for which of the following change in airplane performance?

answers.A: A fast rate of climb and a slow rate of descent.
answers.B: A sudden change in airspeed.
answers.C: A sudden surge of thrust.

explanations.A: because a fast rate of climb and a slow rate of descent are usually not a safety problem, as the reverse could be.
explanations.B: When climbing through an inversion or wind-shear zone, the danger is a sudden change in airspeed. If the airplane were to move abruptly from a headwind to a tailwind, the airspeed would slow dramatically, and a stall or rapid descent could be induced.
explanations.C: because the amount of thrust does not change as a result of wind shears.

questions.question: Which distance is displayed by the DME indicator?

answers.A: Slant range distance in NM.
answers.B: Slant range distance in SM.
answers.C: Line-of-sight direct distance from aircraft to VORTAC in SM.

explanations.A: DME (distance measuring equipment) displays line-of-sight direct distance, i.e., slant range, from the aircraft to the VORTAC in nautical miles.
explanations.B: because the measurement is in nautical miles, not statute miles.
explanations.C: because the measurement is in nautical miles, not statute miles.

questions.question: As a rule of thumb, to minimize DME slant range error, how far from the facility should you be to consider the reading as accurate?

answers.A: Two miles or more for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.B: One or more miles for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.C: No specific distance is specified since the reception is line-of-sight.

explanations.A: because the accuracy is 1 NM, not 2 NM, for each 1,000 ft. AGL.
explanations.B: You should consider the DME slant range error negligible if the airplane is 1 NM or more from the ground facility for each 1,000 ft. of altitude above the elevation of the facility.
explanations.C: because a specific distance is required because the reception is line-of-sight.

answers.B: One or more miles for each 1,000 feet of altitude above the facility.
answers.C: No specific distance is specified since the reception is line-of-sight.

explanations.C: because a specific distance is required because the reception is line-of-sight.

questions.question: Where does the DME indicator have the greatest error between ground distance to the VORTAC and displayed distance?

answers.A: High altitudes far from the VORTAC.
answers.B: High altitudes close to the VORTAC.
answers.C: Low altitudes far from the VORTAC.

explanations.A: because, as you get farther away from the ‘station, the slant range error of the DME becomes minimal.
explanations.B: Because the DME reads slant range distance, its greatest error occurs at high altitudes very close to the VORTAC. For example, if one were at 12,000 ft. directly over the VOR, the DME would show a distance from the VOR of approximately 2 NM.
explanations.C: because the DME has the greatest error at high, not low, altitudes close to, not far from, the VORTAC.

questions.question: Which DME indication should you receive when you are directly over a VORTAC site at approximately 6,000 feet AGL?

explanations.A: because the DME would only indicate Zero if you were at ground level next to the VORTAC.
explanations.B: Because the DME indicates slant range distance, it will indicate your altitude if you are directly above the VORTAC. One nautical mile equals approximately 6,000 ft., so the DME would read 1 NM.
explanations.C: because it would mean that your altitude was about 8,000 ft. AGL (6,000 x 1.3).

questions.question: By which means may a pilot determine if a Loran C equipped aircraft is approved for IFR operations?

answers.A: Not necessary; Loran C is not approved for IFR.
answers.B: Check aircraft logbook.
answers.C: Check the Airplane Flight Manual Supplement.

explanations.A: because some LORAN C receivers are approved for IFR operations by the FAA.
explanations.B: because the operational approval level may be found in the aircraft maintenance records, not necessarily the aircraft logbook.
explanations.C: Pilots must be aware of the authorized operational approval level (e.g., VFR or IFR) of a LORAN receiver installed in their aircraft. Approval information is contained in the Aircraft Flight Manual Supplement, on FAA Form 337, in aircraft maintenance records, or possibly on a placard installed near or on the control panel.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 107.) Where should the bearing pointer be located relative to the wing-tip reference to maintain the 16 DME range in a right-hand arc with a right crosswind component?

answers.A: Behind the right wing-tip reference for VOR-2.
answers.B: Ahead of the right wing-tip reference for VOR-2.
answers.C: Behind the right wing-tip reference for VOR-1.

explanations.A: because the bearing pointer would be behind the wing-tip reference if you were crabbed away from the VORTAC such as ina left-hand crosswind and a right-hand arc.
explanations.B: Normally when flying a DME arc with an RMI, the RMI needle will point directly to the VORTAC, and ina no-wind situation it will be on either a 90° or 3 o'clock (for right-hand arc) or 270° or 9 o'clock (for left-hand arc) indication. Since you are flying a right-hand arc, you should be using VOR 2, which points to the right. The right crosswind component will be blowing you away from the VORTAC. You should crab to the right so the VOR 2 bearing pointer is in front of the right wing-tip reference. This indicates you are correcting back into the wind [> Ile
explanations.C: because VOR 1 is pointing toward the left, which would indicate a left-hand, not right-hand, DME arc.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 108.) Where should the bearing pointer be located relative to the wing-tip reference to maintain the 16 DME range in a left-hand arc with a left crosswind component?

answers.A: Ahead of the left wing-tip reference for the VOR-2.
answers.B: Ahead of the right wing-tip reference for the VOR-1.
answers.C: Behind the left wing-tip reference for the VOR-2.

explanations.A: Since you are flying a left-hand arc, you should be using VOR 2, which points to the left. The left crosswind component will be blowing you away from the VORTAC. You should crab to the left so the VOR 2 bearing pointer is in front of the left wing-tip reference. This indicates you are correcting back into the wind and toward the VORTAC.
explanations.B: because you should use VOR 2 as you are making a left-hand, not right-hand, turn.
explanations.C: because the needle would be behind the wing-tip if you were crabbed away from, not toward, the VORTAC.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 104.) If the radio magnetic indicator is tuned to a VOR, which illustration indicates the aircraft is on the 010° radial?

explanations.C: A radio magnetic indicator (RMI) consists of a rotating compass card and one or more indicators which point to stations. The tail of the indicator tells you what radial you are on. RMI 3 shows the tail of the indicator on 010°, which means that you are on the 010° radial.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 104.) If the radio magnetic indicator is tuned to a VOR, which illustration indicates the aircraft is on the 115° radial?

questions.question: In which publication can the VOR receiver ground checkpoint(s) for a particular airport be found?

answers.B: En Route Low Altitude Chart.
answers.C: Airport/Facility Directory.
answers.A: Airman's Information Manual

explanations.A: because the Aeronautical Information Manual contains general flight information, not data concerning specific airports.
explanations.B: because En Route Low Altitude Charts do not indicate VOR receiver ground checkpoints, only VOT frequencies.
explanations.C: The Airport/Facility Directory provides a listing of available VOR receiver ground checkpoints.

questions.question: Which is the maximum tolerance for the VOR indication when the CDI is centered and the aircraft is directly over the airborne checkpoint?

answers.A: Plus or minus 6° of the designated radial.
answers.B: Plus 6° or minus 4° of the designated radial.
answers.C: Plus or minus 4° of the designated radial.

explanations.A: Airborne checkpoints consist of certified radials that should be received over specific landmarks while airborne in the immediate vicinity of an airport. The maximum tolerance when the CDI is centered is +6°.
explanations.B: because the tolerance for an airborne checkpoint is +6°, not +6° or -4°.
explanations.C: because the tolerance for an airborne checkpoint is +6°, not +4°, which is the tolerance for a ground checkpoint or a VOT.

questions.question: When the CDI needle is centered during an airborne VOR check, the omni-bearing selector and the TO/FROM indicator should read

answers.B: within 6° of the selected radial.
answers.C: 0° TO, only if you are due south of the VOR.
answers.A: within 4° of the selected radial.

explanations.A: because the maximum error for a ground, not airborne, VOR check is +4°.
explanations.B: Airborne VOR checkpoints consist of certified radials that should be received over specific landmarks. Ifno checkpoint is available, a prominent ground point should be selected more than 20 NM from a VOR station that is along an established VOR airway. Once over this point with the CDI centered, the OBS should indicate within 6° of the published radial.
explanations.C: because you should use a certified airborne checkpoint or select a ground reference that is under an established VOR airway, not a randomly selected radial.

questions.question: When making an airborne VOR check, what is the maximum allowable tolerance between the two indicators of a dual VOR system (units independent of each other except the antenna)?

answers.A: 4° between the two indicated radials of a VOR.
answers.B: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR.
answers.C: 6° between the two indicated radials of a VOR.

explanations.A: If a dual system VOR (units independent of each other except for the antenna) is installed in the airplane, one system may be checked against the other in place of other VOR check procedures. The test consists of tuning both systems to the same VOR and centering the CDI needles, then noting the bearing variation between the two VOR units. It should be less than 4°.
explanations.B: because the CDIs are to be centered, not set to the same radials.
explanations.C: because it is a maximum tolerance of 4°, not 6°.

questions.question: While airborne, what is the maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings when checking one VOR system against the other?

answers.B: 4° between the two indicated bearings to a VOR.
answers.C: Plus or minus 6° when set to identical radials of a VOR.
answers.A: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR

explanations.A: because the CDIs must be centered, not set to identical radials.
explanations.B: If a dual system VOR (units independent of each other except for the antenna) is installed in the airplane, one system may be checked against the other in place of other check procedures. The test consists of tuning both systems to the same VOR with the CDI centered and noting the bearing variation between the two VOR units. It should be less than 4°.
explanations.C: because it is a maximum permissible variation of 4°, not 6°, between the indicated bearings.

questions.question: How should the pilot make a VOR receiver check when the aircraft is located on the designated checkpoint on the airport surface?

answers.A: With the aircraft headed directly toward the VOR and the OBS set to 000°, the CDI should center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a TO indication.
answers.B: Set the OBS on the designated radial. The CDI must center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a FROM indication.
answers.C: Set the OBS on 180° plus or minus 4°; the CDI should center with a FROM indication.

explanations.A: because VOR indications are given the same no matter which heading the aircraft is on. The VOR indication is based upon position, not heading.
explanations.B: A VOR receiver check is a checkpoint on the airport surface near a VOR. When the aircraft is on the checkpoint, the designated radial should be set on the OBS. The CDI must then center within 4° of the radial. Also, there will be a FROM indication.
explanations.C: because the specified radial, not 180°, should be set on the OBS.

questions.question: How should the pilot make a VOR receiver check when the aircraft is located on the designated checkpoint on the airport surface?

answers.A: Set the OBS on 180° plus or minus 4°; the CDI should center with a FROM indication.
answers.B: Set the OBS on the designated radial. The CD! must center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a FROM indication.
answers.C: With the aircraft headed directly toward the VOR and the OBS set to 000°, the CDI should center within plus or minus 4° of that radial with a TO indication.

explanations.A: because the specified radial, not 180°, should be set on the OBS.
explanations.B: A VOR receiver check is a checkpoint on the airport surface near a VOR. When the airplane is on the checkpoint, the designated radial should be set on the OBS. The CDI must then center within 4° of the radial. Also, there will be a FROM indication.
explanations.C: because VOR indications are given the same no matter which heading the aircraft is on. The VOR indication is based upon position, not heading.

questions.question: Where can the VOT frequency for a particular airport be found?

answers.A: On the IAP Chart and in the Airport/Facility Directory.
answers.B: Only in the Airport/Facility Directory.
answers.C: In the Airport/Facility Directory and on the A/G Voice Communication Panel of the En Route Low Altitude Chart.

explanations.A: because VOT frequencies are not listed ‘on approach charts.
explanations.B: because VOT frequencies are also published in En Route Low Altitude Charts.
explanations.C: Both the Airport/Facility Directory and the AIG voice communication panel of the En Route Low Altitude Chart provide a listing of the VOT frequency for a particular airport.

questions.question: When using VOT to make a VOR receiver check, the CDI should be centered and the OBS should indicate that the aircraft is on the

answers.A: 090 radial.
answers.B: 180 radial.
answers.C: 360 radial.

explanations.A: because the VOT transmits only the 360°, not 090°, radial in all directions.
explanations.B: because the VOT transmits only the 360°, not 180°, radial in all directions.
explanations.C: A VOT transmits only the 360° radial. Thus, with the CDI centered, the OBS should indicate 0° with a FROM indication and 180° with a TO indication.

questions.question: Which indications are acceptable tolerances when checking both VOR receivers by use of the VOT?

answers.A: 360° TO and 003° TO, respectively.
answers.B: 001° FROM and 005° FROM, respectively.
answers.C: 176° TO and 003° FROM, respectively.

explanations.A: because at 000°, FROM, not TO, should be indicated.
explanations.B: because it exceeds the 4° maximum error limit.
explanations.C: A VOT transmits a 360° radial in all directions. Thus, with the course deviation indicator (CDI) centered, the omnibearing selector (OBS) should read 0° with the TO-FROM indicator showing FROM, or the OBS should read 180° with the TO-FROM indicator showing TO, with a maximum. error of 4°.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 81.) When checking a dual VOR system by use of a VOT, which illustration indicates the VOR's are satisfactory?

explanations.A: A VOT transmits a 360° radial in all directions. Thus, when using an RMI, the tail of each indicator should point to 360°, +4°.
explanations.B: because illustration 2 shows the head, not the tail, of one indicator pointing to 360°.
explanations.C: because illustration 4 shows the heads, not the tails, of both indicators pointing to 360°.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 82.) Which is an acceptable range of accuracy when performing an operational check of dual VOR's using one system against the other?

explanations.A: because, in illustration 1, the needles have a 180° difference.
explanations.B: because, in illustration 2, there is a 10° difference.
explanations.C: When performing an operational check of dual VORs using one system against the other, the difference between the two indicated bearings must be 4° or less. On an RMI, which has two VOR indicators, the VORs should point in the same direction, as in illustration 4 of Fig. 82.

questions.question: What indication should a pilot receive when a VOR station is undergoing maintenance and may be considered unreliable?

answers.A: No coded identification, but possible navigation indications.
answers.B: Coded identification, but no navigation indications.
answers.C: Avoice recording on the VOR frequency announcing that the VOR is out of service for maintenance.

explanations.A: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by Morse Code identification and/or by the recorded voice identification, which is always indicated by use of the word "VOR" following the VOR name. During periods of maintenance, the facility identification is removed, although navigational signals may still be transmitted.
explanations.B: because the coded identi fication is removed when the station is undergoing maintenance.
explanations.C: because an out-of-service VOR is not announced by a voice recording.

questions.question: A particular VOR station is undergoing routine maintenance. This is evidenced by

answers.A: removal of the navigational feature.
answers.B: broadcasting a maintenance alert signal on the voice channel.
answers.C: removal of the identification feature.

explanations.A: because the navigational signals may Continue even though they are not accurate.
explanations.B: because an out-of-service VOR is not announced by a voice recording.
explanations.C: The only positive method of identifying a VOR is by Morse Code identification or by the recorded voice identification, which is always indicated by use of the word "VOR" following the VOR name. During periods of maintenance, the coded and/or voice facility identification is removed, although navigational signals may still be transmitted.

questions.question: When a VOR/DME is collocated under frequency pairings and the VOR portion is inoperative, the DME identifier will repeat at an interval of

answers.B: 30 second intervals at 1350 Hz.
answers.C: 60 second intervals at 1350 Hz.
answers.A: 20 second intervals at 1020 Hz.

explanations.A: because the DME identifier repeats at 30-sec., not 20-sec., intervals at 1350 Hz, not 1020 Hz.
explanations.B: The DME/TACAN coded identification is transmitted at 1350 Hz once for each three or four times the VOR or localizer coded identification is transmitted. When either the VOR or the DME is operative, but not both, it is important to recognize which identifier is retained for the operative facility. A single-coded identification repeated at intervals of approximately 30 sec. indicates that the DME is operative and the VOR is not.
explanations.C: because the DME identifier repeats at 30-sec., not 60-sec., intervals.

questions.question: What is the meaning of a single coded identification received only once approximately every 30 seconds from a VORTAC?

answers.A: The VOR and DME components are operative.
answers.B: VOR and DME components are both operative, but voice identification is out of service.
answers.C: The DME component is operative and the VOR component is inoperative.

explanations.A: because a constant series of identity codes indicates that both the VOR and DME are operative.
explanations.B: because voice identification operates independently of the identity codes.
explanations.C: The DME/TACAN coded identification is transmitted at 1350 Hz once for each three or four times the VOR or localizer coded identification is transmitted. When either the VOR or the DME is operative, but not both, it is important to recognize which identifier is retained for the operative facility. A single-coded identification repeated at intervals of approximately 30 sec. indicates that the DME is operative and the VOR is not.

questions.question: What angular deviation from a VOR course centerline is represented by a full-scale deflection of the CDI? A4. B.5°.

explanations.A: because 4° is indicated by a 2-dot deflection on a 5-dot VOR scale.
explanations.B: because 5° is indicated by a 2-dot deflection on a 4-dot VOR scale.
explanations.C: On VORs, full needle deflection from the center position to either side of the dial indicates that the aircraft is 10° or more off course, assuming normal needle sensiti

questions.question: Full scale deflection of a CDI occurs when the course deviation bar or needle

answers.A: deflects from left side of the scale to right side of the scale.
answers.B: deflects from the center of the scale to either far side of the scale.
answers.C: deflects from half scale left to half scale right.

explanations.A: because it indicates moving from a left full deflection to a right full deflection, i.e., 10° left of course to 10° right of course.
explanations.B: Full-scale deflection of a CDI occurs when the needle deflects from the center of the scale to either far side of the scale. This indicates that the aircraft is 10° or more off course, assuming normal needle sensitivity.
explanations.C: because it indicates moving from a left half deflection to a right half deflection, i.e., 5° left of course to 5° right of course.

questions.question: For operations off established airways at 17,000 feet MSL in the contiguous U.S., (H) Class VORTAC facilities used to define a direct route of flight should be no farther apart than

answers.A: 75 NM.

explanations.A: because 75 NM is the range of an (HH) Class NDB facility, not an (H) Class VORTAC.
explanations.B: because 100 NM is the range of an (H) Class VORTAC at 17,000 ft. MSL; thus the distance between two (H) Class VORTAC facilities can be 200 NM.
explanations.C: (H) Class VORTAC facilities have a range of 100 NM from 14,500 ft. AGL up to 18,000 ft. Thus, (H) Class VORTAC facilities should be no farther apart than 200 NM.

questions.question: For IFR operations off of established airways below 18,000 feet, VOR navigational aids used to describe the "route of flight" should be no more than

answers.A: 80 NM apart.
answers.B: 40 NM apart.
answers.C: 70 NM apart.

explanations.A: (H) Class VOR facilities have a range of 40 NM from 1,000 ft. AGL up to 14,500 ft. AGL, and a range of 100 NM from 14,500 ft. AGL up to 18,000 ft. Thus, in general, VOR navigational aids used to describe a route of flight off of established airways below 18,000 ft. (more-specifically, below 14,500 ft. AGL) should be no more than 80 NM apart.
explanations.B: because 40 NM is the range of an (H) Class VOR from 1,000 ft. AGL to 14,500 ft. AGL. VORs used to describe a route of flight off of established airways below 14,500 ft. AGL should be no more than 80 NM apart.
explanations.C: because VORs should be no more than 80 NM, not 70 NM, apart to define a route of flight off of established airways below 14,500 ft. AGL.

questions.question: When using VOR for navigation, which of the following should be considered as station passage?

answers.A: The first movement of the CDI as the airplane enters the zone of confusion.
answers.B: The moment the TO-FROM indicator becomes blank.
answers.C: The first positive, complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

explanations.A: because it indicates flight into the zone of confusion over the VOR, not station passage.
explanations.B: because it is an indication that you are in the zone of confusion over the VOR, not an indication of station passage.
explanations.C: When approaching a VOR, the TO-FROM indicator and the CDI flicker as the airplane flies into the zone of confusion (no signal area). Station passage is shown by complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

questions.question: Which of the following should be considered as station passage when using VOR?

answers.A: The first flickering of the TO-FROM indicator and CDI as the station is approached.
answers.B: The first full-scale deflection of the CDI.
answers.C: The first complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

explanations.A: because it indicates flight into the zone of confusion over the VOR, not station passage.
explanations.B: because it is an indication that you are in the zone of confusion over the VOR, not an indication of station passage.
explanations.C: When approaching a VOR, the TO-FROM indicator and the CDI flicker as the airplane flies into the zone of confusion (no signal area). Station passage is shown by complete reversal of the TO-FROM indicator.

questions.question: When checking the sensitivity of a VOR receiver, the number of degrees in course change as the OBS is rotated to move the CDI from center to the last dot on either side should be between

explanations.A: because 5° to 6° of course change should result in a %-scale, not full-scale, needle deflection.

explanations.C: In addition to VOR receiver checks, course sensitivity may be checked by noting the number of degrees of change in the course selected as you rotate the OBS to move the CDI from center to the last dot on either side. This range should be between 10° and 12°.

questions.question: A VOR receiver with normal five-dot course sensitivity shows a three-dot deflection at 30 NM from the station. The aircraft would be displaced approximately how far from the course centerline?

answers.A: 2NM.
answers.B: 3NM.
answers.C: 5NM.

explanations.A: because two dots, not three dots, indicate 2 NM off course.
explanations.B: Airplane displacement from a course is approximately 200 ft. per dot per nautical mile for VORs. For example, at 30 NM from the station, a one-dot deflection indicates approximately 1 NM displacement of the airplane from the course centerline. A full course deflection is 5 dots. With a 3-dot deflection, one would be about 3 NM from the course centerline.
explanations.C: because five dots, not three dots, indicate 5 NM off course.

questions.question: An aircraft which is located 30 miles from a VOR station and shows a % scale deflection on the CDI would be how far from the selected course centerline?

answers.A: 1½ miles.
answers.B: 2½ miles.
answers.C: 3½ miles.

explanations.A: because 1½ mi. would be indicated by a 1½-dot deflection.
explanations.B: Airplane displacement from a course is approximately 200 ft. per dot per nautical mile for VORs. For example, at 30 NM from the station, a 1-dot deflection indicates approximately 1 NM displacement of the airplane from the course centerline. A full course deflection is 5 dots. Since a ½-scale deflection on the CDI would be 2½ dots, the airplane would be about 2½ mi. from the course centerline.
explanations.C: because 3½ mi. would be indicated by a 3½-dot deflection.

questions.question: What angular deviation from a VOR course centerline is represented by a % scale deflection of the CDI?

questions.question: After passing a VORTAC, the CDI shows % scale deflection to the right. What is indicated if the deflection remains constant for a period of time?

answers.A: The airplane is getting closer to the radial.
answers.B: The OBS is erroneously set on the reciprocal heading.
answers.C: The airplane is flying away from the radial.

explanations.A: because a steady deflection would indicate the airplane is getting closer to the radial if it were flying TO, not FROM, the station.
explanations.B: because, if you use the reciprocal heading, you get reverse indications from the CDI.
explanations.C: If the CDI shows a %-scale deflection to the right, the airplane is flying 5° to the left of course. Ifit is constant, it means the airplane is flying away from the radial because the 5° off course increases in actual distance as one gets farther away from the VORTAC.

questions.question: Determine the approximate time and distance to a station if a 5° wingtip bearing change occurs in 1.5 minutes with a true airspeed of 95 knots.

answers.A: 16 minutes and 14.3 NM.
answers.B: 18 minutes and 28.5 NM.
answers.C: 18 minutes and 33.0 NM.

Thus, itis 18 min. to the station, which is less than 1/3 of an hour. One-third of 95 is less than 33, and thus must be 28.5 rather than 33.0. On the computer side of your flight computer, put 95 kt. on the outer scale over 60 on the inner scale. Find 18 min. on the inner scale; 28.5 NM is on the outer scale.

explanations.A: because airplane 9 would require a TO, not FROM, indication and a left, not right, bar deflection.
explanations.B: because airplane 13 is to the right of the 360/180 radials, which would require a TO, not FROM, indication.
explanations.C: On Figs. 98 and 99, HSI"B" has a VOR course selection of 270° with a FROM indication, meaning that the airplane is to the left of the 360/180 radials. Since it has a tight deflection, the airplane is south of R-270. Given a heading of 135°, airplane 19 is described.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 98 and 99.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "C" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 6 is north of the 270/090 radials, which would require a FROM, not TO, indication and has a north, not 310°, heading.
explanations.B: because airplane 7 is north of the 270/090 radials, which would require a FROM, not TO, indication.
explanations.C: On Figs. 98 and 99, HSI""C" has a VOR course selection of 360° with a TO indication, meaning the airplane is south of the 270/090 radials. Since the course deflection bar is to the left, the airplane is to the east of the 180° radial. Given a 310° heading, airplane 12 is described.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 98 and 99.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "D" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 4 is north of the 270/090 radials, which would have a TO, not FROM, indication.
explanations.B: because airplane 15 would have a centered deflection bar and a north, not 180°, heading.
explanations.C: On Figs. 98 and 99, HSI"D" has a VOR course selection (OBS) of 180°. Its FROM indication means the airplane is south of R-270/90. Since the course deflection bar is to the left, the airplane is west of R-180. Given the heading of 180°, the position describes airplane 17.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 98 and 99.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "E" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 5 would require a centered deflection bar, and has a south, not 360°, heading.
explanations.B: On Figs. 98 and 99, HSI'"E" has a VOR course selection of 360°. Its FROM indication means the airplane is north of R-270/90. Given the course deflection bar to the left, the airplane is to the east of the 360° radial. Given the 360° heading, the position describes airplane 6.
explanations.C: because airplane 15 is south of the 270/090 radials, which would require a centered deflection bar and a TO, not FROM, indication.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 98 and 99.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "E" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 10 is east of the 360/180 radials and north of the 270/090 radials, which would Tequire a bar deflection, not a centered bar, and a TO, not FROM, indication.
explanations.B: because airplane 14 is east of the 360/180 radials, which would require a bar deflection, not a centered bar.
explanations.C: On Figs. 98 and 99, HSI "F" has a VOR course selection of 180° with a FROM indication, meaning that the airplane is south of the 270/90 radials. Since the course deflection bar is centered, the airplane is on R-180. Givena heading of 045° (at the top of the HSI), airplane 16 is described.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 110.) In which general direction from the VORTAC is the aircraft located?

answers.B: Northwest.
answers.C: Northeast.
answers.A: Southwest.

explanations.A: because southwest would require a TO, not FROM, indication.
explanations.B: because northwest would require a full right, not a %-scale, deflection.
explanations.C: The course indicator arrow (OBS) is set to 60°, and the TO-FROM indicates FROM (opposite the head of the arrow), which means the airplane is northeast of the VORTAC. Since the course deviation bar indicates a deflection of 3 dots to the right, the airplane is to the north of the 60° radial by 6°, which is in the northeast.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 111.) In which general direction from the VORTAC is the aircraft located?

answers.B: Southeast.
answers.C: Northwest.
answers.A: Northeast.

explanations.A: because a left, not right, deflection would indicate the airplane is in the northeast.
explanations.B: because a TO, not FROM, indication. would indicate the airplane is south of the VORTAC.
explanations.C: The course indicator arrow (OBS) is set to 360°, and the TO-FROM indicator is FROM, which means the airplane is north of the VORTAC. Since the course deviation bar is to the right, the airplane is to the west of the 360° radial of the VORTAC. Accordingly, the airplane is to the northwest of the VORTAC.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position(s) does HSI presentation "A" correspond?

answers.A: 9 and 6.

explanations.B: because the indication will be the same on either localizer.
explanations.C: because the indication will be the same ‘on either localizer.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position(s) does HSI presentation "B" correspond? A11.

answers.A: 11 only.
answers.B: 5 and 13.
answers.C: 7 and 11.

explanations.B: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI "B" has a heading of 090°. It has localizer course setting of 090° with a right deflection, meaning the airplane is south of the localizer. Both airplanes 5 and 13 are described. Note the backcourse setting. If the front course 270° (instead of 90°) had been set, normal (rather than reverse) sensing would be indicated.
explanations.C: because airplanes 7 and 11 have 270°, not 090°, headings.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "C" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 9 has a 360°, not 090°, heading.
explanations.B: because airplane 4 has a 270°, not 090°, heading.
explanations.C: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI"C" has a heading of 090° with a centered course deviation bar; thus the airplane is on the localizer with a 090° heading, which describes airplane 12. The backcourse setting (090) has no effect because ‘the deviation bar is centered.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "D" correspond?

explanations.A: because airplane 1 has a heading of 215°, not 315°.
explanations.B: because airplane 10 has a heading of 135°, not 315°.
explanations.C: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI"D" has a heading of 315°. Airplane 2 is the only one with a northwest heading.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position(s) does HSI presentation "E" correspond?

answers.B: 3 only.
answers.C: 8 and 3.

explanations.A: because airplane 3 is also south of the localizer with a 045° heading.
explanations.B: because airplane 8 also has a 045° heading and is south of the localizer.
explanations.C: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI"E" has a heading of 045°. It has a right deflection with a backcourse HSI setting of 090. This results in reverse sensing, meaning the airplane is south of the localizer. Thus, airplanes 3 and 8 are described.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "E" correspond?

explanations.A: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI "F" has a setting of 270° with a centered bar and a 270° heading, which corresponds to airplane 4.
explanations.B: because airplane 11 would have a left, not centered, course deviation bar.
explanations.C: because airplane 5 has a heading of 090°, not 270°.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "H" correspond?

explanations.B: On Figs. 96 and 97, HSI'"H" has a heading of 215°. Airplane / is the only one with a southwest heading.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position(s) does HSI presentation "G" correspond?

answers.B: 7 and 11.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 96 and 97.) To which aircraft position does HSI presentation "I" correspond?
