questions.question: How cana pilot determine if a Global Positioning System (GPS) installed in an aircraft is approved for IFR en route and IFR approaches?

answers.A: Flight manual supplement.
answers.B: GPS operator's manual.
answers.C: Aircraft owner's handbook.

explanations.A: A supplement to the aircraft's POH (flight manual) is required for newly installed equipment. A supplement should state that the GPS is approved for IFR operations (en route and approaches).
explanations.B: because the GPS operator's manual will describe how to operate the GPS unit but will not provide approval for its use in a particular aircraft.
explanations.C: because the aircraft owner's handbook (i-e., information manual or POH) may not have any information ona GPS unit unless the unit was installed as a standard feature.

questions.question: Hand-held GPS systems, and GPS systems certified for VFR operation, may be used during IFR operations as

answers.A: the principal reference to determine en route waypoints.
answers.B: an aid to situational awareness.
answers.C: the primary source of navigation.

explanations.A: because hand-held and VFR-only GPS systems are not approved for IFR operations, and may only be used as an aid to situational awareness. Passage of en route reporting points and fixes (i.e., waypoints) must be verified by some other means (e.g., VOR, ADF, radar, etc.).
explanations.B: In order to use a GPS as the primary means of navigation under IFR or to perform instrument approaches, both the GPS receiver and the aircraft installation must FAA-approved. Additionally, the receiver must have a current database of waypoints and instrument approach procedures. Hand-held GPS systems and VFR- only GPS systems are not FAA-approved for IFR operations, and may only be used during IFR operations as an aid to situational awareness.
explanations.C: because hand-held and VFR-only GPS systems are not approved as the primary source of navigation under IFR; they may only be used as an aid to situational awareness.

questions.question: During IFR en route and terminal operations using an approved GPS system for navigation, ground based navigational facilities

answers.A: are only required during the approach portion of the flight.
answers.B: must be operational along the entire route.
answers.C: must be operational only if RAIM predicts an outage.

explanations.A: because ground-based navigational facilities appropriate to the route must be available and operational along the entire route of flight, not just the approach portion.
explanations.B: In order to conduct IFR en route and terminal operations using an approved GPS system, the avionics necessary to receive all of the ground-based facilities that are appropriate for the route to the destination airport and to any alternate airport must be installed and operational, and the ground-based facilities necessary for these routes must be operational.
explanations.C: because ground-based navigational facilities appropriate to the route must be available and operational regardless of Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) status. However, unless RAIM predicts an outage, active monitoring of these facilities is not necessary.

questions.question: During IFR operation using an approved GPS system for navigation,

answers.A: no other navigation system is required.
answers.B: active monitoring of an alternate navigation system is always required.
answers.C: the aircraft must have an approved and operational alternate navigation system appropriate for the route.

explanations.A: because aircraft using an approved GPS system for IFR operations must be equipped with an approved and operational alternate means of navigation appropriate to the flight.
explanations.B: because active monitoring of an alternate navigation system is only required when GPS RAIM capability is lost or when an outage is predicted, not at all times.
explanations.C: Aircraft using GPS under IFR must be equipped with an approved and operational alternate means of navigation appropriate for the route. Active monitoring of alternative navigation equipment is not required if the GPS receiver uses Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM). However, active monitoring of an alternate means of navigation is required when the RAIM capability of the GPS equipment is lost, or if RAIM predicts an outage.

questions.question: Under which condition must the pilot in command of a civil aircraft have at least an instrument rating?

answers.A: When operating in Class E airspace.
answers.B: For a flight in VFR conditions while on an IFR flight plan.
answers.C: For any flight above an altitude of 1,200 feet AGL, when the visibility is less than 3 miles.

explanations.A: because an instrument rating is required at all times when operating in Class A, not Class E, airspace.
explanations.B: No person may act as pilot in command of
explanations.C: because VFR is permitted in uncontrolled airspace during the day with visibilities of as little as 1 SM when more than 1,200 ft. AGL but below 10,000 ft. MSL.

questions.question: The pilot in command of a civil aircraft must have an instrument rating only when operating

answers.A: under IFR in positive control airspace.
answers.B: under IFR, in weather conditions less than the minimum for VFR flight or in Class A airspace.
answers.C: in weather conditions less than the minimum prescribed for VFR flight.

explanations.A: because you must have an instrument tating when operating under IFR, in weather conditions less than ‘the minimum for VFR flight, or in Class A airspace, not only under IFR in positive control airspace. Positive control airspace means that ATC will provide separation to all aircraft within that airspace.
explanations.B: No person may act as pilot in command of
explanations.C: because it omits flying in VFR conditions with an IFR clearance.

questions.question: Which flight time may be logged as instrument time when on an instrument flight plan?

answers.A: All of the time the aircraft was not controlled by ground references.
answers.B: Only the time you controlled the aircraft solely by reference to flight instruments.
answers.C: Only the time you were flying in IFR weather conditions.

explanations.A: because VFR flight can be conducted above a cloud layer without visual ground references, i.e., VFR-on-top.
explanations.B: A pilot may log as instrument flight time ‘only that time during which (s)he operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions.
explanations.C: because time under the hood (i.e., simulated IFR) as well as actual IFR conditions counts as instrument time.

questions.question: What portion of dual instruction time may a certificated instrument flight instructor log as instrument flight time?

answers.A: All time during which the instructor acts as instrument instructor, regardless of weather conditions.
answers.B: All time during which the instructor acts as instrument instructor in actual instrument weather conditions.
answers.C: Only the time during which the instructor flies the aircraft by reference to instruments.

explanations.A: because the flight conditions must be IMC. for the instructor to log flight instruction as instrument time.
explanations.B: An instrument flight instructor may log as instrument time that time during which (s)he acts as instrument flight instructor in actual instrument weather conditions.
explanations.C: because instructing in (as well as flying in) actual IFR weather conditions can be logged as instrument time by the instructor.

questions.question: To meet instrument experience requirements of CFR Part 61, section 61.57(c), a pilot enters the condition of flight in the pilot logbook as simulated instrument conditions, what other qualifying information must also be entered?

answers.A: Location and type of each instrument approach completed and name of safety pilot.
answers.B: Number and type of instrument approaches completed and route of flight.
answers.C: Name and pilot certificate number of safety pilot and type of approaches completed.

explanations.A: A pilot may log as instrument flight time ‘only that time during which (s)he operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions. Each entry must include the location and type of each instrument approach completed and the name of the safety pilot for each simulated instrument flight.
explanations.B: because the location and type of instrument approaches must be entered along with the safety pilot's name, not the route of flight.
explanations.C: because the location is required, but the ‘safety pilot's certificate number is not.

questions.question: How long does a pilot meet the recency of experience requirements for IFR flight after successfully completing an instrument proficiency check if no further IFR flights are made?

answers.A: 90 days.
answers.B: 6 calendar months.
answers.C: 12 calendar months.

explanations.A: because 90 days refers to takeoff and landing currency to carry passengers.
explanations.B: No pilot may act as pilot in command when operating under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR unless (s)he has, within the past 6 months, logged instrument time under actual or simulated IFR conditions in the category of aircraft involved or in an appropriate flight simulator or flight training device and has performed at least ‘six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems. An alternative way to remain current is to pass an instrument proficiency check in the category of aircraft involved.
explanations.C: because 12 months is the time whereafter another instrument proficiency check is required.

questions.question: No pilot may act as pilot-in-command of an aircraft, under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR unless that pilot has, within the preceding 6 calendar months, completed at least

answers.A: six instrument approaches, holding procedures, intercepting and tracking courses using navigational systems, or passed an instrument proficiency check.
answers.B: six instrument flights under actual IFR conditions.
answers.C: three instrument approaches and logged 3 hours.

explanations.A: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR unless, within the preceding 6 calendar months, that person has performed and logged under actual or simulated instrument conditions, either in flight in the appropriate category of aircraft for the instrument privileges sought or in a flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of the aircraft category for the instrument privileges sought, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems. Alternatively, the pilot may pass an instrument proficiency check in the category of aircraft involved.
explanations.B: because a pilot must complete, under actual or simulated instrument conditions, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, not six instrument flights under actual IFR conditions.
explanations.C: because a pilot must complete at least six, not three, instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems. There is no required minimum number of hours to be logged.

questions.question: To meet the minimum required instrument flight experience to act as pilot in command of an aircraft under IFR, you must have logged within the preceding 6 calendar months in the same category of aircraft: six instrument approaches,

answers.A: holding procedures, intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems.
answers.B: three of which must be in the same category and class of aircraft to be flown, and 6 hours of instrument time in any aircraft.
answers.C: and 6 hours of instrument time in any aircraft.

explanations.A: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than VFR minimums unless, within the preceding 6 calendar months, (s)he has performed and logged, under actual or simulated instrument conditions, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, in the category of aircraft to be flown.
explanations.B: because all six, not three, approaches must be in the same category and aircraft. Additionally, you must have accomplished holding procedures and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, not accumulated 6 hr. of instrument time.
explanations.C: because you must have also accomplished holding procedures and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems in the same category and class of aircraft, not accumulated 6 hr. of instrument time in any aircraft.

questions.question: To meet the minimum instrument experience requirements, within the last 6 calendar months you need

answers.A: six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses in the appropriate category of aircraft.
answers.B: six hours in the same category aircraft.
answers.C: six hours in the same category aircraft, and at least 3 of the 6 hours in actual IFR conditions.

explanations.A: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than VFR minimums unless, within the preceding 6 calendar months, (s)he has performed and logged, under actual or simulated instrument conditions, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, in the category of aircraft to be flown.
explanations.B: because, to be current for IFR, you must have performed six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses in the same category of aircraft, not accumulated 6 hr. in the same category of aircraft.
explanations.C: because, to be current for IFR, you must have performed six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses in the same category of aircraft, not accumulated 6 hr. in the same category aircraft with at least 3 hr. in actual IFR conditions.

questions.question: What recent instrument flight experience requirements must be met before you may act as pilot in command of an airplane under IFR?

answers.A: A minimum of six instrument approaches in an airplane, or an approved simulator (airplane) or ground trainer, within the preceding 6 calendar months.
answers.B: A minimum of six instrument approaches, at least three of which must be in an aircraft within the preceding 6 calendar months.
answers.C: A minimum of six instrument approaches in an aircraft, at least three of which must be in the same category within the preceding 6 calendar months.

explanations.A: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than VFR minimums unless, within the preceding 6 calendar months, (s)he has performed and logged, under actual or simulated instrument conditions, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, in the category of aircraft to be flown, in an approved simulator or flight training device, or in any combination of these.
explanations.B: because all six approaches may be done in an approved flight simulator or flight training device; none are required to be done in an aircraft.
explanations.C: because all six approaches may be done in an approved flight simulator or flight training device; none are required to be done in an aircraft. In addition, all six approaches, not just three, must be done in the same category of aircraft or a ‘simulator or flight training device representative of that aircraft category.

questions.question: An instrument rated pilot, who has not logged any instrument experience in 1 year or more, cannot serve as pilot in command under IFR, unless the pilot

answers.A: completes the required 6 hours and six approaches, followed by an instrument proficiency check given by an FAA-designated examiner.
answers.B: passes an instrument proficiency check in the category of aircraft involved, given by an approved FAA examiner, instrument instructor, or FAA inspector.
answers.C: passes an instrument proficiency check in the category of aircraft involved, followed by 6 hours and six instrument approaches, 3 of those hours in the category of aircraft involved.

explanations.A: because an instrument proficiency check by itself provides currency. Additional time and approaches are not required.
explanations.B: A pilot who does not meet the recent instrument experience requirements during the prescribed time or 6 months thereafter may not serve as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR until (s)he passes an instrument proficiency check in the category of aircraft involved, given by an FAA inspector, a member of an armed force of the U.S. authorized to conduct flight tests, an FAA-approved check pilot, or a certificated instrument flight instructor. The proficiency check may be completed in an appropriate flight simulator or flight training device.
explanations.C: because an instrument proficiency check by itself provides currency. Additional time and approaches are not required.

questions.question: After your recent IFR experience lapses, how much time do you have before you must pass an instrument proficiency check to act as pilot in command under IFR?

answers.A: 6 months.
answers.B: 90 days.
answers.C: 12 months.

explanations.A: A pilot who does not meet the recent instrument experience requirements during the prescribed time or 6 months thereafter may not serve as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR until (s)he passes an instrument proficiency check.
explanations.B: because 90 days refers to the takeoff and landing currency requirements to carry passengers.
explanations.C: because 12 months is the time from when you gain IFR currency to when you are required to pass another instrument proficiency check (assuming you have not maintained currency since you gained proficiency).

questions.question: What minimum conditions are necessary for the instrument approaches required for IFR currency?

answers.A: The approaches may be made in an aircraft, approved instrument ground trainer, or any combination of these.
answers.B: At least three approaches must be made in the same category of aircraft to be flown.
answers.C: The approaches must be made in the same category and class of aircraft to be flown.

explanations.A: For IFR currency, the six instrument approaches must be made either in the same category of aircraft to be flown or ina flight simulator or training device representative of the aircraft category to be flown, or in any combination of these.
explanations.B: because all six approaches may be done in an approved flight simulator or training device, not necessarily in an airplane.
explanations.C: because all six approaches may be done in an approved flight simulator or training device, not necessarily in an airplane.

questions.question: Apilot's recent IFR experience expires on July 1 of this year. What is the latest date the pilot can meet the IFR experience requirement without having to take an instrument proficiency check?

answers.A: December 31, this year.
answers.B: June 30, next year.
answers.C: July 31, this year.

explanations.A: A pilot who does not meet the recent instrument experience requirements during the prescribed time or 6 months thereafter may not serve as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR until (s)he passes an instrument proficiency check. If the 6 months' recency experience period expires on July 1, the 6 months thereafter would expire on December 31 this year.
explanations.B: because this date represents 12 months instead of 6 months.
explanations.C: because this date represents 1 month instead of 6 months.

questions.question: How may a pilot satisfy the recent flight experience requirement necessary to act as pilot in command in IMC in powered aircraft? Within the previous 6 calendar months, logged

answers.A: six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses using navigational systems.
answers.B: six instrument approaches and 3 hours under actual or simulated IFR conditions within the last 6 months; three of the approaches must be in the category of aircraft involved.
answers.C: 6 hours of instrument time under actual or simulated IFR conditions within the last 3 months, including at least six instrument approaches of any kind. Three of the 6 hours must be in flight in any category aircraft.

explanations.A: No pilot may act as pilot in command of a powered aircraft under IFR or in weather conditions less than VFR minimums unless, within the preceding 6 calendar months, (s)he has performed and logged, under actual or simulated instrument conditions, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems, in the category of aircraft to be flown or in an airplane flight simulator or training device.
explanations.B: because there is no instrument flight time requirement. In addition to the six instrument approaches, you must also log holding procedures and intercepting and tracking courses using navigational systems.
explanations.C: because there is no instrument flight time fequirement. You must log six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses using navigational systems within the past 6 months, not 3 months.

questions.question: Which additional IFR experience is required for you to meet the recent flight experience requirements to act as pilot in command of an airplane under IFR? Your present instrument experience within the preceding 6 calendar months is 1. three hours with holding, intercepting and tracking courses in an approved airplane flight simulator. 2. two instrument approaches in an airplane.

answers.A: Three hours of simulated or actual instrument flight time in a helicopter and two instrument approaches in an airplane or helicopter.
answers.B: Four instrument approaches in an airplane, or an approved airplane flight simulator or training device.
answers.C: Three instrument approaches in an airplane.

explanations.A: because no minimum time is required; four, not two, more approaches are required; and all approaches must be in an airplane or flight simulator or flight training device representative of an airplane, not a helicopter.
explanations.B: No person may act as pilot in command under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR, unless within the preceding 6 calendar months that person has performed and logged under actual or simulated instrument conditions, either in flight in the appropriate category of aircraft for the instrument privileges being sought or ina flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of the aircraft category for the instrument privileges sought; at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigation systems. Having logged only two instrument approaches, the pilot must log four more.
explanations.C: because four, not three, more approaches are required to have the required minimum of six.

questions.question: To carry passengers for hire in an airplane on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM from the departure airport, the pilot in command is required to hold at least

answers.A: a Category Il pilot authorization.
answers.B: a First-Class Medical certificate.
answers.C: a Commercial Pilot Certificate with an instrument rating.

explanations.A: because Category Il refers to an authorization for reduced ILS approach minimums.
explanations.B: because a first-class medical certificate is required for operations requiring an airline transport pilot Certificate.
explanations.C: To carry passengers for hire, the pilot in command is required to hold at least a commercial pilot certificate. Additionally, to carry those passengers for hire in an airplane on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM (or at night), (s)he must also hold an instrument rating on the commercial certificate.

questions.question: Which limitation is imposed on the holder of a Commercial Pilot Certificate if that person does not hold an instrument rating?

answers.A: That person is limited to private pilot privileges at night.
answers.B: The carrying of passengers or property for hire on cross-country flights at night is limited to a radius of 50 NM.
answers.C: The carrying of passengers for hire on cross-country flights is limited to 50 NM and the carrying of passengers for hire at night is prohibited.

explanations.A: because that person may exercise commercial pilot privileges at night, but with limitations.
explanations.B: because no passengers may be carried at night without an instrument rating.
explanations.C: The applicant for a commercial pilot certificate must hold an instrument rating (airplane), or the commercial pilot certificate must be endorsed with a limitation prohibiting the carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM or at night.

questions.question: What limitation is imposed on a newly certificated commercial airplane pilot if that person does not hold an instrument pilot rating?

answers.A: The carrying of passengers or property for hire on cross-country flights at night is limited to a radius of 50 nautical miles (NM).
answers.B: The carrying of passengers for hire on cross-country flights is limited to 50 NM for night flights, but not limited for day flights.
answers.C: The carrying of passengers for hire on cross-country flights is limited to 50 NM and the carrying of passengers for hire at night is prohibited.

explanations.A: because the carriage of property (freight) is not limited at night.
explanations.B: because no passengers may be carried at night and the flight is limited to 50 NM, not unlimited, for day flights without an instrument rating.
explanations.C: The applicant for a commercial pilot certificate must hold an instrument rating (airplane), or the commercial pilot certificate must be endorsed with a limitation prohibiting the carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM or at night.

questions.question: A certificated commercial pilot who carries passengers for hire at night or in excess of 50 NM is required to have at least

answers.A: an associated type rating if the airplane is of the multiengine class.
answers.B: a First-Class Medical Certificate.
answers.C: aninstrument rating in the same category and class of aircraft.

explanations.A: because, even if the airplane requires a type rating, the commercial pilot must have at least an instrument rating to carry passengers for hire at night or in excess of 50 NM.
explanations.B: because only a second-class medical certificate is required of commercial pilots. First-class medical certificates are required of airline transport pilots.
explanations.C: A certificated commercial pilot who carries passengers for hire at night or in excess of 50 NM is required to have an instrument rating.

questions.question: You intend to carry passengers for hire on a night VFR flight in a single-engine airplane within a 25-mile radius of the departure airport. You are required to possess at least which rating(s)?

answers.A: A Commercial Pilot Certificate with a single-engine land rating.
answers.B: A Commercial Pilot Certificate with a single-engine and instrument (airplane) rating.
answers.C: A Private Pilot Certificate with a single-engine land and instrument airplane rating.

explanations.A: because, to carry passengers for hire at night, one must have an instrument rating as well as a commercial pilot certificate.
explanations.B: A commercial pilot certificate with a single-engine airplane rating is required for a pilot to carry passengers for hire and to operate that class of aircraft. Also, an applicant for a commercial pilot certificate must hold an instrument rating (airplane), or the commercial pilot certificate will be endorsed with a limitation prohibiting carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights of more than 50 NM or at night.
explanations.C: because a commercial, not private, pilot certificate is required to carry passengers for hire.

questions.question: Who is responsible for determining that the altimeter system has been checked and found to meet 14 CFR Part 91 requirements for a particular instrument flight?

answers.A: Owner.
answers.B: Operator.
answers.C: Pilot in command.

explanations.A: because the owner is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft, but the pilot in command is responsible for determining that the aircraft is airworthy.
explanations.B: because the operator is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft, but the pilot in command is responsible for determining that the aircraft is airworthy.
explanations.C: The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the airworthiness and operation of that aircraft.

questions.question: The use of certain portable electronic devices is prohibited on aircraft that are being operated under.

answers.A: IFR.
answers.B: VER.
answers.C: DVFR.

explanations.A: The use of portable electronic devices in Carrier aircraft and other aircraft operated under IFR is prohibited. This prohibition does not apply to portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers, electric shavers, and other devices which do not interfere with the aircraft's navigation and communication systems.
explanations.B: because portable electronic devices are not prohibited in aircraft operated under VFR.
explanations.C: because portable electronic devices are not prohibited in aircraft operated under DVFR (defense VFR).

questions.question: Before beginning any flight under IFR, the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. In addition, the pilot must

answers.B: list an alternate airport on the flight plan and confirm adequate takeoff and landing performance at the destination airport.
answers.A: list an alternate airport on the flight plan and become familiar with the instrument approaches to that airport.
answers.C: be familiar with the runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed.

explanations.A: because listing an alternate airport is not required for all IFR flights, ie., when the destination is forecast to have ceilings above 2,000 ft. and visibility of at least 3 SM.
explanations.B: because listing an alternate airport is not required for all IFR flights, ie., when the destination is forecast to have ceilings above 2,000 ft. and visibility of at least 3 SM.
explanations.C: Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, familiarize hinVherseff with all available information concerning that flight. For a flight under IFR or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, this information should include weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays of which (s)he has been advised by ATC. For any flight, the preflight information should include runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance data.

questions.question: Before beginning any flight under IFR, the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information concerning that flight including:

answers.A: all instrument approaches at the destination airport.
answers.B: an alternate airport and adequate takeoff and landing performance at the destination airport.
answers.C: the runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the aircraft's takeoff and landing data.

explanations.A: because, while knowing what approaches are available is a good operating procedure, it is not a required preflight action.
explanations.B: because a pilot must be familiar with the airplane's takeoff and landing performance at all airports of intended use, not just the destination airport.
explanations.C: Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, familiarize him/herself with all available information concerning that flight. For a flight under IFR or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, this information should include weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays of which (s)he has been advised by ATC. For any flight, the preflight information should include runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance information.

questions.question: What are the minimum qualifications for a person who occupies the other control seat as safety pilot during simulated instrument flight?

answers.A: Private pilot certificate with appropriate category and class ratings for the aircraft.
answers.B: Private pilot with instrument rating.
answers.C: Private pilot with appropriate category, class, and instrument ratings.

explanations.A: No person may operate a civil aircraft in simulated instrument flight unless the other control seat is occupied by a safety pilot who possesses at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown.
explanations.B: because the safety pilot's certificate must carry an appropriate category and class (but not instrument) rating, e.g., a private pilot (helicopter) may not act as safety pilot in an airplane.
explanations.C: because the safety pilot does not need to be instrument rated.

questions.question: When may ATC request a detailed report of an emergency even though a rule has not been violated?

answers.A: When priority has been given.
answers.B: Any time an emergency occurs.
answers.C: When the emergency occurs in controlled airspace.

explanations.A: Each pilot in command who is given priority by ATC in an emergency (even though no FAR has been violated) shall, if requested by ATC, submit a detailed report of that emergency within 48 hr. to the manager of that ATC facility.
explanations.B: because a written report may be requested when priority is given in an emergency, not any time an emergency occurs.
explanations.C: because a written report may be Tequested when priority is given in an emergency, regardless of where the emergency occurs.

questions.question: While on an FR flight, a pilot has an emergency which causes a deviation from an ATC clearance. What action must be taken?

answers.A: Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible.
answers.B: Squawk 7700 for the duration of the emergency.
answers.C: Submit a detailed report to the chief of the ATC facility within 48 hours.

explanations.A: Each pilot in command who, in an emergency, deviates from an ATC clearance or instruction shall notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible.
explanations.B: because, in an emergency, you must report a deviation from an ATC clearance as soon as possible, not just squawk 7700 during the emergency.
explanations.C: because a report in 48 hr. is required only if you are given priority during the emergency and ATC requests such a report.

questions.question: During an IFR flight in IMC, a distress condition is encountered, (fire, mechanical, or structural failure). The pilot should

answers.A: not hesitate to declare an emergency and obtain an amended clearance.
answers.B: wait until the situation is immediately perilous before declaring an emergency.
answers.C: contact ATC and advise that an urgency condition exists and request priority consideration.

explanations.A: Distress is a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance. Thus, during an IFR flight in IMC, if a distress Condition is encountered, you should immediately declare an emergency and obtain an amended clearance.
explanations.B: because a distress condition is perilous and you should not hesitate to declare an emergency.
explanations.C: because you should contact ATC and declare that an emergency, not urgency, condition exists and obtain an amended clearance, not a request for consideration.

questions.question: In addition to a VOR receiver and two-way communications capability, which additional equipment is required for IFR operation in Class B airspace?

answers.B: Standby communications receiver, DME, and coded transponder.
answers.C: An operable coded transponder having Mode C capability.

questions.question: Which of the following is required equipment for operating an aircraft within Class B airspace?

An operable 4096-code transponder having Mode C capability, and 3. For IFR operations, an operable VOR or TACAN receiver.
explanations.B: because DME is not required and a VOR receiver is only required when operating IFR.

questions.question: When are you required to have an instrument rating for flight in VMC?

answers.C: Flight into Class A airspace.

explanations.C: No person may operate an aircraft within Class A airspace at any time unless (s)he is rated for instrument flight and is on an instrument flight plan.

questions.question: When is an IFR clearance required during VFR weather conditions?

answers.A: When operating in the Class E airspace.

answers.C: When operating in airspace above 14,500 feet.

explanations.A: because an IFR clearance is not required in VMC in Class E airspace.

answers.B: Class E airspace with IMC and Class A airspace.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 92.) What is the minimum in-flight visibility and distance from clouds required for an airplane operating less than 1,200 feet AGL under special VFR during daylight hours in area 5?

answers.C: From 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA, forecast ceiling 2,000, and visibility 3 miles.

explanations.A: because the destination weather condition forecast is from 1 hr., not 2 hr., before and after ETA, and the visibility must be at least 3 SM, not 2% SM.
explanations.B: because the destination weather condition forecast is from 1 hr., not 2 hr., before and after ETA, and the ceiling must be at least 2,000 ft. AGL, not 3,000 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: An alternate airport is not required to be listed on an IFR flight plan if the destination airport has a standard instrument approach procedure available and, for at least 1 hr. before and 1 hr. after the estimated time of arrival, the weather reports or forecasts, or any combination of them, indicate 1. The ceiling will be at least 2,000 ft. above the airport elevation; and 2. The visibility will be at least 3 SM.

questions.question: What are the minimum weather conditions that must be forecast to list an airport as an alternate when the airport has no approved IAP?

answers.A: The ceiling and visibility at ETA, 2,000 feet and 3 miles, respectively.
answers.B: The ceiling and visibility from 2 hours before until 2 hours after ETA, 2,000 feet and 3 miles, respectively.
answers.C: The ceiling and visibility at ETA must allow descent from MEA, approach, and landing, under basic VFR.

explanations.A: because an alternate must be listed on your IFR flight plan unless the weather at your destination is forecast, from 1 hr. before to 1 hr. after ETA, to have a ceiling of 2,000 ft. and visibility of 3 SM.
explanations.B: because an alternate must be listed on your IFR flight plan, unless the weather at your destination is forecast, from 1 hr., not 2 hr., before to 1 hr. after ETA, to have at least a 2,000-ft. ceiling and visibility of 3 SM.
explanations.C: Unless otherwise authorized, no one may include an alternate airport that has no instrument approach in an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that, at the ETA at the alternate airport, the ceiling and visibility will allow descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR.

questions.question: What standard minimums are required to list an airport as an alternate on an IFR flight plan if the airport has VOR approach only?

answers.A: Ceiling and visibility at ETA, 800 feet and 2 miles, respectively.
answers.B: Ceiling and visibility from 2 hours before until 2 hours after ETA, 800 feet and 2 miles, respectively.
answers.C: Ceiling and visibility at ETA, 600 feet and 2 miles, respectively.

explanations.A: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may include an alternate airport that has only a VOR (ie., nonprecision) approach in an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that at the ETA at the alternate airport the ceiling is at least 800 ft. and visibility is 2 SM.
explanations.B: because the alternate airport weather minimums apply to the ETA, not 2 hr. plus or minus.
explanations.C: because 600 ft. and 2 SM are the alternate airport weather minimums for a precision approach, ie., ILS.

questions.question: For aircraft other than helicopters, what minimum weather conditions must be forecast for your ETA at an alternate airport that has a precision approach procedure, with standard alternate minimums, in order to list it as an alternate for the IFR flight?

answers.A: 600-foot ceiling and 2 SM visibility at your ETA.
answers.B: 600-foot ceiling and 2 SM visibility from 2 hours before to 2 hours after your ETA.
answers.C: 800-foot ceiling and 2 SM visibility at your ETA.

explanations.A: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may include an alternate airport that has a precision (ILS) approach in an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that at the ETA at the alternate airport the ceiling is at least 600 ft. and visibility is 2 SM.
explanations.B: because the alternate airport weather minimums apply to the ETA, not 2 hr. plus or minus.
explanations.C: because 800 ft. and 2 SM are the alternate airport minimums for a nonprecision approach.

questions.question: What are the alternate minimums that must be forecast at the ETA for an airport that has a precision approach procedure?

answers.A: 400-foot ceiling and 2 miles visibility.
answers.B: 600-foot ceiling and 2 miles visibility.
answers.C: 800-foot ceiling and 2 miles visibility.

explanations.A: because 400 ft. is not a standard minimum ceiling used as an alternative airport minimum.
explanations.B: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may include an alternate airport that has a precision (ILS) approach in an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that at the ETA at the alternate airport the ceiling is at least 600 ft. and visibility is 2 SM.
explanations.C: because 800 ft. and 2 SM are the alternate airport minimums for nonprecision approaches.

questions.question: An airport without an authorized IAP may be included on an IFR flight plan as an alternate, if the current weather forecast indicates that the ceiling and visibility at the ETA will

answers.A: allow for descent from the IAF to landing under basic VFR conditions.
answers.B: be at least 1,000 feet and 1 mile.
answers.C: allow for a descent from the MEA, approach, and a landing under basic VFR conditions.

explanations.A: because descent must be possible from the MEA, not the IAF (initial approach fix), under basic VFR conditions.
explanations.B: because 800 ft., not 1,000 ft, and 2 SM, not 1 SM, are the standard alternate airport weather minimums at ETA for a nonprecision approach procedure.
explanations.C: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may include an alternate airport that does not have a standard instrument approach on an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that at the ETA at the alternate airport the ceiling and visibility will allow for a descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR conditions.

questions.question: When an alternate airport is required, what are the weather minimums that must be forecast at the ETA for an alternate airport that has a precision approach procedure?

answers.A: Ceiling 200 feet above the approach minimums and at least 1 statute mile visibility, but not less than the minimum visibility for the approach.
answers.B: 600 foot ceiling and 2 statute miles visibility.
answers.C: Ceiling 200 feet above field elevation and visibility 1 statute mile, but not less than the minimum visibility for the approach.

explanations.A: because 600 ft., not 200 ft. above imums, is the minimum ceiling; and 2 SM, not 1 SM, is the minimum visibility required to list an airport with a precision approach as an alternate.
explanations.B: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may include an alternate airport that has a precision (ILS) approach in an IFR flight plan unless current weather forecasts indicate that at the ETA at the alternate airport the ceiling is at least 600 ft. and visibility is 2 SM.
explanations.C: because 600 ft., not 200 ft., and 2 SM, not 1 SM, are the alternate minimums for airports with precision approaches.

questions.question: What record shall be made in the aircraft log or other permanent record by the pilot making the VOR operational check?

answers.A: The date, place, bearing error, and signature.
answers.B: The date, frequency of VOR or VOT, number of flight hours since last check, and signature.
answers.C: The date, place, bearing error, aircraft total time, and signature.

explanations.A: Each person making the VOR operational check shall enter the date, place, and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record.
explanations.B: because VOR frequency and number of flight hr. since last check are not required.
explanations.C: because the aircraft's total time is not required.

questions.question: When must an operational check on the aircraft VOR equipment be accomplished when used to operate under IFR?

answers.A: Within the preceding 10 days or 10 hours of flight time.
answers.B: Within the preceding 30 days or 30 hours of flight time.
answers.C: Within the preceding 30 days.

explanations.A: because it must be checked every 30 days, not 10 days or 10 hr.
explanations.B: because there is no time requirement regarding hours of flight time.
explanations.C: No person may operate a civil aircraft under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the VOR equipment of that aircraft is maintained, checked, and inspected under an approved procedure, or has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and was found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing error.

questions.question: Which data must be recorded in the aircraft log or other appropriate log by a pilot making a VOR operational check for IFR operations?

answers.A: VOR name or identification, date of check, amount of bearing error, and signature.
answers.B: Place of operational check, amount of bearing error, date of check, and signature.
answers.C: Date of check, VOR name or identification, place of operational check, and amount of bearing error.

explanations.A: because the place of operational check rather than the VOR name or identification is required.
explanations.B: Each person making the VOR operational check shall enter the date, place, and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record.
explanations.C: because a signature is required, but the VOR name is not required.

questions.question: When making an airborne VOR check, what is the maximum allowable tolerance between the two indicators of a dual VOR system (units independent of each other except the antenna)?

answers.A: 4° between the two indicated bearings of a VOR.
answers.B: Plus or minus 4° when set to identical radials of a VOR.
answers.C: 6° between the two indicated radials of a VOR.

explanations.A: If a dual VOR system (units independent of each other except the antenna) is installed in the aircraft, you may check one system against the other. You tune both systems to the same VOR station and note the indicated bearings to that station. The maximum permissible variation between the two indicated bearings is 4°.
explanations.B: because you center the CDI and note the bearing, not set both VORs to the same radial.
explanations.C: because the maximum allowable difference between the two VORs is 4°, not 6°, of the indicated radial.

questions.question: Which checks and inspections of flight instruments or instrument systems must be accomplished before an aircraft can be flown under IFR?

answers.A: VOR within 30 days, altimeter systems within 24 calendar months, and transponder within 24 calendar months.
answers.B: ELT test within 30 days, altimeter systems within 12 calendar months, and transponder within 24 calendar months.
answers.C: VOR within 24 calendar months, transponder within 24 calendar months, and altimeter system within 12 calendar months.

explanations.A: No person may operate a civil aircraft under IFR using the VOR system of radio navigation unless the VOR equipment of that aircraft is maintained, checked, and inspected under an approved procedure, or has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and was found to be within the limits of the permissible indicated bearing error. Also, within the preceding 24 calendar months, each altimeter system and transponder must be tested, inspected, and found to comply with the regulations.
explanations.B: because check and inspection of the altimeter system is required every 24 months, not 12 months, and ELTs must be inspected every 12 months, not tested within 30 days.
explanations.C: because VORs must be checked within 30 days, not 24 months, and altimeter systems must be inspected within 24 months, not 12 months.

questions.question: What is the maximum tolerance allowed for an operational VOR equipment check when using a VOT?

answers.B: Plus or minus 6°.
answers.C: Plus or minus 8°.
answers.A: Plus or minus 4°.

explanations.A: When using a VOT for an operational VOR equipment check, the maximum permissible indicated bearing error is plus or minus 4°.
explanations.B: because plus or minus 6° is the maximum error allowed when using an airborne checkpoint.
explanations.C: because plus or minus 8° is not an acceptable error for any type of VOR equipment check.

questions.question: When departing from an airport located outside controlled airspace during IMC, you must file an IFR flight plan and receive a clearance before

answers.B: entering IFR conditions.
answers.A: takeoff.
answers.C: entering Class E airspace.

explanations.A: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.
explanations.B: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.
explanations.C: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless (s)he has filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance.

questions.question: To operate an aircraft under IFR, a flight plan must have been filed and an ATC clearance received prior to

answers.A: controlling the aircraft solely by use of instruments.
answers.B: entering weather conditions in any airspace.
answers.C: entering controlled airspace.

explanations.A: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.
explanations.B: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.
explanations.C: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless (s)he has filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance.

questions.question: To operate under IFR below 18,000 feet, a pilot must file an IFR flight plan and receive an appropriate ATC clearance prior to

answers.A: entering controlled airspace.
answers.B: entering weather conditions below VFR minimums.
answers.C: takeoff.

explanations.A: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless (s)he has filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance.
explanations.B: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.
explanations.C: because an IFR flight plan and clearance are not required until you enter controlled airspace.

questions.question: Prior to which operation must an IFR flight plan be filed and an appropriate ATC clearance received?

answers.A: Flying by reference to instruments in controlled airspace.
answers.B: Entering controlled airspace when IMC exists.
answers.C: Takeoff when IFR weather conditions exist.

explanations.A: because you may fly by reference to instruments with a safety pilot in VFR weather conditions without an lFR flight plan or an IFR clearance.
explanations.B: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless (s)he has filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance.
explanations.C: because an IFR flight plan is not required until you enter controlled airspace.

questions.question: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless he/she files a flight plan

answers.A: and receives a clearance by telephone prior to takeoff.
answers.B: prior to takeoff and requests the clearance upon arrival on an airway.
answers.C: and receives a clearance prior to entering controlled airspace.

explanations.A: because it does not matter how the clearance is obtained.
explanations.B: because a person must file an IFR flight plan and receive clearance before operating in controlled airspace, e.g., a federal airway.
explanations.C: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless (s)he has filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance.

questions.question: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing or unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator, the minimum altitude for IFR flight is

answers.A: 3,000 feet over all terrain.
answers.B: 3,000 feet over designated mountainous terrain; 2,000 feet over terrain elsewhere.
answers.C: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle over designated mountainous terrain; 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle over terrain elsewhere.

explanations.A: because the minimum IFR altitude is 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle over mountainous terrain or 1,000 ft. over the highest obstacle over terrain elsewhere, not 3,000 ft. over all terrain.
explanations.B: because the minimum IFR altitude is 2,000 ft., not 3,000 ft., above the highest obstacle over mountainous terrain, or 1,000 ft., not 2,000 ft., above the highest obstacle over terrain elsewhere.
explanations.C: Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown over designated mountainous terrain, or 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown over terrain elsewhere.

questions.question: What minimum navigation equipment is required for IFR flight?

answers.A: VORILOC receiver, transponder, and DME.
answers.B: VOR receiver and, if in ARTS Ill environment, a coded transponder equipped for altitude reporting.
answers.C: Navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities to be used.

explanations.A: because a VOR/LOC receiver and DME are required only if VORTAC stations will be used for navigation and DME fixes need to be identified. If you are using alternative means of navigation (e.g., LORAN), this equipment is not needed. A transponder is not a navigation system.
explanations.B: because a VOR is required only if using VOR stations for navigation. If using NDB stations, a VOR is not required. A transponder is not a navigation system.
explanations.C: The minimum navigation equipment requirement for IFR flight is navigation equipment that is appropriate to the ground facilities to be used.

questions.question: Where is DME required under IFR?

answers.A: At or above 24,000 feet MSL if VOR navigational equipment is required.
answers.B: In positive control airspace.
answers.C: Above 18,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A: If VOR navigational equipment is required, no person may operate a U.S.-registered civil aircraft within the 50 states and the District of Columbia, at or above 24,000 ft. MSL (FL 240), unless that aircraft is equipped with approved distance measuring equipment (DME).
explanations.B: because, if VOR navigational equipment is required, DME is required at or above FL 240, not only in positive control airspace. Positive control airspace is that airspace in which ATC separates all aircraft, e.g., Class A, Class B, Class C.
explanations.C: because Class A airspace begins at 18,000 ft. MSL and DME is required at or above FL 240, if VOR navigational equipment is required.

questions.question: An aircraft operated during IFR under 14 CFR Part 91 is required to have which of the following?

answers.B: Dual VOR system.
answers.C: Gyroscopic direction indicator.
answers.A: Radar altimeter.

explanations.A: because only a sensitive altimeter, not a radar altimeter, is required.
explanations.B: because, if VOR navigation is to be used, ‘only one, not two, VOR is required under FAR Part 91.
explanations.C: An aircraft operated during IFR under FAR Part 91 is required to have a gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent).

questions.question: Aircraft being operated under IFR are required to have, in addition to the equipment required for VFR and night, at least

answers.A: asilip skid indicator.
answers.B: dual VOR receivers.
answers.C: distance measuring equipment.

explanations.A: An aircraft operated under FAR Part 91 under IFR is required to have a slip-skid indicator (e.g., the ball of the turn coordinator).
explanations.B: because the requirement is for navigational equipment appropriate to the ground facilities to be used, not necessarily dual VOR receivers.
explanations.C: because DME is required only above 24,000 ft. MSL when VOR navigational equipment is required.

questions.question: To meet the requirements for flight under IFR, an aircraft must be equipped with certain operable instruments and equipment. One of those required is

answers.A: a radar altimeter.
answers.B: a transponder with altitude reporting capability.
answers.C: a clock with sweep second pointer or digital presentation.

explanations.A: because a radio (radar) altimeter is required under some circumstances for Category Il operations with decision heights below 150 ft. AGL, not for all flights under IFR.
explanations.B: because a transponder with altitude encoding capability is required in certain airspace areas, not for all flights under IFR.
explanations.C: An aircraft operated under FAR Part 91 under IFR is required to have a clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation.

questions.question: What is the oxygen requirement for an unpressurized aircraft at 15,000 feet?

answers.A: All occupants must use oxygen for the entire time at this altitude.
answers.B: Crew must start using oxygen at 12,000 feet and passengers at 15,000 feet.
answers.C: Crew must use oxygen for the entire time above 14,000 feet and ngers must be provided supplemental oxygen only above 15,000 feet.

explanations.A: because the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen above 14,000 ft. MSL and others must be provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.B: because the crew must start using oxygen at 14,000 ft. MSL or after 30 min. above 12,500 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes. At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 ft. MSL, each passenger must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

questions.question: What is the maximum IFR altitude you may fly in an unpressurized aircraft without providing passengers with supplemental oxygen?

explanations.A: because, at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL, only the minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is more than 30 min. duration.
explanations.B: because, at cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 ft. MSL, only the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen.
explanations.C: At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 ft. MSL, each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen.

questions.question: What is the maximum cabin pressure altitude at which a pilot can fly for longer than 30 minutes without using supplemental oxygen?

explanations.A: because supplemental oxygen is not required at any time at 10,500 ft.
explanations.B: because supplemental oxygen is not required at any time at 12,000 ft.
explanations.C: No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required minimum flight crew uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration.

questions.question: if an unpressurized aircraft is operated above 12,500 feet MSL, but not more than 14,000 feet MSL, for a period of 2 hours 20 minutes, how long during that time is the minimum flightcrew required to use supplemental oxygen?

answers.A: 2 hours 20 minutes.
answers.B: 1 hour 20 minutes.
answers.C: 1 hour 50 minutes.

explanations.A: because one may fly for 30 min. without supplemental oxygen between 12,500 ft. MSL and 14,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.B: because 30 min. of flight, not 1 hr., is permitted without supplemental oxygen between 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: No one may operate a U.S. civil aircraft at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft. MSL up to and including 14,000 ft. MSL unless the required imum flight crew uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 min. duration. If the flight lasts 2 hr. and 20 min., the crew must use supplemental oxygen for all but 30 min., or 1 hr. and 50 min.

questions.question: Inthe 48 contiguous states, excluding the airspace at or below 2,500 feet AGL, an operable coded transponder equipped with Mode C capability is required in all controlled airspace at and above

answers.A: 12,500 feet MSL.
answers.B: 10,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: Flight level (FL) 180.

explanations.A: because 12,500 ft. MSL pertains to supplemental oxygen, not Mode C, requirements.
explanations.B: Unless otherwise authorized or directed by ATC, no person may operate an aircraft in the 48 contiguous states at and above 10,000 ft. MSL, excluding the airspace at or below 2,500 ft. AGL, unless the aircraft is equipped with an operable Mode C transponder.
explanations.C: because FL 180 is the floor of Class A airspace.

questions.question: A coded transponder equipped with altitude reporting capability is required in all controlled airspace AGL.

answers.B: at and above 2,500 feet above the surface.
answers.A: at and above 10,000 feet MSL, excluding at and below 2,500 feet
answers.C: below 10,000 feet MSL, excluding at and below 2,500 feet AGL.

explanations.A: Unless otherwise authorized or directed by ATC, no person may operate an aircraft in the 48 contiguous states at and above 10,000 ft. MSL, excluding the airspace at or below 2,500 ft. AGL, unless the aircraft is equipped with an operable Mode C transponder.
explanations.B: because the airspace above 2,500 ft. AGL must also be at or above 10,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: because the limit is at and above, not below, 10,000 ft. MSL.

questions.question: Prior to operating an aircraft not equipped with a transponder in Class B airspace, a request for a deviation must be submitted to the

answers.A: FAA Administrator at least 24 hours before the proposed operation.
answers.B: nearest FAA General Aviation District Office 24 hours before the proposed operation.
answers.C: controlling ATC facility at least 1 hour before the proposed flight.

explanations.A: because a request for a deviation to operate in Class B airspace in an airplane not equipped with a transponder must be submitted to the controlling ATC facility at least 1 hr. before the proposed flight, not to the FAA Administrator at least 24 hr. before the operation.
explanations.B: because a request for a deviation to operate in Class B airspace in an airplane not equipped with a transponder must be submitted to the controlling ATC facility at least 1 hr. before the proposed flight, not to the nearest FSDO. (formerly called GADO) 24 hr. before the proposed operation.
explanations.C: ATC may authorize deviations ona continuing basis, or for individual flights, for operations of aircraft without a transponder. The request for a deviation must be submitted to the ATC facility having jurisdiction over the airspace concerned at least 1 hr. before the proposed operation.

questions.question: When an aircraft is not equipped with a transponder, what requirement must be met before ATC will authorize a flight within Class B airspace?

answers.A: Arequest for the proposed flight must be made to ATC at least 1 hour before the flight.
answers.B: The proposed flight must be conducted when operating under instrument flight rules.
answers.C: The proposed flight must be conducted in visual meteorological conditions (VMC).

explanations.A: Requests for ATC authorized deviations must be made to the ATC facility having jurisdiction over the concerned airspace. A request for a deviation from the transponder equipment requirement in Class B airspace must be made to the controlling ATC facility at least 1 hr. before the flight.
explanations.B: because you must request a deviation from the transponder equipment requirement from ATC. The requirement is not that the proposed flight be conducted under IFR.
explanations.C: because you must request a deviation from the transponder equipment requirement from ATC. The requirement is not that the proposed flight be conducted in VMC.

questions.question: If the aircraft's transponder fails during flight within Class B airspace,

answers.A: the pilot should immediately request clearance to depart the Class B airspace.
answers.B: ATC may authorize deviation from the transponder requirement to allow aircraft to continue to the airport of ultimate destination.
answers.C: aircraft must immediately descend below 1,200 feet AGL and proceed to destination.

explanations.A: because ATC can immediately authorize
explanations.B: If an aircraft's transponder fails during flight within Class B airspace, ATC may authorize deviation from the transponder requirement to allow the aircraft to continue to the airport of ultimate destination, including any intermediate stops, or to proceed to a place where suitable repairs can be made, or both.
explanations.C: because a pilot may descend only if clearance from ATC is obtained.

questions.question: Your aircraft had the static pressure system and altimeter tested and inspected on January 5, of this year, and was found to comply with FAA standards. These systems must be reinspected and approved for use in controlled airspace under IFR by

answers.A: January 5, next year.
answers.B: January 5, 2 years hence.
answers.C: January 31, 2 years hence.

explanations.A: because these tests must be completed every 24 calendar months, not 1 year from the date of the last inspection.
explanations.B: because these tests must be completed within the preceding 24 calendar months, not 2 years from the date of the last inspection.
explanations.C: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested, inspected, and found to comply with the regulations. The 24-calendar-month period following January of this year begins February 1, this year, and ends on January 31, 2 years hence.

questions.question: An aircraft altimeter system test and inspection must be accomplished within

answers.A: 12 calendar months.
answers.B: 18 calendar months.
answers.C: 24 calendar months.

explanations.A: because an annual inspection, not the altimeter system, must be accomplished within the preceding 12 calendar months.
explanations.B: because the aircraft's altimeter system must be tested and inspected within 24, not 18, calendar months.
explanations.C: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested, inspected, and found to comply with the regulations.

questions.question: Which publication covers the procedures required for aircraft accident and incident reporting responsibilities for pilots?

answers.B: FAR Part 91.
answers.C: NTSB Part 830.
answers.A: FAR Part 61

explanations.A: because FAR Part 61 concerns certification of pilots, flight instructors, and ground instructors.
explanations.B: because FAR Part 91 concerns general operating and flight rules.
explanations.C: NTSB Part 830 contains rules pertaining to the following: 1. Notification and reporting aircraft accidents and incidents and certain other occurrences in the operation of aircraft when they involve civil aircraft of the U.S. wherever they occur, or foreign civil aircraft when such events occur in the U.S., its territories, or possessions. 2. Reporting aircraft accidents and listed incidents in the operation of aircraft when they involve certain public aircraft. 3. Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo, and records involving all civil aircraft in the U.S., its territories, or possessions.

chapters.section: Airports, Air Traffic Control, and Airspace

questions.question: (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (A) from the beginning of the runway to the fixed distance marker?

answers.A: 500 feet.
answers.B: 1,000 feet.
answers.C: 1,500 feet.

explanations.A: because the six parallel lines (somewhat lighter and narrower than the fixed distance marker) 500 ft. from the threshold of the runway are the touchdown zone marker.
explanations.B: The fixed distance marker on precision instrument runways consists of two heavy lines parallel to the direction of the runway, 1,000 ft. from the runway threshold.
explanations.C: because the marker at roughly 1,500 ft. from the threshold is the next marker beyond the fixed distance marker, not the fixed distance marker.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (B) from the beginning of the runway to the touchdown zone marker?

answers.A: 250 feet.
answers.B: 500 feet.
answers.C: 750 feet.

explanations.A: because there is no standardized marking 250 ft. from the beginning of the runway.
explanations.B: The distance from the runway threshold to the touchdown zone marker is 500 ft. The touchdown zone marker consists of six lines parallel to the runway.
explanations.C: because there is no standardized marking 750 ft. from the beginning of the runway.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 137.) What is the distance (C) from the beginning of the touchdown zone marker to the beginning of the fixed distance marker?

answers.A: 1,000 feet.
answers.B: 500 feet.
answers.C: 250 feet.

explanations.A: because 1,000 ft. is the distance from the beginning of the runway to the fixed distance marker.
explanations.B: Since the touchdown zone marker is 500 ft. from the runway threshold and the fixed distance marker is 1,000 ft. from the runway threshold, the distance from the beginning of the touchdown zone marker to the beginning of the fixed distance marker is 500 ft. (1,000 - 500).
explanations.C: because 250 ft. is not a standard distance between runway markings.

questions.question: The primary purpose of runway end identifier lights, installed at many airfields, is to provide

answers.A: rapid identification of the approach end of the runway during reduced visibility.
answers.B: a warning of the final 3,000 feet of runway remaining as viewed from the takeoff or approach position.
answers.C: rapid identification of the primary runway during reduced visibility.

explanations.A: Runway end identifier lights (REIL) are effective for rapid and positive identification of the approach end of a runway which is surrounded by a preponderance of other lighting, which lacks contrast with surrounding terrain, and/or which has reduced visibility. They are white strobe lights, one on each side of the runway threshold.
explanations.B: because it describes runway remaining lights in the center of the runway, not REIL.
explanations.C: because REIL of other than the primary runway may be used to help identify the airport. In other words, REIL may be flashing at the end of a runway which is not the primary runway.

questions.question: Which type of runway lighting consists of a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold?

answers.B: HIRL.
answers.C: REIL.
answers.A: RAIL.

explanations.A: because RAIL refers to runway alignment indicator lights, which are sequenced flashing lights that are used in combination with other approach lighting systems.
explanations.B: because HIRL refers to high-intensity runway lights, which are a runway edge light system.
explanations.C: Runway end identifier lights (REIL) consist of a pair of synchronized flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold.

questions.question: Which runway marking indicates a displaced threshold on an instrument runway?

answers.A: Arrows leading to the threshold mark.
answers.B: Centerline dashes starting at the threshold.
answers.C: Red chevron marks in the nonlanding portion of the runway.

explanations.A: On any runway, a displaced threshold is marked with a series of arrows in the middle of the runway pointing to the threshold mark, which is a solid line across the runway. A displaced threshold is available for taxiing, landing rollout, and takeoff, but not landing.
explanations.B: because it describes the centerline marking of a runway.
explanations.C: because chevron marks are usually yellow. They indicate a nonusable portion of the runway that is only available for emergency use (overrun and stopway areas).

questions.question: (Refer to figure 138.) What night operations, if any, are authorized between the approach end of the runway and the threshold lights?

answers.A: No aircraft operations are permitted short of the threshold lights.
answers.B: Only taxi operations are permitted in the area short of the threshold lights.
answers.C: Taxi and takeoff operations are permitted, providing the takeoff operations are toward the visible green threshold lights.

explanations.A: because overrun areas are areas where ‘only emergency operations are permitted. Overrun areas do not have any runway edge lights.
explanations.B: because landing rollout and takeoff operations are also permitted behind displaced thresholds.
explanations.C: On displaced thresholds, runway edge lights appear red when taxiing toward the green threshold lights and white when taxiing away from the threshold to the departure end of the runway. The area behind the displaced runway threshold is available for taxiing, landing rollout, and takeoff of aircraft.

questions.question: Under which conditions is hydroplaning most likely to occur?

answers.A: When rudder is used for directional control instead of allowing the nosewheel to contact the surface early in the landing roll on a wet runway.
answers.B: During conditions of standing water, slush, high speed, and smooth runway texture.
answers.C: During a landing on any wet runway when brake application is delayed until a wedge of water begins to build ahead of the tires.

explanations.A: because the nosewheel cannot hydroplane if it is not put down to the runway surface.
explanations.B: In hydroplaning, the aircraft tire is separated from the runway by water. It is more apt to happen at higher speeds, with standing water or slush on the runway, and on
explanations.C: because hydroplaning occurs regardless of brake timing.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) Mandatory airport instruction signs are designated by having

answers.A: yellow lettering with a black background.
answers.B: white lettering with a red background.
answers.C: black lettering with a yellow background.

explanations.A: because yellow lettering on a black background denotes taxiway or runway location signs (where the aircraft is located).
explanations.B: Mandatory airport instruction signs have a red background with white lettering and are used to denote an entrance to a runway or critical area, and areas where an aircraft is prohibited from entering.
explanations.C: because black lettering on a yellow background denotes direction, destination, and information signs.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) What sign is designated by illustration 7?

answers.A: Location sign.
answers.B: Mandatory instruction sign.
answers.C: Direction sign.

explanations.A: because location signs use yellow lettering on a black background.
explanations.B: Mandatory instruction signs have a red background with white lettering. The sign designated by illustration 7 (15-APCH) protects the approach to RWY 15 and/or the departure for RWY 33.
explanations.C: because direction signs use black lettering on a yellow background.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) What colors are runway holding position signs?

answers.A: White with a red background.
answers.B: Red with a white background.
answers.C: Yellow with a black background.

explanations.A: Runway holding position signs, like other mandatory instruction signs, have white lettering on a red background. Runway holding position signs are located at the holding position on taxiways that intersect a runway or on runways that intersect other runways.
explanations.B: because red lettering on a white background is used on the landing area of a hospital heliport but is not used on any airport signs.
explanations.C: because taxiway and runway location signs, not runway holding position signs, have yellow lettering on

questions.question: (Refer to figure 94.) Hold line markings at the intersection of taxiways and runways consist of four lines that extend across the width of the taxiway. These lines are

answers.A: white, and the dashed lines are nearest the runway.
answers.B: yellow, and the dashed lines are nearest the runway.
answers.C: yellow, and the solid lines are nearest the runway.

explanations.A: because the lines are yellow, not white.
explanations.B: Runway holding position markings on taxiways identify the location where you are supposed to stop when you do not have a clearance to proceed onto the runway. These markings consist of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, spaced 6 inches apart and extending across the width of the taxiway, with the dashed lines nearest the runway. The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft is to hold. Cc vellow and the soli lines are nearest the runway.
explanations.C: because solid lines are always on the holding side, not the runway side.

questions.question: The "runway hold position" sign denotes

answers.A: intersecting runways.
answers.B: an entrance to runway from a taxiway
answers.C: an area protected for an aircraft approaching a runway.
