explanations.A: because a runway hold position sign is used only to denote an intersecting runway when that runway is used for “Land, Hold Short" operations or as a taxiway.
explanations.B: Runway holding position signs, consisting of white numbering on a red background, are found adjacent to runway holding position markings that are painted on a taxiway or
explanations.C: because a runway approach area holding position sign, not a runway holding position sign, denotes an area protected for aircraft approaching or departing a runway.

questions.question: "Runway hold position" markings on the taxiway

answers.A: identifies where aircraft hold short of the runway.
answers.B: identifies area where aircraft are prohibited.
answers.C: allows an aircraft permission onto the runway.

explanations.A: Runway holding position markings on taxiways identify the location where you are supposed to stop when you do not have an ATC clearance to proceed at an airport with an operating control tower or without making sure of adequate separation at an airport without an operating control tower. These markings consist of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, spaced 6 inches apart and extending across the width of the taxiway, with the dashed lines nearest the runway. The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft is to hold.
explanations.B: because a no entry sign, not a runway hold position marking, identifies an area where aircraft are prohibited.
explanations.C: because runway holding position markings indicate that aircraft should hold short of the runway, not taxi onto it, until a clearance to proceed onto the runway is received.

questions.question: The "No Entry" sign identifies

answers.A: the exit boundary for the runway protected area.
answers.B: an area that does not continue beyond intersection.
answers.C: paved area where aircraft entry is prohibited.

explanations.A: because a runway boundary sign, not a no entry sign, identifies the boundary of the runway protected area for aircraft leaving the runway. Runway boundary signs consist of a black depiction of a runway holding position marking ona yellow background.
explanations.B: because a taxiway ending marker sign, not a no entry sign, indicates that a taxiway does not continue beyond the next intersection. Taxiway ending marker signs consist of alternating yellow and black diagonal stripes.
explanations.C: No entry signs consist of a white horizontal line surrounded by a white circle on a red background. These signs are posted at points where aircraft entry is prohibited. These signs are typically found on taxiways that are intended to be used in only one direction and at the intersection of vehicle roadways with runways, taxiways, or ramp areas where the roadway may be mistaken for a taxiway or other aircraft movement area.

questions.question: When turning onto a taxiway from another taxiway, the "taxiway directional sign" indicates

answers.A: direction to the take-off runway.
answers.B: designation and direction of taxiway leading out of an intersection.
answers.C: designation and direction of exit taxiway from runway.

explanations.A: because outbound destination signs, not direction signs, indicate the direction that must be taken out of an intersection in order to follow the preferred taxi route to a runway.
explanations.B: Direction signs consist of black lettering on
explanations.C: because the question specifies that you are turning onto a taxiway from another taxiway, not from a runway.

questions.question: Which approach and landing objective is assured when the pilot remains on the proper glidepath of the VASI?

answers.A: Continuation of course guidance after transition to VFR.
answers.B: Safe obstruction clearance in the approach area.
answers.C: Course guidance from the visual descent point to touchdown.

explanations.A: because VASI does not provide course guidance.
explanations.B: The VASI system provides visual descent guidance and provides safe obstruction clearance within plus or minus 10° of the extended runway centerline from as far as 4 NM from the runway threshold.
explanations.C: because VASI does not provide course guidance.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 134.) Unless a higher angle is necessary for obstacle clearance, what is the normal glidepath angle for a 2-bar VASI?

explanations.A: because the normal glide path angle for a 2-bar VAST is 3°, not 2.75°.
explanations.B: Two-bar VASI installations provide one visual glide path, which is normally set at 3°. Angles at some locations may be as high as 4.5°, however, to give proper obstacle clearance. This greater angle may necessitate increased runway for landing and rollout of some high-performance airplanes.
explanations.C: because 3.25° is the normal upper glide path provided by a 3-bar VASI.

questions.question: Which of the following indications would a pilot see while approaching to land on a runway served by a 2-bar VASI?

answers.A: If on the glidepath, the near bars will appear red, and the far bars will appear white.
answers.B: If departing to the high side of the glidepath, the far bars will change from red to white.
answers.C: If on the glidepath, both near bars and far bars will appear white.

explanations.A: because, if you are on the glide slope, the near bars are white, not red, and the far bars are red, not white (the opposite is impossible).
explanations.B: As you move to the high side of a VASI glide slope, the far bar will change from red to white. When you are on the glide slope, the far bar is red. When you are above the glide slope, the far bar is white.
explanations.C: because, if both near and far bars are white, you are above, not on, the glide slope.

questions.question: When on the proper glidepath of a 2-bar VASI, the pilot will see the near bar as

answers.B: red and the far bar as white.
answers.C: white and the far bar as white.
answers.A: white and the far bar as red.

explanations.A: When you are on the proper glide path of a 2-bar VASI, the near lights will be white and the far lights red.
explanations.B: because white over red is impossible.
explanations.C: because white over white means you are above, not on, the glide path.

questions.question: if an approach is being made to a runway that has an operating 3-bar VASI and all the VASI lights appear red as the airplane reaches the MDA, the pilot should

answers.A: start a climb to reach the proper glidepath.
answers.B: continue at the same rate of descent if the runway is in sight.
answers.C: level off momentarily to intercept the proper approach path.

explanations.A: because a climb is not necessary. If you level off you will soon be back on the glide path.
explanations.B: because you should briefly stop, not continue, your rate of descent to get back on the desired glide path.
explanations.C: If all three VASI bars are red, you are beneath both glide paths and should level off momentarily to intercept the proper approach path.

questions.question: The middle and far bars of a 3-bar VASI will

answers.A: both appear white to the pilot when on the upper glidepath.
answers.B: constitute a 2-bar VASI for using the lower glidepath.
answers.C: constitute a 2-bar VASI for using the upper glidepath.

explanations.A: because, when both the middle and far bars are white, the airplane is above both glide paths.
explanations.B: because the near and middle bars are used for the lower glide path.
explanations.C: On 3-bar VASIs, the lower glide path is provided by the near and middle bars at a 3° glide slope. The middle and far bars normally have a 1/4° greater glide slope and are used for the upper glide path.

questions.question: Tricolor Visual Approach Indicators normally consist of

answers.A: asingle unit, projecting a three-color visual approach path.
answers.B: three separate light units, each projecting a different color approach path.
answers.C: three separate light projecting units of very high candle power with a daytime range of approximately 5 miles.

explanations.A: Tricolor visual approach indicators consist of a single light unit projecting a three-color visual approach path. The unit has a useful range of % to 1 mi. in daylight and as much as 5 mi. at night.
explanations.B: because tricolor visual approach indicators have only one light unit and only one glide path.
explanations.C: because tricolor VASIs have only one projecting unit with a daytime range of about 1, not 5, mi.

questions.question: Which is a feature of the tricolor VASI?

answers.A: One light projector with three colors: red, green, and amber.
answers.B: Two visual glidepaths for the runway.
answers.C: Three glidepaths, with the center path indicated by a white light.

explanations.A: Tricolor VASIs normally consist of a single light unit projecting a three-color visual approach path. The colors are amber (above the glide path), green (on the path), and red (below the path).
explanations.B: because having two visual glide paths for the runway is a feature of a 3-bar, not tricolor, VASI.
explanations.C: because it is a nonsense concept; i.e., there is not a three-glide path VASI.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 135.) Unless a higher angle is required for obstacle clearance, what is the normal glidepath for a 3-bar VASI?

explanations.A: because 2.3° is not a VASI glide path angle.
explanations.B: because 2.75° is not a VASI glide path angle.
explanations.C: The normal glide path for a 3-bar VASI (the lower glide path) is 3°. The upper glide path is usually a 3.25° slope. Higher-angle glide slopes, up to 4.5°, are used in some places for adequate obstruction clearance.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 135.) Which illustration would a pilot observe when on the lower glidepath?

explanations.A: because illustration 4 indicates that you are below both glide paths.
explanations.B: On the lower glide path of a 3-bar VASI, the near lights should be white and the middle and far bars should be red, which is illustration 5.
explanations.C: because illustration 6 indicates that you are on the upper glide path.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 135.) Which illustration would a pilot observe if the aircraft is above both glidepaths?

explanations.A: because illustration 5 indicates that you are on the lower glide path.
explanations.B: because illustration 6 indicates that you are on the upper glide path. C7.
explanations.C: If you are above both glide paths ona 3-bar VASI, you will observe that all three rows of lights appear white, which is illustration 7.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 135.) Which illustration would a pilot observe if the aircraft is below both glidepaths?

explanations.A: If you are below both glide paths ona 3-bar VASI, you will observe that all three rows of lights appear red, which is illustration 4.
explanations.B: because illustration 5 indicates that you are on the lower glide path. C6.
explanations.C: because illustration 6 indicates that you are on the upper glide path.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 136.) Which illustration depicts an "on glidepath" indication?

explanations.A: because illustration 8 indicates that you are above the glide slope.
explanations.B: The precision approach path indicator (PAPI) uses light units similar to the VASI, but they are installed in
explanations.C: because illustration 11 indicates that you are slightly below (2.8°) the glide slope.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 136.) Which illustration depicts a "slightly low" (2.8°) indication?

explanations.A: because illustration 9 indicates that you are slightly above (3.2°) the glide path.
explanations.B: because illustration 10 indicates that you are on (3.0°) the glide path.
explanations.C: On PAPI, you are slightly below (2.8°) the glide path when three of the four lights indicate red as in illustration 11.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 136.) Which illustration would a pilot observe if the aircraft is on a glidepath higher than 3.5°?

explanations.A: Higher than the glide path on PAPIs means 3.5° or more, which is indicated by all white lights as in illustration 8.
explanations.B: because illustration 9 indicates that you are slightly high (3.2°).
explanations.C: because illustration 11 indicates that you are slightly low (2.8°).

questions.question: (Refer to figure 136.) Which illustration would a pilot observe if the aircraft is “slightly high" (3.2°) on the glidepath?

explanations.A: because illustration 8 indicates a glide slope that is high or more than 3.5°.
explanations.B: Slightly high on a PAPI is about 3.2°, which is indicated by three white lights out of four. The remaining light is red as in illustration 9.
explanations.C: because illustration 11 indicates a glide slope that is slightly low or about 2.8°.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 136.) Which illustration would a pilot observe if the aircraft is less than 2.5°?

explanations.A: because illustration 10 indicates that you are on the glide path (3.0°).
explanations.B: because illustration 11 indicates that you are slightly low (2.8°).
explanations.C: On PAPI systems, low is indicated by all Ted lights as in illustration 12. Low means the aircraft is on a glide slope of less than 2.5°.

questions.question: What wind condition prolongs the hazards of wake turbulence on a landing runway for the longest period of time?

answers.A: Direct headwind.
answers.B: Direct tailwind.
answers.C: Light quartering tailwind.

explanations.A: because a direct headwind will permit the vortices to move away from each side of the runway.
explanations.B: because a direct tailwind will permit the vortices to move away from each side of the runway.
explanations.C: Light quartering tailwinds require maximum caution because they can move the vortices of preceding aircraft forward into the touchdown zone and hold the upwind vortex on the runway.

questions.question: Wake turbulence is near maximum behind a jet transport just after takeoff because

answers.A: the engines are at maximum thrust output at slow airspeed.
answers.B: the gear and flap configuration increases the turbulence to maximum.
answers.C: of the high angle of attack and high gross weight.

explanations.A: because vortices have to do with airflows about the wingtips, not the engines.
explanations.B: because the gear and flap con figuration will change the characteristics of the vortex.
explanations.C: The greatest vortex strength occurs when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean, and slow, such as in takeoff climbout. At this time there is a high gross weight and also a high angle of attack.

questions.question: What effect would a light crosswind of approximately 7 knots have on vortex behavior?

answers.A: The light crosswind would rapidly dissipate vortex strength.
answers.B: The upwind vortex would tend to remain over the runway.
answers.C: The downwind vortex would tend to remain over the runway.

explanations.A: because strong, not light, winds would help rapidly dissipate vortex strength.
explanations.B: A light crosswind of 1 to 7 kt. could result in the upwind vortex of a preceding aircraft remaining in the touchdown zone for a period of time. Also, it could hasten the drift of the downwind vortex toward another runway.
explanations.C: because the upwind, not downwind, vortex would tend to remain over the runway in a light crosswind.

questions.question: When landing behind a large jet aircraft, at which point on the runway should you plan to land?

answers.A: If any crosswind, land on the windward side of the runway and prior to the jet's touchdown point.
answers.B: At least 1,000 feet beyond the jet's touchdown point.
answers.C: Beyond the jet's touchdown point.

explanations.A: because you must land beyond, not prior to, the touchdown point.
explanations.B: because there is no minimum distance (Le., 1,000 ft.) that you should land beyond the jet's touchdown point.
explanations.C: When landing behind a large aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above the large aircraft's final approach flight path, and land beyond its touchdown point.

questions.question: Which procedure is recommended while climbing to an assigned altitude on the airway?

answers.A: Climb on the centerline of the airway except when maneuvering to avoid other air traffic in VFR conditions.
answers.B: Climb slightly on the right side of the airway when in VFR conditions.
answers.C: Climb far enough to the right side of the airway to avoid climbing or descending traffic coming from the opposite direction if in VFR conditions.

explanations.A: When climbing to an assigned altitude on an airway, one should use the centerline except to avoid other aircraft when in VFR conditions. This procedure is specified in FAR 91.181, which requires aircraft to operate along the centerline of federal airways.
explanations.B: because you are required to maintain the centerline, not remain on the right side, while operating ona federal airway.
explanations.C: because you are required to maintain the centerline, not remain on the right side, while operating ona federal airway.

questions.question: What is expected of you as pilot on an IFR flight plan if you are descending or climbing in VFR conditions?

answers.A: If on an airway, climb or descend to the right of the centerline.
answers.B: Advise ATC you are in visual conditions and will remain a short distance to the right of the centerline while climbing.
answers.C: Execute gentle banks, left and right, at a frequency which permits continuous visual scanning of the airspace about you.

explanations.A: because you are required to maintain, not remain to the right of, the centerline while operating on a federal airway, except when maneuvering to avoid other traffic in VFR conditions.
explanations.B: because you are not required to advise ATC that you are in visual conditions, but you are required to maintain, not remain to the right of, the centerline while operating on a federal airway, except when maneuvering to avoid other traffic in VFR conditions.
explanations.C: During climbs and descents in VFR conditions, pilots should execute gentle banks left and right to permit continual scanning of surrounding airspace.

questions.question: When is a pilot on an IFR flight plan responsible for avoiding other aircraft?

answers.B: When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether operating under IFR or VFR.
answers.C: Only when advised by ATC.
answers.A: Atall times when not in radar contact with ATC.

explanations.A: because, if weather conditions permit, each pilot is responsible for avoiding other aircraft, whether in tadar contact or not.
explanations.B: When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether an operation is conducted under IFR or VFR, each pilot shall maintain vigilance in order to see and avoid other aircraft.
explanations.C: because, if weather conditions permit, each pilot, not ATC, is responsible for avoiding other aircraft.

questions.question: What responsibility does the pilot in command of an IFR flight assume upon entering VFR conditions?

answers.A: Report VFR conditions to ARTCC so that an amended clearance may be issued.
answers.B: Use VFR operating procedures.
answers.C: To see and avoid other traffic.

explanations.A: because VFR conditions are not reported unless so requested by ATC.
explanations.B: because IFR operating procedures are to be followed on an IFR flight.
explanations.C: When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether an operation is conducted under IFR or VER, each pilot shall maintain vigilance in order to see and avoid other aircraft.

questions.question: The most current en route and destination flight information for planning an instrument flight should be obtained from

answers.B: the FSS.
answers.C: Notices to Airmen (Class Il).
answers.A: the ATIS broadcast.

explanations.A: because the ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) broadcasts only information pertaining to landing and departing operations at one airport. ATIS does not provide any en route information.
explanations.B: The FAA urges every pilot to receive a preflight briefing, which may be obtained from a Flight Service Station (FSS) by telephone, radio, or personal visit. The preflight briefing should cover weather, airport, and en route navigation data.
explanations.C: because Notices to Airmen Publication (formerly Class Il) is published every 28 days and contains NOTAMs still in effect but not transmitted with weather information. It is only one aspect of a complete flight briefing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FDC NOTAMs?

answers.A: To provide the latest information on the status of navigation facilities to all FSS facilities for scheduled broadcasts.
answers.B: To issue notices for all airports and navigation facilities in the shortest possible time.
answers.C: To advise of changes in flight data which affect instrument approach procedures (IAP), aeronautical charts, and flight restrictions prior to normal publication.

explanations.A: because NOTAMs (D), not FDC NOTAMs, provide information for the status of navigational facilities. These NOTAMs are appended to the hourly weather reports.
explanations.B: because the purpose of NOTAMs (D) or (L) is to issue notices for all public-use airports and navigation facilities in the shortest possible time.
explanations.C: FDC (Flight Data Center) NOTAMs are regulatory in nature and issued to establish restrictions to flight or amend charts or published instrument approach procedures. FDC NOTAMs are published as needed and indexed in the Notices to Airmen Publication.

questions.question: From what source can you obtain the latest FDC NOTAM's?

answers.B: FAAAFSSIFSS.
answers.C: Airport/Facility Directory.
answers.A: Notices to Airmen Publication.

explanations.A: because the Notices to Airmen Publication is published every 28 days. The FSSs may have more current data.
explanations.B: The National Flight Data Center occasionally publishes regulatory changes (either permanent or temporary) in FDC (Flight Data Center) NOTAMs. They are also used to advertise temporary flight restrictions caused by such things as natural disasters, large public events, and other events that may generate congested air traffic. FSSs are required to keep a file of current FDC NOTAMs.
explanations.C: because the Airport/Facility Directory is only published every 56 days. The A/FD includes only permanent changes that were known at the time of publication.

questions.question: Which sources of aeronautical information, when used collectively, provide the latest status of airport conditions (e.g., runway closures, runway lighting, snow conditions)?

answers.B: Airport Facility Directory, FDC NOTAM's, and Local (L) NOTAM's.
answers.C: Airport Facility Directory, Distant (D) NOTAM's, and Local (L) NOTAM's.
answers.A: Aeronautical Information Manual, aeronautical charts, and Distant (D) Notice to Airmen (NOTAM's).

explanations.A: because the Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) is a source of basic flight information and ATC. procedures, not specific airport information, and aeronautical charts do not indicate the latest status of runway conditions.
explanations.B: because FDC NOTAMs deal with regulatory changes or unusual air traffic congestion, not local airport conditions.
explanations.C: The latest status of airport conditions can be determined by using the Airport/Facility Directory for items that have been known for some time, and distant (D) NOTAMs and local (L) NOTAMs, which contain the most up-to-date data.

questions.question: When are ATIS broadcasts updated?

answers.A: Every 30 minutes if weather conditions are below basic VFR; otherwise, hourly.
answers.B: Upon receipt of any official weather, regardless of content change or reported values.
answers.C: Only when the ceiling and/or visibility changes by a reportable value.

explanations.A: because the frequency of ATIS updates does not differ under VFR or IFR conditions.
explanations.B: ATIS broadcasts are updated upon the receipt of any official weather regardless of content change or reported values. A new recording will also be made when there is
explanations.C: because the recording will be updated whenever official weather is received, even if there is no change.

questions.question: Absence of the sky condition and visibility on an ATIS broadcast specifically implies that

answers.A: the ceiling is more than 5,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more.
answers.B: the sky condition is clear and visibility is unrestricted.
answers.C: the ceiling is at least 3,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more.

explanations.A: The ATIS broadcast generally includes the latest weather sequence, sky conditions, temperature, dew point, wind direction and velocity, altimeter, runways in use, etc. Absence of the sky condition and visibility on an ATIS broadcast specifically implies that the ceiling is more than 5,000 ft. and visibility is more than 5 SM.
explanations.B: because the absence of the sky condition and visibility on an ATIS broadcast implies that ceilings are more than 5,000 ft., not clear, and visibility is 5 SM or more, not unrestricted.
explanations.C: because the absence of the sky condition ‘on an ATIS broadcast implies a ceiling of more than 5,000 ft, not at least 3,000 ft.

questions.question: The operation of an airport rotating beacon during daylight hours may indicate that

answers.A: the in-flight visibility is less than 3 miles and the ceiling is less than 1,500 feet within Class E airspace.
answers.B: the ground visibility is less than 3 miles and/or the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet in Class B, C, or D airspace.
answers.C: anlFR clearance is required to operate within the airport traffic area.

explanations.A: because the operation of an airport rotating beacon during daylight hours at an airport located in Class E airspace may indicate that in-flight visibility (if ground is not reported) is less than 3 SM and/or the ceiling is less than 4,000 ft, not 1,500 ft.
explanations.B: In Class B, C, D, and E surface areas, operation of an airport beacon during daylight hours often indicates that the ground visibility is less than 3 SM and/or the Ceiling is less than 1,000 ft. Pilots should not rely solely on the beacon to indicate weather conditions because there is no regulatory requirement for daylight operation of the airport's rotating beacon.
explanations.C: because an IFR clearance is required only in controlled airspace when IMC exists, not at an airport that is operating a rotating beacon during the day.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 1.) Which item(s) should be checked in block 1 for a composite flight plan?

answers.A: VER with an explanation in block 11.
answers.B: IFR with an explanation in block 11.
answers.C: VFR and IFR.

explanations.A: because both VFR and IFR should be checked.
explanations.B: because both VFR and IFR should be checked.
explanations.C: If you are filing a composite VFRAFR flight plan, you should check both VFR and IFR in Block 1 of the flight plan. A DVFR flight plan is required for flights through air defense identification zones (ADIZ) for national security reasons.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 1.) Which equipment determines the code to be entered in block 3 as a suffix to aircraft type on the flight plan form?

answers.A: DME, ADF, and airborne radar.
answers.B: DME, transponder, and ADF.
answers.C: DME, transponder, and RNAV.

explanations.A: because you need not report ADF (automatic direction finder) or airborne radar.
explanations.B: because an ADF is not considered a special type of navigation equipment.
explanations.C: Block 3 asks for the aircraft type and ‘special equipment. After the aircraft type, a slash is followed by a letter indicating the combination of transponder, DME, and area navigation (RNAV) equipment that you have in the airplane.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 1.) What information should be entered in block 7 of an IFR flight plan if the flight has three legs, each at a different altitude?

answers.B: Altitude for first leg and highest altitude.
answers.C: Highest altitude.
answers.A: Altitude for first leg.

explanations.A: Block 7 of IFR flight plans is for altitude. You should enter only the initial request for altitude. When more than one altitude or flight level is desired along the route of flight, it is best to make subsequent requests direct to the controller.
explanations.B: because initial, not highest, altitude is to be submitted on your flight plan.
explanations.C: because initial, not highest, altitude is to be entered on your flight plan.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 1.) The time entered in block 12 for an IFR flight should be based on which fuel quantity?

answers.A: Total fuel required for the flight.
answers.B: Total useable fuel on board.
answers.C: The amount of fuel required to fly to the destination airport, then to the alternate, plus a 45-minute reserve.

explanations.A: because total fuel required for the flight is determined in your flight planning but is not an item that is listed on an FR flight plan.
explanations.B: Block 12 should be filled in with the time at normal cruising speed using total usable fuel on board. It should be computed from the departure point.
explanations.C: because it describes the IFR fuel requirement.

questions.question: What point at the destination should be used to compute estimated time en route on an IFR flight plan?

answers.A: The final approach fix on the expected instrument approach.
answers.B: The initial approach fix on the expected instrument approach.
answers.C: The point of first intended landing.

explanations.A: because, due to varying weather conditions, runways in use, traffic, etc., there is no way of accurately telling which approach will be used.
explanations.B: because, due to varying weather Conditions, runways in use, traffic, etc., there is no way of accurately telling which approach will be used.
explanations.C: Estimated time en route on an IFR flight plan should be the time from takeoff at the departure airport to touchdown at the point of first intended landing.

questions.question: When may a pilot file a composite flight plan?

answers.A: When requested or advised by ATC.
answers.B: Any time a portion of the flight will be VFR.
answers.C: Any time a landing is planned at an intermediate airport.

explanations.A: because ATC does not request or advise on the type of flight plan to file other than IFR flight plans required in certain weather conditions and in the positive control area.
explanations.B: A composite flight plan should be filed whenever VFR operation is specified for one portion of the flight and IFR for another portion.
explanations.C: because you are not required to convert a flight plan from or to IFR or VFR when landing is planned at an intermediate airport.

questions.question: When filing a composite flight plan where the first portion of the flight is IFR, which fix(es) should be indicated on the flight plan form?

answers.B: Only the fix where you plan to terminate the IFR portion of the flight.
answers.C: Only those compulsory reporting points on the IFR route segment.
answers.A: All points of transition from one airway to another, fixes defining direct route segments, and the clearance limit fix.

explanations.A: On composite flight plans for which the first portion of the flight is IFR, the flight plan should be a standard IFR flight plan, which includes points of transition from one airway to another, fixes defining direct route segments, and the clearance limit fix.
explanations.B: because you have to define the route to get to your clearance limit fix.
explanations.C: because compulsory reporting points are not listed on an IFR flight plan unless they define a point of transition, direct route segments, or the clearance limit fix.

questions.question: What is the recommended procedure for transitioning from VFR to IFR ona composite flight plan?

answers.A: Prior to transitioning to IFR, contact the nearest FSS, close the VER portion, and request ATC clearance.
answers.B: Upon reaching the proposed point for change to IFR, contact the nearest FSS and cancel your VFR flight plan, then contact ARTCC and request an IFR clearance.
answers.C: Prior to reaching the proposed point for change to IFR, contact ARTCC, request your IFR clearance, and instruct them to cancel the VFR flight plan.

explanations.A: Prior to transitioning from VFR to IFR, you should close the VFR portion with FSS and request ATC clearance. You must remain in VFR weather conditions until Operating in accordance with the IFR clearance.
explanations.B: because you must obtain an |FR clearance before beginning IFR operations.
explanations.C: because you should cancel your VFR flight plan with FSS, not ATC.

questions.question: When may a pilot cancel the IFR flight plan prior to completing the flight?

answers.B: Only if an emergency occurs.
answers.C: Only in VFR conditions when not in Class A airspace.
answers.A: Any time.

explanations.A: because you cannot proceed under VFR when IFR conditions exist or when you are flying above FL 180 (i-e., in Class A airspace).
explanations.B: because ATC will provide needed assistance in emergencies while you are operating under an IFR flight plan.
explanations.C: An IFR flight plan may be canceled at any time you are operating in VFR conditions when not in Class A airspace by stating, "Cancel my IFR flight plan" to ATC. Once accepted by ATC, you should change to the appropriate communications frequency, transponder code, and altitude.

questions.question: How is your flight plan closed when your destination airport has IFR conditions and there is no control tower or flight service station (FSS) on the field?

answers.A: The ARTCC controller will close your flight plan when you report the runway in sight.
answers.B: You may close your flight plan any time after starting the approach by contacting any FSS or ATC facility.
answers.C: Upon landing, you must close your flight plan by radio or by telephone to any FSS or ATC facility.

explanations.A: because you, not ATC, must close your IFR flight plan at airports without an operating control tower or FSS on the field.
explanations.B: because, when an airport has IFR conditions, you must have IFR clearances until you have safely landed.
explanations.C: IFR flight plans are automatically closed by ATC if you land at an airport with an operating control tower. However, if operating under an IFR flight plan to an airport with no functioning control tower, you must cancel the IFR flight plan. You may cancel your IFR flight plan while airborne only if weather permits. If your destination airport has IFR conditions and there is no tower or FSS on the field, you should close your IFR flight plan upon landing by radio or telephone to any FSS or ATC facility.

questions.question: What is a way point when used for an IFR flight?

answers.A: Apredetermined geographical position used for an RNAV route or an RNAV instrument approach.
answers.B: A reporting point defined by the intersection of two VOR radials.
answers.C: A location on a victor airway which can only be identified by VOR and DME signals.

explanations.A: A way point on an FR flight is a predetermined geographical position used for an RNAV route or an RNAV instrument approach definition or progress-reporting purposes. It is defined relative to a VORTAC position or in terms of latitude/longitude coordinates.
explanations.B: because a point defined by the intersection of two VOR radials is called an intersection, not a way point.
explanations.C: because a location on a victor airway which can be identified only by VOR and DME signals is called a DME fix, not a way- point.

questions.question: What response is expected when ATC issues an IFR clearance to pilots of airbome aircraft?

answers.A: Read back the entire clearance as required by regulation.
answers.B: Read back those parts containing altitude assignments or vectors and any part requiring verification.
answers.C: Read-back should be unsolicited and spontaneous to confirm that the pilot understands all instructions.

explanations.A: because the read-back is an expected procedure, but there is no regulatory requirement to read back an ATC clearance. Only those parts containing altitude assignments or vectors and any part requiring verification, not the entire clearance, should be read back.
explanations.B: Pilots of airborne aircraft should read back those parts of ATC clearances and instructions containing altitude assignments or vectors and any part requiring verification. The read-back serves as a double-check between pilots and ATC and reduces the kinds of communications errors that occur when a number is either misheard or incorrect.
explanations.C: because only those parts containing altitude assignments or vectors and any part requiring verification, not all instructions, should be read back.

questions.question: Which clearance items are always given in an abbreviated IFR departure clearance? (Assume radar environment.)

answers.A: Altitude, destination airport, and one or more fixes which identify the initial route of flight.
answers.B: Destination airport, altitude, DP Name, Number, and/or Transition, if appropriate.
answers.C: Clearance limit, DP Name, Number, and/or Transition, if appropriate.

explanations.A: because the fixes are already included in the flight plan and do not need to be repeated in an abbreviated IFR departure clearance.
explanations.B: An abbreviated IFR departure clearance will include the destination airport. En route altitude will be stated in the clearance, and the pilot will be advised to expect an assigned or filed altitude within a given time or at a certain point after departure. Any DP (instrument departure procedure) will also be specified by ATC stating the DP name, the current number, and the DP transition name.
explanations.C: because an en route altitude is always given in an abbreviated IFR departure clearance.

questions.question: Which information is always given in an abbreviated departure clearance?

answers.B: Name of destination airport or specific fix and altitude.
answers.C: Altitude to maintain and code to squawk.
answers.A: DP or transition name and altitude to maintain.

explanations.A: because the destination airport or clearance limit is always given in an abbreviated clearance.
explanations.B: An abbreviated IFR departure clearance always contains the name of your destination airport or clearance limit; altitude; and, if a DP is to be flown, the DP name, the current number, and the DP transition name.
explanations.C: because the destination airport or clearance limit is always given in an abbreviated clearance.

questions.question: An abbreviated departure clearance "...CLEARED AS FILED..." will always contain the name

answers.A: and number of the STAR to be flown when filed in the flight plan.
answers.B: of the destination airport filed in the flight plan.
answers.C: of the first compulsory reporting point if not in a radar environment.

explanations.A: because a STAR, when filed in a flight plan, is considered a part of the filed route of flight and will not normally be stated in an initial departure clearance.
explanations.B: An abbreviated IFR departure clearance will include the destination airport. En route altitude will be stated, and the pilot will be advised to expect an assigned or filed altitude by a certain time or at a certain point after departure either separately or as part of a DP. The abbreviated clearance also includes the DP name-number-transition, if appropriate.
explanations.C: because compulsory reporting points are not given in an abbreviated clearance.

questions.question: On the runup pad, you receive the following clearance from ground control: CLEARED TO THE DALLAS-LOVE AIRPORT AS FILED - MAINTAIN SIX THOUSAND - SQUAWK ZERO SEVEN ZERO FOUR JUST BEFORE DEPARTURE - DEPARTURE CONTROL WILL BE ONE TWO FOUR POINT NINER. An abbreviated clearance, such as this, will always contain the

answers.A: departure control frequency.
answers.B: transponder code.
answers.C: destination airport and route.

explanations.A: because if the abbreviated clearance contains a DP, the departure control frequency may not be given if the frequency is published in the DP.
explanations.B: because "Cleared to (destination) airport as filed" does NOT include the en route altitude filed (requested) in the flight plan. An en route altitude will be stated in the clearance or the pilot will be advised to expect an assigned or filed altitude.
explanations.C: An IFR departure clearance will always contain the destination airport and the route of flight. The route of flight will either be given fix-by-fix by the controller, or it will be given “as filed," in which case the route on the IFR flight plan is the assigned route. The statement, “Cleared to the Dallas-Love airport as filed," contains the destination airport and the specific route to be taken (the filed route).

questions.question: When departing from an airport not served by a control tower, the issuance of a Clearance containing a void time indicates that

answers.A: ATC will assume the pilot has not departed if no transmission is received before the void time.
answers.B: The pilot must advise ATC as soon as possible, but no later than 30 minutes, of their intentions if not off by the void time.
answers.C: ATC will protect the airspace only to the void time.

explanations.A: because ATC will assume a departure unless it hears from the pilot.
explanations.B: If operating from an airport not served by a control tower, the pilot may receive a clearance containing a provision that, if the flight has not departed by a specific eke (void time), the clearance is void. In this situation, the pilot who does not depart prior to the void time must advise ATC of his/her intentions as soon as possible, but no later than 30 min. after the void time.
explanations.C: because the airspace is protected until ATC hears from the pilot.

questions.question: What is the significance of an ATC clearance which reads "... CRUISE SIX THOUSAND..."?

answers.A: The pilot must maintain 6,000 until reaching the IAF serving the destination airport, then execute the published approach procedure.
answers.B: It authorizes a pilot to conduct flight at any altitude from minimum IFR altitude up to and including 6,000.
answers.C: The pilot is authorized to conduct flight at any altitude from minimum IFR altitude up to and including 6,000, but each change in altitude must be reported to ATC.

explanations.A: because the pilot need not maintain 6,000 ft.
explanations.B: The term "cruise" in a clearance assigns a pilot a block of airspace from the minimum IFR altitude up to and including the specified altitude (e.g., 6,000 ft. MSL). The pilot may level off at any intermediate altitude within this block of airspace. Climb and descent within the block are to be made at the discretion of the pilot. However, once the pilot starts descent and verbally reports leaving an altitude in the block, (s)he may not return to that altitude without additional ATC clearance.
explanations.C: because the pilot may change altitude without reporting to ATC.

questions.question: What is the significance of an ATC clearance which reads "... CRUISE SIX THOUSAND..."?

answers.A: The pilot must maintain 6,000 feet until reaching the IAF serving the destination airport, then execute the published approach procedure.
answers.B: Climbs may be made to, or descents made from, 6,000 feet at the pilot's discretion.
answers.C: The pilot may utilize any altitude from the MEA/MOCA to 6,000 feet, but each change in altitude must be reported to ATC.

explanations.A: because the pilot need not maintain 6,000 ft.
explanations.B: The term "cruise" in a clearance assigns a pilot a block of airspace from the minimum IFR altitude up to and including the specified altitude (e.g., 6,000 ft. MSL). The pilot may climb to, level off at, or descend from any intermediate altitude within this block of airspace. Once the pilot starts descent and verbally reports leaving an altitude in the block, however, (s)he may not return to that altitude without additional ATC clearance.
explanations.C: because the pilot is assigned all the airspace from the minimum IFR altitude to 6,000 ft. MSL and may change altitudes without reporting to ATC.

questions.question: A"CRUISE FOUR THOUSAND FEET" clearance would mean that the pilot is authorized to

answers.A: vacate 4,000 feet without notifying ATC.
answers.B: climb to, but not descend from 4,000 feet, without further ATC clearance.
answers.C: use any altitude from minimum IFR to 4,000 feet, but must report leaving each altitude.

explanations.A: The term "cruise" in a clearance assigns a pilot a block of airspace from the minimum IFR altitude up to and including the specified altitude (e.g., 4,000 ft. MSL). The pilot may level off at any intermediate altitude within this block of airspace. Climb and descent within the block are to be made at the discretion of the pilot. However, once the pilot starts descent and verbally reports leaving an altitude in the block, (s)he may not return to that altitude without additional ATC clearance.
explanations.B: because any airspace between the minimum IFR altitude and 4,000 ft. MSL may be used without further ATC clearance.
explanations.C: because cruise clearances do not require reporting a change in altitude to ATC.

questions.question: When should pilots state their position on the airport when calling the tower for takeoff?

answers.A: When visibility is less than 1 mile.
answers.B: When parallel runways are in use.
answers.C: When departing from a runway intersection.

explanations.A: because a pilot is not expected to state his/her position on the airport when calling the tower for takeoff when visibility is less than 1 mile.
explanations.B: because a pilot is not expected to state his/her position on the airport when calling the tower for takeoff when parallel runways are in use.
explanations.C: You should state your position on the airport when calling the tower for takeoff from a runway intersection. Additionally, you are expected to request from ground control approval for the intersection departure (i.e., a departure from any runway intersection except the end of the runway) prior to taxi.

questions.question: During a takeoff into IFR conditions with low ceilings, when should the pilot contact departure control?

answers.A: Before penetrating the clouds.
answers.B: When advised by the tower.
answers.C: Upon completing the first turn after takeoff or upon establishing cruise climb on a straight-out departure.

explanations.A: because the tower will advise the pilot when to contact departure control, and such contact is not based on whether the aircraft has penetrated the clouds.
explanations.B: A pilot should not change to the departure control frequency until advised by ATC. Because the pilot maintains continuous contact with assigned ATC frequencies, all frequency changes are at the direction of ATC.
explanations.C: because the tower will advise the pilot when to contact departure control, which may or may not be upon completion of the first turn after takeoff or establishment of a cruise climb on departure.

questions.question: What is the recommended climb procedure when a nonradar departure control instructs a pilot to climb to the assigned altitude?

answers.A: Maintain a continuous optimum climb until reaching assigned altitude and report passing each 1,000 foot level.
answers.B: Climb at a maximum angle of climb to within 1,000 feet of the assigned altitude, then 500 feet per minute the last 1,000 feet.
answers.C: Maintain an optimum climb on the centerline of the airway without intermediate level-offs until 1,000 feet below assigned altitude, then 500 to 1,500 feet per minute.

explanations.A: because the pilot is not required to report passing each 1,000 ft. of altitude.
explanations.B: because one should normally use a cruise climb rather than a maximum angle of climb.
explanations.C: When ATC clearances are given to descend or climb to a certain altitude, the pilot should use the optimum rate consistent with the operating characteristics of the aircraft to 1,000 ft. above or below the assigned altitude and then attempt to descend or climb at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm until reaching the assigned altitude. Also, on airways, one should climb and descend on the centerline of the airway with no intermediate level-offs.

questions.question: To comply with ATC instructions for altitude changes of more than 1,000 feet, what rate of climb or descent should be used?

answers.A: As rapidly as practicable to 500 feet above/below the assigned altitude, and then at 500 feet per minute until the assigned altitude is reached.
answers.B: 1,000 feet per minute during climb and 500 feet per minute during descents until reaching the assigned altitude.
answers.C: As rapidly as practicable to 1,000 feet above/below the assigned altitude, and then between 500 and 1,500 feet per minute until reaching the assigned altitude.

explanations.A: because the rate should be between 500 and 1,500 fpm after you are within 1,000 ft., not 500 ft., of the target altitude.
explanations.B: because the rate of climb and descent should be based upon aircraft capability. Also, when 1,000 ft. above or below the assigned altitude, the pilot should attempt to descend or climb at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm until the assigned altitude is reached.
explanations.C: When ATC clearances are given to descend or climb to a certain altitude, the pilot should use the optimum rate consistent with the operating characteristics of the aircraft to 1,000 ft. above or below the assigned altitude and then attempt to descend or climb at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm until reaching the assigned altitude. Also, one should climb and descend on the centerline of the airway with no intermediate level-offs.

questions.question: When ATC has not imposed any climb or descent restrictions and aircraft are within 1,000 feet of assigned altitude, pilots should attempt to both climb and descend at a rate of between

answers.A: 500 feet per minute and 1,000 feet per minute.
answers.B: 500 feet per minute and 1,500 feet per minute.
answers.C: 1,000 feet per minute and 2,000 feet per minute.

explanations.A: because, within 1,000 ft. of the assigned altitude, pilots should attempt to climb/descend at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm, not 1,000 fpm.
explanations.B: When ATC clearances are given to descend or climb to a certain altitude, the pilot should use the optimum rate consistent with the operating characteristics of the aircraft to 1,000 ft. above or below the assigned altitude and then attempt to descend or climb at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm until reaching the assigned altitude. Also, on airways, one should climb and descend on the centerline of the airway with no intermediate level-offs.
explanations.C: because, within 1,000 ft. of the assigned altitude, pilots should attempt to climb/descend at a rate of between 500 and 1,500 fpm, not 1,000 and 2,000 fpm.

questions.question: Which report should be made to ATC without a specific request when not in radar contact?

answers.A: Entering instrument meteorological conditions.
answers.B: When leaving final approach fix in bound on final approach.
answers.C: Correcting an E.T.A. any time a previous E.T.A. is in error in excess of 2 minutes.

explanations.A: because a report should be made to ATC. whether or not in radar contact anytime you encounter any type of weather conditions that have not been forecast. If IMC were forecast, no report is necessary.
explanations.B: The following reports (in addition to those that are made at all times) should be made to ATC without a specific request when not in radar contact: 1. Areport when leaving final approach fix in bound on final approach (nonprecision approach) or when leaving the outer marker or fix used in lieu of the outer marker in bound on final approach (precision approach). 2. Position reports over compulsory reporting points. 3. A corrected ETA to a reporting point at any time it becomes apparent that an estimate as previously submitted is in error in excess of 3 min.
explanations.C: because a report should be made to ATC when correcting an ETA anytime a previous ETA is in error in excess of 3 min., not 2 min.

questions.question: For IFR planning purposes, what are the compulsory reporting points when using VOR/DME or VORTAC fixes to define a direct route not on established airways?

answers.B: There are no compulsory reporting points unless advised by ATC.
answers.C: At the changeover points.
answers.A: Fixes selected to define the route.

explanations.A: When using VOR/DME or VORTAC fixes to define a direct route not on an established airway, those fixes selected to define the route automatically become compulsory reporting points (when not in radar contact) for the flight.
explanations.B: because, on a direct flight, the compulsory reporting points are those fixes used to define the route.
explanations.C: because some navigation systems used on direct flights do not require COPs to prevent the loss of navigation guidance, e.g., GPS.

questions.question: When should your transponder be on Mode C while on an IFR flight?

answers.A: Only when ATC requests Mode C.
answers.B: At all times if the equipment has been calibrated, unless requested otherwise by ATC.
answers.C: When passing 12,500 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because Mode C should be turned off, not on, only when directed by ATC.
explanations.B: If your airplane's transponder is equipped to reply on Mode C, it should be on at all times unless deactivation is directed by ATC.
explanations.C: because Mode C is a requirement anytime you are flying above 10,000 ft. MSL, not 12,500 ft. MSL.

questions.question: During a flight, the controller advises "traffic 2 o'clock 5 miles southbound.” The pilot is holding 20° correction for a crosswind from the right. Where should the pilot look for the traffic?

answers.A: 40° to the right of the aircraft's nose.
answers.B: 20° to the right of the aircraft's nose.
answers.C: Straight ahead.

explanations.A: ATC issues traffic advisories in terms of the aircraft's course (i.e., ground track), not its heading. Allowance must be made for drift correction or course change made simultaneously with the radar traffic information. 2 o'clock is approximately 60° to the right of the aircraft's course. Since the pilot is already holding a 20° right-wind correction, (s)he should look only 40° to the right of the aircraft's nose for the traffic.
explanations.B: because 20° to the right of the aircraft's nose is 40° to the right of the aircraft's track, which is between 1 and 2 o'clock.
explanations.C: because straight ahead is 20° (wind correction) to the right of the aircraft's track, which is between 12 and 1 o'clock.

questions.question: During the en route phase of an IFR flight, the pilot is advised "Radar service terminated." What action is appropriate?

answers.A: Set transponder to code 1200.
answers.B: Resume normal position reporting.
answers.C: Activate the IDENT feature of the transponder to re-establish radar contact.

explanations.A: because you should set the transponder to code 1200 (VFR) only when you cancel your IFR flight plan with ATC and you are instructed to squawk VFR.
explanations.B: During the en route phase of an IFR flight, if you are advised of "radar service terminated" or "radar contact lost," you should resume normal position reporting as required when not in radar contact.
explanations.C: because you should activate the IDENT feature of the transponder only upon the request of ATC.

questions.question: What does the ATC term "Radar Contact" signify?

answers.A: Your aircraft has been identified and you will receive separation from all aircraft while in contact with this radar facility.
answers.B: Your aircraft has been identified on the radar display and radar flight-following will be provided until radar identification is terminated.
answers.C: You will be given traffic advisories until advised the service has been terminated or that radar contact has been lost.

explanations.A: because separation from all aircraft occurs only in Class A, B, and C airspace.
explanations.B: The term "radar contact" is used by ATC to inform an aircraft that it is identified on the radar display and that tadar flight following will be provided until radar service is terminated. Reporting over compulsory reporting points is not required when an aircraft is in radar contact.
explanations.C: because traffic advisory service is provided only to the extent possible. Higher-priority duties take precedence, such as controlling or other limitations, volume of traffic, frequency congestion, or controller workload.

questions.question: What is meant when departure control instructs you to "resume own navigation" after you have been vectored to a Victor airway?

answers.A: You should maintain the airway by use of your navigation equipment.
answers.B: Radar service is terminated.
answers.C: You are still in radar contact, but must make position reports.

explanations.A: Assuming you have been vectored to an airway on your intended route of flight, you should maintain your course along the airway by use of your navigation equipment when ATC advises you to resume your own navigation.
explanations.B: because "resume navigation" means that the radar controller will stop vectoring you, not stop observing you.
explanations.C: because position reporting is not required when you are in radar contact with ATC.

questions.question: Upon intercepting the assigned radial, the controller advises you that you are on the airway and to "RESUME OWN NAVIGATION." This phrase means that

answers.A: You are still in radar contact, but must make position reports.
answers.B: Radar services are terminated and you will be responsible for position reports.
answers.C: You are to assume responsibility for your own navigation.

explanations.A: because position reporting is not required when in radar contact.
explanations.B: because "resume navigation" means only that the radar controller is going to stop vectoring you, not stop observing you.
explanations.C: Assuming you have been vectored to an airway on your intended route of flight, you should maintain your course along the airway by use of your navigation equipment when ATC advises you to resume your own navigation.

questions.question: What service is provided by departure control to an IFR flight when operating from an airport within the outer area of Class C airspace?

answers.A: Separation from all aircraft.
answers.B: Position and altitude of all traffic within 2 miles of the IFR pilot's line of flight and altitude.
answers.C: Separation from all IFR aircraft and participating VFR aircraft.

explanations.A: because an IFR flight is provided traffic advisories and conflict resolution with other IFR aircraft and with only participating VFR aircraft within the outer area of Class C airspace.
explanations.B: because ATC provides position and altitude of aircraft that may conflict, not position and altitude of all traffic within 2 NM of your line of flight.
explanations.C: In the outer area of Class C airspace, ATC provides an IFR flight with separation from all IFR aircraft and ipating VFR aircraft. VFR aircraft participation in the outer area is voluntary.

questions.question: If during a VFR practice instrument approach, Radar Approach Control assigns an altitude or heading that will cause you to enter the clouds, what action should be taken?

answers.A: Enter the clouds, since ATC authorization for practice approaches is considered an IFR clearance.
answers.B: Avoid the clouds and inform ATC that altitude/heading will not permit VFR.
answers.C: Abandon the approach.

explanations.A: because pilots may not enter clouds without an IFR clearance.
explanations.B: During a VFR practice instrument approach, you are responsible to comply with basic visual flight tules. Thus, if radar approach assigns an altitude or heading that will cause you to enter the clouds, you must avoid the clouds and inform ATC that that altitude/heading will not permit VFR.
explanations.C: because the pilot need only modify, not abandon the approach, to maintain VFR.

questions.question: You are being vectored to the ILS approach course, but have not been cleared for the approach. It becomes evident that you will pass through the localizer course. What action should be taken?

answers.A: Tur outbound and make a procedure turn.
answers.B: Continue on the assigned heading and query ATC.
answers.C: Start a turn to the inbound heading and inquire if you are cleared for the approach.

explanations.A: because, while you are being radar vectored, you are not authorized to make a procedure turn unless cleared by ATC.
explanations.B: Normally, you will be informed by ATC. when it is necessary to vector across the final approach course for spacing or other reasons. If you have not been cleared for the approach and it becomes evident that you will cross the approach course, you must continue on your assigned heading and question ATC.
explanations.C: because you must maintain your assigned heading, not turn inbound on the final approach course.

questions.question: What is the pilot in command's responsibility when flying a propeller aircraft within 20 miles of the airport of intended landing and ATC requests the pilot to reduce speed to 160? (Pilot complies with speed adjustment.)

answers.A: Reduce TAS to 160 knots and maintain until advised by ATC.
answers.B: Reduce IAS to 160 MPH and maintain until advised by ATC.
answers.C: Reduce IAS to 160 knots and maintain that speed within 10 knots.

explanations.A: because ATC speed restrictions are based on indicated airspeed (IAS), not true airspeed (TAS).
explanations.B: because airspeeds are given in knots, not MPH.
explanations.C: ATC will express all speed adjustments in terms of knots based on indicated airspeed (IAS) in 10-kt. increments below FL 240. When complying with an ATC speed adjustment to reduce to 160, you should reduce IAS to 160 kt. and maintain that speed within 10 kt.

questions.question: For which speed variation should you notify ATC?

answers.A: When the ground speed changes more than 5 knots.
answers.B: When the average true airspeed changes 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater.
answers.C: Any time the ground speed changes 10 MPH.

explanations.A: because ATC should be notified if TAS, not ground speed, varies more than 10 kt., not 5 kt., or 5%, whichever is greater.
explanations.B: There are a number of things a pilot needs to report to ATC without being requested. One is a change in the average TAS at cruising altitude when it varies by 5% or 10 kt. (whichever is greater) from that filed in the flight plan.
explanations.C: because ATC should be notified if TAS, not ground speed, varies more than 10 kt., not 10 MPH, or 5%, whichever is greater.

questions.question: When are you required to establish communications with the tower (Class

answers.A: Immediately after canceling the flight plan.
answers.B: When advised by ARTCC.
answers.C: Before entering Class D airspace.
answers.D: airspace), if you cancel your IFR flight plan 10 miles from the destination?

explanations.A: because, while it is a good operating practice to make an initial call to the tower up to 15 mi. froma Class D airport, it is required only before entering Class D airspace.
explanations.B: because, while ARTCC may advise you to contact the tower when the controller accepts your IFR flight plan cancellation, you are required to contact the tower only prior to entering Class D airspace.
explanations.C: You must establish two-way radio communication with the tower before entering Class D airspace. Thus, if you cancel your IFR flight plan, you must notify the tower of your position and intentions prior to entering Class D airspace.

questions.question: If a control tower and an FSS are located on the same airport, which function is provided by the FSS during those periods when the tower is closed?

answers.A: Automatic closing of the IFR flight plan.
answers.B: Approach control services.
answers.C: Airport Advisory Service.

explanations.A: because the pilot must initiate cancellation of the IFR plan if operating IFR to an airport with no functioning control tower.
explanations.B: because FSS personnel can only issue advisories, not provide ATC services, to pilots.
explanations.C: An FSS located on an airport will provide Local Airport Advisory (LAA) service at that airport when there is no operating control tower. This service provides arriving and departing aircraft with wind direction and speed, favored runway, altimeter setting, pertinent known traffic, pertinent known field condition, and airport taxi routes and traffic patterns. The information is advisory in nature.

questions.question: Which service is provided for IFR arrivals by a FSS located on an airport without a control tower?

answers.A: Automatic closing of the IFR flight plan.
answers.B: Airport advisories.
answers.C: All functions of approach control.

explanations.A: because the pilot must initiate cancellation of the IFR plan if operating IFR to an airport with no operating control tower.
explanations.B: An FSS located on an airport will provide Local Airport Advisory (LAA) service at that airport if there is no operating control tower. This service provides arriving and departing aircraft with wind direction and speed, favored runway, altimeter setting, pertinent known traffic, pertinent known field Condition, and airport taxi routes and traffic patterns. The information is advisory in nature.
explanations.C: because FSS personnel can issue only advisories, not ATC clearances and instructions, to pilots.

questions.question: What does declaring "minimum fuel" to ATC imply?

answers.A: Traffic priority is needed to the destination airport.
answers.B: Emergency handling is required to the nearest useable airport.
answers.C: Merely an advisory that indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.

explanations.A: because priority may be issued when declaring an emergency, not when declaring minimum fuel.
explanations.B: because minimum fuel advisory is not an emergency situation.
explanations.C: You should advise ATC of your minimum fuel status when your fuel supply has reached a state in which, upon reaching your destination, you cannot accept any undue delay. Be aware that this is not an emergency situation, but merely an advisory that indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.

questions.question: You enter a holding pattern (at a fix that is not the same as the approach fix) with an EFC time of 1530. At 1520 you experience complete two-way communications failure. Which procedure should you follow to execute the approach to a landing?

answers.A: Depart the holding fix to arrive at the approach fix as close as possible to the EFC time and complete the approach.
answers.B: Depart the holding fix at the EFC time, and complete the approach.
answers.C: Depart the holding fix at the earliest of the flight planned ETA or the EFC time, and complete the approach.

explanations.A: because you leave for, not arrive at, the approach fix at the EFC time.
explanations.B: If you experience two-way radio communication failure at a holding fix that is not the same as the approach fix, leave the holding fix at the EFC time, and complete the approach.
explanations.C: because the EFC time takes precedence over the flight plan ETA.

questions.question: Which procedure should you follow if you experience two-way communications failure while holding at a holding fix with an EFC time? (The holding fix is not the same as the approach fix.)

answers.A: Depart the holding fix to arrive at the approach fix as close as possible to the EFC time.
answers.B: Depart the holding fix at the EFC time.
answers.C: Proceed immediately to the approach fix and hold until EFC.

explanations.A: because you would leave for, not arrive at, the approach fix at the EFC time.
explanations.B: If you experience two-way radio communication failure at a holding fix that is not the same as the approach fix, leave the holding fix at the EFC time, and complete the approach.
explanations.C: because you should not leave the holding fix to go to the approach fix until the EFC time.

questions.question: You are in IMC and have two-way radio communications failure. If you do not exercise emergency authority, what procedure are you expected to follow?

answers.A: Set transponder to code 7600, continue flight on assigned route and fly at the last assigned altitude or the MEA, whichever is higher.
answers.B: Set transponder to code 7700 for 1 minute, then to 7600, and fly to an area with VFR weather conditions.
answers.C: Set transponder to 7700 and fly to an area where you can let down in VFR conditions.

explanations.A: When you lose two-way radio capability, you should alert ATC by changing your transponder to code 7600. If you experience two-way radio communication failure while in IMC, continue your flight on the assigned route and maintain the last assigned altitude or the MEA, whichever is higher.
explanations.B: because the transponder should be set on 7600 at all times, not 7700 for 1 min., and you must maintain your assigned route and altitude (or MEA). If VMC are encountered, continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
explanations.C: because you should set the transponder to 7600. While in IMC, you must maintain your assigned route and altitude (or MEA).

questions.question: What altitude and route should be used if you are flying in IMC and have two-way radio communications failure?

answers.A: Continue on the route specified in your clearance, fly at an altitude that is the highest of last assigned altitude, altitude ATC has informed you to expect, or the MEA.
answers.B: Fly direct to an area that has been forecast to have VFR conditions, fly at an altitude that is at least 1,000 feet above the highest obstacles along the route.
answers.C: Descend to MEA and, if clear of clouds, proceed to the nearest appropriate airport. If not clear of clouds, maintain the highest of the MEA's along the clearance route.

explanations.A: When you lose two-way radio communication in IMC, continue the flight by the route assigned by the last ATC clearance, by the route that ATC has advised may be expected to be assigned, or by the flight plan. Use the highest of the altitude assigned in the last ATC clearance, the MEA, or the flight level ATC may be expected to assign.
explanations.B: because you should continue the assigned route.
explanations.C: because you should use the highest of the altitude assigned, the altitude expected to be assigned, or MEA.

questions.question: Which procedure should you follow if, during an IFR flight in VFR conditions, you have two-way radio communications failure?

answers.A: Continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
answers.B: Continue the flight at assigned altitude and route, start approach at your ETA, or, if late, start approach upon arrival.
answers.C: Land at the nearest airport that has VFR conditions.

explanations.A: If a radio failure occurs during an IFR flight in VFR conditions or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, the pilot should continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
explanations.B: because this procedure applies only if you are in instrument meteorological conditions, not VFR.
explanations.C: because the pilot retains the prerogative of exercising good judgment and is not required to land at an unauthorized airport or an airport unsuitable for the type of aircraft flown, nor is the pilot required to land only minutes short of the destination.

questions.question: While flying on an IFR flight plan, you experience two-way communications radio failure while in VFR conditions. In this situation, you should continue your flight under

answers.A: VER and land as soon as practicable.
answers.B: IFR and maintain the last assigned route and altitude to your flight plan destination.
answers.C: VFR and proceed to your flight plan destination.

explanations.A: If a radio failure occurs during an IFR flight in VFR conditions or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, the pilot should continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
explanations.B: because this procedure applies only if you are in instrument meteorological conditions, not VFR.
explanations.C: because you should land as soon as practicable rather than proceeding to your flight plan destination.

questions.question: What action should you take if your DME fails at FL 240?

answers.A: Advise ATC of the failure and land at the nearest available airport where repairs can be made.
answers.B: Notify ATC that it will be necessary for you to go to a lower altitude, since your DME has failed.
answers.C: Notify ATC of the failure and continue to the next airport of intended landing where repairs can be made.

explanations.A: because you can continue to your destination, not the nearest airport, and have repairs made there.
explanations.B: because you need not descend to a lower altitude after you notify ATC. You may continue to operate at or above FL 240.
explanations.C: When required DME fails at or above FL 240, the pilot should notify ATC immediately and may continue operations at and above FL 240 to the next airport of intended landing at which repairs or replacement of the equipment can be made.

questions.question: What is the procedure when the DME malfunctions at or above 24,000 feet MSL?

answers.A: Notify ATC immediately and request an altitude below 24,000 feet.
answers.B: Continue to your destination in VFR conditions and report the malfunction.
answers.C: After immediately notifying ATC, you may continue to the next airport of intended landing where repairs can be made.

explanations.A: because there is no need to descend to a lower altitude. You may continue to your destination and have repairs made there.
explanations.B: because you may continue your flight as normal, even under IFR, and make repairs at your destination.
explanations.C: When required DME fails at or above FL 240, the pilot should notify ATC immediately and may continue operations at and above FL 240 to the next airport of intended landing at which repairs or replacement of the equipment can be made.

questions.question: What action should you take if your No. 1 VOR receiver malfunctions while operating in controlled airspace under IFR? Your aircraft is equipped with two VOR receivers. The No. 1 receiver has Omni/Localizer/Glide Slope capability, and the No. 2 receiver has only VOR/Localizer capability.

answers.A: Report the malfunction immediately to ATC.
answers.B: Continue the flight as cleared; no report is required.
answers.C: Continue the approach and request a VOR or NDB approach.

explanations.A: When operating under IFR in controlled airspace, you must immediately report to ATC as soon as practical any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight. Each report should include the following: 1. Aircraft identification, 2. Equipment affected, 3. Degree to which the capability of the pilot to operate under IFR inthe ATC system is impaired, and 4. Nature and extent of assistance desired from ATC.
explanations.B: because a report to ATC is required.
explanations.C: because ATC will know that you need a VOR or NDB approach if you report the ILS receiver inoperative.

questions.question: Which types of airspace are depicted on the En Route Low Altitude Chart?

answers.A: Class D, Class C, Class B, Class E, and special use airspace.
answers.B: Class A, special use airspace, Class D, and Class E.
answers.C: Special use airspace, Class E, Class D, Class A, Class B, and Class C.

explanations.A: En Route Low Altitude Charts depict Class B, Class C, Class D, Class E, and special-use airspace up to but not including 18,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.B: because Class A airspace is airspace above FL 180. It is not depicted on En Route Low-Altitude Charts.
explanations.C: because Class A airspace is not depicted on En Route Low-Altitude Charts.

questions.question: Class G airspace is that airspace where

answers.A: ATC does not control air traffic.
answers.B: ATC controls only IFR flights.
answers.C: the minimum visibility for VFR flight is 3 miles.

explanations.A: Class G airspace is that portion of the airspace that has not been designated as Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class E. In Class G airspace, ATC has neither the authority nor the responsibility for exercising control over air traffic in any weather condition.
explanations.B: because ATC does not control IFR flight in Class G airspace.
explanations.C: because the minimum visibility for VFR flight is 1 SM, not 3 SM, in Class G airspace during the day when below 10,000 ft. MSL.

questions.question: Which airspace is defined as a transition area when designated in Conjunction with an airport which has a prescribed IAP?

answers.A: The Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet or more above the surface and terminating at the base of the overlying controlled airspace.
answers.B: That Class D airspace extending from the surface and terminating at the base of the continental control area.
answers.C: The Class C airspace extending from the surface to 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, where designated.

explanations.A: Transition areas are Class E airspace that extends upward from 700 ft. or more above the surface when designated in conjunction with an airport for which an instrument approach procedure (IAP) has been prescribed. Class E airspace extends up to but does not include 18,000 ft. MSL, i-e., the base of Class A airspace.
explanations.B: because a transition area is classified as Class E, not Class D, airspace.
explanations.C: because transition areas are Class E, not Class C, airspace and extend upward from, not to, 700 ft.

questions.question: What are the vertical limits of a transition area that is designated in Conjunction with an airport having a prescribed IAP?

answers.A: Surface to 700 feet AGL.
answers.B: 1,200 feet AGL to the base of the overlying controlled airspace.
answers.C: 700 feet AGL or more to the base of the overlying controlled airspace.

explanations.A: because a transition area begins at 700 ft. AGL, not the surface, when it is designated in conjunction with an lAP.
explanations.B: because transition areas begin at 1,200 ft. AGL when designated in conjunction with an airway route structure or segment, not with an airport with an instrument approach.
explanations.C: Transition areas are controlled airspace extending upward from 700 ft. or more above the surface when designated in conjunction with an airport for which an instrument approach procedure has been prescribed. Transition areas terminate at the base of overlying controlled airspace (i.e., Class A airspace).

questions.question: The vertical extent of the Class A airspace throughout the conterminous U.S. extends from

answers.A: 18,000 feet to and including FL 450.
answers.B: 18,000 feet to and including FL 600.
answers.C: 12,500 feet to and including FL 600.

explanations.A: because FL 450 is the top of the jet routes.
explanations.B: Class A airspace extends from 18,000 ft. MSL to and including FL 600.
