explanations.C: because the base of Class A airspace is 18,000 ft. MSL, not 12,500 ft. MSL.

questions.question: MOAs are established to

answers.A: prohibit all civil aircraft because of hazardous or secret activities.
answers.B: separate certain military activities from IFR traffic.
answers.C: restrict civil aircraft during periods of high-density training activities.

explanations.A: because a prohibited area, not an MOA, prohibits all aircraft for reasons of national security.
explanations.B: MOAs consist of airspace of defined vertical and lateral limits established for the purpose of separating certain military training activities from IFR traffic. When an MOA is in use, nonparticipating IFR traffic may be cleared to fly through if ATC can provide IFR separation. Otherwise, ATC will reroute or restrict nonparticipating IFR traffic.
explanations.C: because a restricted area, not an MOA, is used to restrict aircraft during certain periods.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What is the floor of Class E airspace when designated in Conjunction with an airway?

answers.A: 700 feet AGL.
answers.B: 1,200 feet AGL.
answers.C: 1,500 feet AGL.

explanations.A: because 700 ft. AGL is the floor of Class E airspace when designated in conjunction with an airport which has an approved IAP, not with an airway.
explanations.B: The floor of Class E airspace when designated in conjunction with an airway is 1,200 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: because the floor of Class E airspace when designated in conjunction with an airway is 1,200 ft. AGL, not 1,500 ft. AGL.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) Which altitude is the normal upper limit for Class D airspace?

answers.A: 1,000 feet AGL.
answers.B: 2,500 feet AGL.
answers.C: 4,000 feet AGL.

explanations.A: because 1,000 ft. AGL is the normal traffic pattern altitude for piston aircraft, not the ceiling of Class
explanations.B: Class D airspace extends from the surface up to and including 2,500 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: because 4,000 ft. AGL is the upper limit for Class C, not Class D, airspace.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What is the floor of Class E airspace when designated in Conjunction with an airport which has an approved IAP?

answers.A: 500 feet AGL.
answers.B: 700 feet AGL.
answers.C: 1,200 feet AGL.

explanations.A: because 500 ft. AGL is not an altitude which defines airspace.
explanations.B: The floor of Class E airspace when designated in conjunction with an airport which has an approved IAP is 700 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: because 1,200 ft. AGL is the floor of Class E airspace when designated in conjunction with an airway, not an approved IAP.

questions.question: New Airspace Classification FL eo MSL. 18,000 | r4s00 me ‘ cusse - Figure 93 cuss

answers.B: 18,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: 60,000 feet MSL.
answers.A: 109. (Refer to figure 93.) Which altitude is the upper limit for Class A airspace? A 14,500 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because 14,500 ft. MSL is the upper limit for Class G, not Class A, airspace.
explanations.B: because 18,000 ft. MSL is the floor, not the upper limit, of Class A airspace.
explanations.C: Class A airspace extends from 18,000 ft. MSL to and including 60,000 ft. MSL (i.e., FL 600).

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What is the maximum altitude that Class G airspace will exist? (Does not include airspace less than 1,500 feet AGL.)

answers.A: 18,000 feet MSL.
answers.B: 14,500 feet MSL.
answers.C: 14,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because 18,000 ft. MSL is the floor of Class A airspace, not the maximum altitude at which Class G airspace will exist.
explanations.B: The maximum altitude at which Class G airspace will exist (not including airspace less than 1,500 ft. AGL) is 14,500 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: because 14,000 ft. MSL is not an altitude which defines airspace.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What is generally the maximum altitude for Class B airspace?

answers.A: 4,000 feet MSL.
answers.B: 10,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: 14,500 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because 4,000 ft. MSL is not an altitude which defines airspace.
explanations.B: The maximum altitude for Class B airspace will generally be 10,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: because 14,500 ft. MSL is the maximum altitude at which Class G, not Class B, airspace will exist.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What are the normal lateral limits for Class D airspace?

answers.A: 8NM.
answers.B: 5NM.
answers.C: 4NM.

explanations.A: because 8 NM is not a defined lateral limit of any class of airspace surface area.
explanations.B: because 5 NM defines the lateral limit of
explanations.C: The normal lateral limit for Class D airspace is approximately 4 NM.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 93.) What is the floor of Class A airspace?

answers.A: 10,000 feet MSL.
answers.B: 14,500 feet MSL.
answers.C: 18,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because 10,000 ft. MSL is the floor of controlled airspace in which a transponder with altitude encoding capability is required, not the floor of Class A airspace.
explanations.B: because 14,500 ft. MSL is a floor of Class E, not Class A, airspace.
explanations.C: Class A airspace extends from 18,000 ft. MSL up to, and including, FL 600.

questions.question: What minimum aircraft equipment is required for operation within Class C airspace?

answers.A: Two-way communications and Mode C transponder.
answers.B: Two-way communications.
answers.C: Transponder and DME.

explanations.A: In Class C airspace, the equipment requirement is an operating two-way communications radio and
explanations.B: because a Mode C transponder is also required.
explanations.C: because two-way communications and Mode C capability are also required and DME is not required.

questions.question: What conditions are necessary before ATC can authorize a visual approach?

answers.A: You must have the preceding aircraft in sight, and be able to remain in VFR weather conditions.
answers.B: You must have the airport in sight or the preceding aircraft in sight, and be able to proceed to, and land in IFR conditions.
answers.C: You must have the airport in sight or a preceding aircraft to be followed, and be able to proceed to the airport in VFR conditions.

explanations.A: because you can have the airport in sight instead of having the preceding aircraft in sight.
explanations.B: because you must be able to land in VFR, not IFR, conditions.
explanations.C: ATC may authorize airplanes to conduct visual approaches to an airport or to follow another airplane when flight to and landing at the airport can be accomplished in VFR weather. You must have the airport or preceding aircraft in sight before the clearance is issued.

questions.question: What are the main differences between a visual approach and a contact approach?

answers.A: The pilot must request a contact approach; the pilot may be assigned a visual approach and higher weather minimums must exist
answers.B: The pilot must request a visual approach and report having the field in sight, ATC may assign a contact approach if VFR conditions exist.
answers.C: Anytime the pilot reports the field in sight, ATC may clear the pilot for a contact approach; for a visual approach, the pilot must advise that the approach can be made under VFR conditions.

explanations.A: Contact approaches can be issued only upon pilot request, but visual approaches may be assigned by ATC. Visual approaches require VFR conditions. Contact approaches require 1 SM flight visibility and the ability to remain clear of clouds.
explanations.B: because ATC may assign visual approaches without pilot request, and ATC cannot issue a contact approach clearance without the pilot's request.
explanations.C: because ATC cannot issue a contact approach clearance without the pilot's request.

questions.question: A contact approach is an approach procedure that may be used

answers.A: inlieu of conducting a SIAP.
answers.B: if assigned by ATC and will facilitate the approach.
answers.C: in lieu of a visual approach.

explanations.A: A contact approach may be requested by the pilot if there is 1 SM flight visibility and the pilot can operate clear of clouds. It is an alternative to a standard instrument approach procedure (SIAP).
explanations.B: because ATC cannot assign a contact approach; pilots must request them.
explanations.C: because using a contact approach is not necessary if a visual approach is possible.

questions.question: You arrive at your destination airport on an IFR flight plan. Whichis a prerequisite condition for the performance of a contact approach?

answers.A: Aground visibility of at least 2 SM.
answers.B: A flight visibility of at least 1/2 NM.
answers.C: Clear of clouds and at least 1 SM flight visibility.

explanations.A: because the flight, not ground, visibility must be at least 1 SM, not 2 SM.
explanations.B: because the flight visibility must be at least 1 SM, not 1/2 NM.
explanations.C: A contact approach may be requested by the pilot if there is 1 SM flight visibility and the pilot can operate clear of clouds.

questions.question: What are the requirements for a contact approach to an airport that has an approved IAP, if the pilot is on an instrument flight plan and clear of clouds?

answers.A: The controller must determine that the pilot can see the airport at the altitude flown and can remain clear of clouds.
answers.B: The pilot must agree to the approach when given by ATC and the controller must have determined that the visibility was at least 1 mile and be reasonably sure the pilot can remain clear of clouds.
answers.C: The pilot must request the approach, have at least 1-mile visibility, and be reasonably sure of remaining clear of clouds.

explanations.A: because the pilot must deter mine whether (s)he can reasonably expect to continue to the airport in at least 1 SM flight visibility and clear of clouds, not the controller.
explanations.B: because the pilot must request a contact approach; ATC does not solicit or assign contact approaches.
explanations.C: Pilots operating in accordance with an IFR flight plan, provided they are clear of clouds, have at least 1 SM flight visi and can reasonably expect to continue to the destination airport in those conditions, may request ATC authorization for a contact approach.

questions.question: Whenis radar service terminated during a visual approach?

answers.A: Automatically when ATC instructs the pilot to contact the tower.
answers.B: Immediately upon acceptance of the approach by the pilot.
answers.C: When ATC advises, "Radar service terminated; resume own. navigation."

explanations.A: During a visual approach, radar service is automatically terminated without advising the pilot once the pilot has been instructed to contact the tower or change to advisory frequency.
explanations.B: because approach clearance is given well before radar service is terminated.
explanations.C: because "resume own navigation" is generally an en route instruction and is not applicable to approaches.

questions.question: When may you obtain a contact approach?

answers.A: ATC may assign a contact approach if VFR conditions exist or you report the runway in sight and are clear of clouds.
answers.B: ATC may assign a contact approach if you are below the clouds and the visibility is at least 1 mile.
answers.C: ATC will assign a contact approach only upon request if the reported visibility is at least 1 mile.

explanations.A: because ATC may assign a visual, not a contact, approach if VFR weather conditions exist. ATC may not assign a contact approach.
explanations.B: because ATC may not assign a contact approach. The pilot must request one.
explanations.C: ATC will assign a contact approach only upon pilot request if the pilot is operating clear of clouds, has at least 1 SM flight visibility, and expects to reach the airport and land in those conditions.

questions.question: What are the main differences between the SDF and the localizer of an ILS?

answers.A: The useable off-course indications are limited to 35° for the localizer and up to 90° for the SDF.
answers.B: The SDF course may not be aligned with the runway and the course may be wider.
answers.C: The course width for the localizer will always be 5° while the SDF course will be between 6° and 12°.

explanations.A: because the off-course indications are limited to 35° for both types of approach.
explanations.B: The approach techniques and procedures. used in performance of an SDF instrument approach are essentially identical to those employed to execute a standard localizer approach, except that the SDF course may not be aligned with the runway and the course may be wider, resulting in less precision.
explanations.C: because the course width for the localizer is usually between 3° and 6°, and SDF is either 6° or 12° (not between).

questions.question: Whatis the difference between a Localizer-Type Directional Aid (LDA) and the ILS localizer?

answers.A: The LDA is not aligned with the runway.
answers.B: The LDA uses a course width of 6° or 12°, while an ILS uses only bie
answers.C: The LDA signal is generated from a VOR-type facility and has no glide slope.

explanations.A: The localizer-type directional aid (LDA) is similar to a localizer but is not part of a complete ILS, and it is not aligned with the runway.
explanations.B: because the LDA uses the same course width as the ILS, i.e., 3° to 6°. The SDF uses 6° or 12°.
explanations.C: because the LDA is a localizer-type, not VOR-type, signal.

questions.question: How wide is an SDF course?

answers.B: Either 6° or 12°.
answers.C: Varies from 5° to 10°.
answers.A: Either 3° or 6°.

explanations.A: because either 3° or 6° is half the course width of an SDF.
explanations.B: The simplified directional facility (SDF) signal is fixed at either 6° or 12° as necessary to provide maximum flyability and optimum course quality.
explanations.C: because a course 5° to 10° wide does not relate to ILS, LDA, or SDF.

questions.question: What is a difference between an SDF and an LDA facility?

answers.B: The SDF course has no glide slope guidance while the LDA does.
answers.C: The SDF has no marker beacons while the LDA has at least an OM.
answers.A: The SDF course width is either 6° or 12° while the LDA course width is approximately 5°.

explanations.A: The localizer-type directional aid (LDA) is of comparable utility and accuracy as a localizer but is not part of
explanations.B: because only some LDA approaches provide glide slope guidance, but this is not a requirement of the system.
explanations.C: because both SDF and LDA may have marker beacons.

questions.question: What does the Runway Visual Range (RVR) value, depicted on certain straight-in IAP Charts, represent?

answers.A: The slant range distance the pilot can see down the runway while crossing the threshold on glide slope.
answers.B: The horizontal distance a pilot should see when looking down the runway from a moving aircraft.
answers.C: The slant visual range a pilot should see down the final approach and during landing.

explanations.A: because RVR is the horizontal, not slant Tange, distance the pilot will see down the runway.
explanations.B: RVR is an instrumentally derived value that represents the horizontal distance the pilot will see down the runway from the approach end. It is based on the measurement of a transmissometer near the touchdown point of the instrument runway and is reported in hundreds of feet.
explanations.C: because RVR is the horizontal, not slant range, distance the pilot will see down the runway, not the final approach.

questions.question: The RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are published in an IAP, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway at the time. Which of the following would apply?

answers.A: RVR minimums which are specified in the procedure should be converted and applied as ground visibility.
answers.B: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing the runway has an operative HIRL system.
answers.C: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing all other components of the ILS system are operative.

explanations.A: If RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are prescribed in an instrument approach procedure, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway of intended operation, the RVR minimum shall be converted to ground visibility and shall be the visibility minimum for takeoff or landing on that runway.
explanations.B: because RVR minimums must be converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.
explanations.C: because RVR minimums must be converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.

questions.question: RVR minimums for landing are prescribed in an IAP, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the intended runway at the time. Which of the following would be an operational consideration?

answers.A: RVR minimums which are specified in the procedures should be converted and applied as ground visibility.
answers.B: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing the runway has an operative HIRL system.
answers.C: RVR minimums may be disregarded, providing all other components of the ILS system are operative.

explanations.A: If RVR minimums for takeoff or landing are prescribed in an instrument approach procedure, but RVR is inoperative and cannot be reported for the runway of intended operation, the RVR minimum shall be converted to ground visibility and shall be the visibility minimum for takeoff or landing on that runway.
explanations.B: because RVR minimums must be converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.
explanations.C: because RVR minimums must be converted to ground visibility, not disregarded.

questions.question: If the RVR equipment is inoperative for an IAP that requires a visibility of 2400 RVR, how should the pilot expect the visibility requirement to be reported in lieu of the published RVR?

answers.A: As a slant range visibility of 2,400 feet.
answers.B: As an RVR of 2,400 feet.
answers.C: As a ground visibility of % SM.

explanations.A: because slant range visibility is not used for approach minimums. Slant range visibility refers to the forward visibility seen by the pilot, while published approach minimums use runway visual range (RVR) or ground visibility.
explanations.B: because RVR cannot be reported if the RVR equipment is inoperative. It must be converted to ground visibility.
explanations.C: An RVR of 2,400 feet converts to 1/2 statute mile ground visibility when RVR equipment is unavailable. Therefore, the visibility requirement is reported as ground visibility of 1/2 SM.

questions.question: If the RVR is not reported, what meteorological value should you substitute for 2400 RVR?

answers.A: Aground visibility of % NM.
answers.B: Asslant range visibility of 2,400 feet for the final approach segment of the published approach procedure.
answers.C: A ground visibility of ¥% SM.

explanations.A: because RVR is converted into statute, not nautical, miles.
explanations.B: because when RVR is not reported, ground visibility, not slant range visibility on approach, is substituted.
explanations.C: Refer to Legend 11 for a chart of RVR\ visibility comparable values. An RVR of 2,400 ft. may be converted to % SM visibility when the RVR is not reported.

questions.question: If an early missed approach is initiated before reaching the MAP, the following procedure should be used unless otherwise cleared by ATC.

answers.A: Proceed to the missed approach point at or above the MDA or DH before executing a turning maneuver.
answers.B: Begin a climbing turn immediately and follow missed approach procedures.
answers.C: Maintain altitude and continue past MAP for 1 minute or 1 mile whichever occurs first.

explanations.A: When an early missed approach is executed, the pilot should, unless otherwise directed by ATC, fly the IAP as specified on the approach plate to the missed approach point at or above the MDA or DH before executing a turning maneuver.
explanations.B: because one should continue to the MAP before executing any turns.
explanations.C: because one need only continue to, not past, the MAP.

questions.question: If the pilot loses visual reference while circling to land from an instrument approach and ATC radar service is not available, the missed approach action should be to

answers.A: execute a climbing turn to parallel the published final approach course and climb to the initial approach altitude.
answers.B: climb to the published circling minimums then proceed direct to the final approach fix.
answers.C: make a climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue the turn until established on the missed approach course.

explanations.A: because the climbing turn should be toward the landing runway; then the pilot should execute the published missed approach procedures.
explanations.B: because there should be a climbing turn toward the landing runway.
explanations.C: If visual reference is lost while circling to land, the missed approach specified for that particular procedure must be followed. To become established on the prescribed missed approach course, the pilot should make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and continue the turn until established on the missed approach course.

questions.question: If all ILS components are operating and the re established, the missed approach should be it ed visual references are not jated upon

answers.A: arrival at the DH on the glide slope.
answers.B: arrival at the middle marker.
answers.C: expiration of the time listed on the approach chart for missed approach.

explanations.A: The missed approach procedure should be executed upon arrival at the decision height (DH) on the glide slope if the visual reference requirements are not met. Thus, DH onan ILS is the MAP.
explanations.B: because the DH rather than the middle marker is the MAP.
explanations.C: because the time listed on the approach chart for missed approaches is used in conjunction with the localizer for a timed approach if the glide slope fails during the ILS approach; i.e., itis not the primary indicator.

questions.question: if during an ILS approach in IFR conditions, the approach lights are not visible upon arrival at the DH, the pilot is

answers.A: required to immediately execute the missed approach procedure.
answers.B: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the localizer MDA.
answers.C: permitted to continue the approach to the approach threshold of the ILS runway.

explanations.A: The missed approach procedure should be executed upon arrival at the decision height (DH) on the glide slope if the visual reference requirements are not met. Thus, the DH onan ILS is the MAP.
explanations.B: because the DH is the MAP on anILS, which is lower than the localizer MDA.
explanations.C: because the pilot may continue the approach below the DH only if the required visual references (e.g., approach lights) are established.

questions.question: How does a pilot determine if DME is available on an ILS/LOC?

answers.B: LOC\DME are indicated on en route low altitude frequency box.
answers.C: LOC\DME frequencies available in the Airman's Information Manual.
answers.A: IAP indicate DME\TACAN channel in LOC frequency box.

explanations.A: If DME is available on an ILS or localizer approach, the DME/TACAN channel will be indicated in the localizer frequency box on the approach plate.
explanations.B: because LOC/DME frequencies are available on approach plates, not en route charts.
explanations.C: because the A/M gives general information on navigation systems, not specific frequencies.

questions.question: Approximately what height is the glide slope centerline at the MM of a typical ILS?

answers.A: 100 feet.
answers.B: 200 feet.
answers.C: 300 feet.

explanations.A: because the glide slope centerline at the inner, not middle, marker on a Category II ILS is at 100 ft. above the TDZE.
explanations.B: The ILS glide path projection angle is normally 3° above horizontal so it intersects the middle marker (MM) at 200 ft. and the outer marker (OM) at about 1,400 ft. above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE).
explanations.C: because the glide slope centerline at the MM is usually 200 ft. AGL, not 300 ft.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 139 and 140.) Which displacement from the localizer and Glide slope at the 1.9 NM point is indicated?

answers.B: 710 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 140 feet above the glide slope.
answers.C: 430 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 28 feet above the glide slope.
answers.A: 710 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 140 feet below the glide slope.

explanations.A: because the airplane is to the right, not left, of the localizer and above, not below, the glide slope.
explanations.B: The airplane is to the right of the localizer and above the glide slope each by 2 dots at 1.9 NM out. Per Fig. 139, 2 dots at 1.9 NM are 140 ft. above the glide slope and 710 ft. to the right of the localizer.
explanations.C: because the 430-ft. and 28-ft. deviations are at 1,300 ft, not 1.9 NM.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 139 and 141.) Which displacement from the localizer centerline and glide slope at the 1,300-foot point from the runway is indicated?

answers.B: 28 feet above the glide slope and approximately 250 feet to the left of the runway centerline.
answers.C: 21 feet above the glide slope and approximately 320 feet to the left of the runway centerline.
answers.A: 21 feet below the glide slope and approximately 320 feet to the fight of the runway centerline.

explanations.A: because the airplane is above, not below, the glide slope, and to the left, not right, of the localizer.
explanations.B: because 28 ft. is 2 dots, and 250 ft. is less than 1% dots.
explanations.C: The airplane is above the glide slope and to the left of the localizer by 1% dots each at 1,300 ft. out. Per extrapolation and Fig. 139, this displacement is 21 ft. above the glide slope and about 320 ft. to the left of the localizer.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 139 and 142.) Which displacement from the localizer and glide slope at the outer marker is indicated?

answers.A: 1,550 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 210 feet below the glide slope.
answers.B: 1,550 feet to the right of the localizer centerline and 210 feet above the glide slope.
answers.C: 775 feet to the left of the localizer centerline and 420 feet below the glide slope.

explanations.A: The airplane is below the glide slope by 1 dot and to the left of the localizer by 2 dots at the outer marker. Per Fig. 139, 1 dot on the glide slope is 210 ft. at the outer marker (OM), and 2 dots on the localizer is 1,550 ft.
explanations.B: because the airplane is to the left, not right, of the localizer, and below, not above, the glide slope.
explanations.C: because at the OM 775 ft. is 1 dot on the localizer, not the glide slope, and 420 ft. is 2 dots on the glide slope, not the localizer.

questions.question: Which range facility associated with the ILS is identified by the last two letters of the localizer identification group?

answers.A: Inner marker.
answers.B: Outer marker.
answers.C: Middle compass locator.

explanations.A: because marker beacons are not identified by letters when they are not compass locators.
explanations.B: because marker beacons are not identified by letters when they are not compass locators.
explanations.C: Compass locators transmit two-letter identification groups. The outer locator transmits the first two letters of the localizer identification group, and the middle locator transmits the last two letters of the localizer identification group.

questions.question: Which indications will a pilot receive where an IM is installed on a front course ILS approach?

answers.A: One dot per second and a steady amber light.
answers.B: Six dots per second and a flashing white light.
answers.C: Alternate dashes and a blue light.

explanations.A: because the middle marker, not the inner marker, has an amber light with 95 dot-dash combinations per minute.
explanations.B: The inner marker (IM) indicates a point at which an airplane is at a designated decision height (DH) on the glide slope between the middle marker and the landing threshold. It is identified with continuous dots keyed at the rate of 6 dots per second and a white marker beacon.
explanations.C: because the outer marker, not the inner marker, has continuous, not alternate, dashes and a blue light.

questions.question: Which range facility associated with the ILS can be identified by a two-letter coded signal?

answers.A: Middle marker.
answers.B: Outer marker.
answers.C: Compass locator.

explanations.A: because marker beacons are not identified by letters when they are not a compass locator.
explanations.B: because marker beacons are not identified by letters when they are not a compass locator.
explanations.C: Each compass locator (middle and outer) is identified by a two-letter coded signal.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Parallel ILS approaches?

answers.A: Parallel ILS approach runway centerlines are separated by at least 4,300 feet and standard IFR separation is provided on the adjacent runway.
answers.B: Parallel ILS approaches provide aircraft a minimum of 1% miles radar separation between successive aircraft on the adjacent localizer course.
answers.C: Landing minimums to the adjacent runway will be higher than the minimums to the primary runway, but will normally be lower than the published circling minimums.

explanations.A: because parallel approach runway centerlines are separated by at least 4,300 ft., a minimum of 2 mi. diagonal radar separation is between successive aircraft, not standard IFR separation.
explanations.B: Aircraft are afforded a minimum of 1% mi. radar separation diagonally between successive aircraft on the adjacent localizer course and a minimum 2% mi. radar separation from aircraft on the same final approach during parallel ILS operations.
explanations.C: because a side-step maneuver, not a parallel ILS approach, will have landing minimums to the adjacent runway which are higher than the minimums to the primary runway, but these minimums will normally be lower than the published circling minimums.

questions.question: Which pilot action is appropriate if more than one component of an ILS is unusable?

answers.A: Use the highest minimum required by any single component that is unusable.
answers.B: Request another approach appropriate to the equipment that is useable.
answers.C: Raise the minimums a total of that required by each component that is unusable.

explanations.A: Landing minimums published on instrument approach procedure charts are based upon full operation of all components and the use of visual aids associated with the particular instrument approach chart. Higher visibility minimums are required with inoperative components or visual aids as specified in FAA tables. If more than one component is inoperative, each minimum is raised to the highest minimum required by any single component that is inoperative.
explanations.B: because an ILS can be used with some components inoperative. Those inoperative components would increase the approach minimums, but you would not need to request another approach appropriate to the equipment that is usable.
explanations.C: because it is not cumulative; you need only use the highest minimum required as a result of any one component's being unusable.

questions.question: Which substitution is permitted when an ILS component is inoperative?

answers.A: Acompass locator or precision radar may be substituted for the ILS outer or middle marker.
answers.B: ADF or VOR bearings which cross either the outer or middle marker sites may be substituted for these markers.
answers.C: DME, when located at the localizer antenna site, should be ‘substituted for the outer or middle marker.

explanations.A: A compass locator or precision radar may be substituted for an inoperative outer or middle marker. Compass locators, precision radar, DME, VOR, or nondirectional fixes authorized in the standard instrument approach or surveillance radar may be substituted for an inoperative outer marker.
explanations.B: because ADF and VOR bearings can be substituted for the outer marker but not the middle marker.
explanations.C: because DME can be substituted for the outer marker but not the middle marker.

questions.question: What facilities, if any, may be substituted for an inoperative middle marker during an ILS approach without affecting the straight-in minimums?

answers.B: Substitution not necessary, minimums do not change.
answers.C: Compass locator, PAR, and ASR.
answers.A: ASR.

explanations.A: because no substitution is necessary for an inoperative MM since the landing minimums do not change.
explanations.B: Refer to Legend 22, Inoperative Components or Visual Aids Table. Note that an inoperative middle marker (MM) is not listed as an inoperative ILS component that would require an increase in the visibility minimum. While a compass locator or PAR may be substituted for an inoperative MM, no substitution is necessary since the landing minimums are not changed.
explanations.C: because no substitution is necessary for an inoperative MM since the landing minimums do not change.

questions.question: Which of these facilities may be substituted for an MM during a complete ILS. IAP?

answers.A: Surveillance and precision radar.
answers.B: Compass locator and precision radar.
answers.C: AVORIDME fix.

explanations.A: because airport surveillance radar may be substituted for the outer marker but not the middle marker.
explanations.B: Compass locators or precision radar may be substituted for the outer or middle marker.
explanations.C: because a VOR/DME fix authorized in the standard instrument approach may only be substituted for the outer marker.

questions.question: When installed with the ILS and specified in the approach procedures, DME may be used

answers.B: in lieu of visibility requirements.
answers.C: to determine distance from TDZ.
answers.A: inlieu of the OM.

explanations.A: When installed with the ILS and specified in the approach procedure, DME may be used in lieu of the outer marker (OM).
explanations.B: because DME has no effect on visibility requirements.
explanations.C: because touchdown zone (TDZ) is the first 3,000 ft. of the runway, not a specific point.

questions.question: Which substitution is appropriate during an ILS approach?

answers.A: AVOR radial crossing the outer marker site may be substituted for the outer marker.
answers.B: LOC minimums should be substituted for ILS minimums whenever the glide slope becomes inoperative.
answers.C: DME, when located at the localizer antenna site, should be substituted for either the outer or middle marker.

explanations.A: because a VOR radial must be authorized in the standard approach procedure to be used as a ‘substitute.
explanations.B: When the glide slope becomes inoperative during an ILS approach, the approach can be conducted as a localizer approach and the LOC minimums apply.
explanations.C: because DME can be substituted for the outer marker, but not the middle marker.

questions.question: Immediately after passing the final approach fix in bound during an ILS approach in IFR conditions, the glide slope warning flag appears. The pilot is

answers.A: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the DH.
answers.B: permitted to continue the approach and descend to the localizer MDA.
answers.C: required to immediately begin the prescribed missed approach procedure.

explanations.A: because, once the glide slope is inoperative, the localizer may be used only for a nonprecision approach, which uses MDA, not DH.
explanations.B: When the glide slope fails, the approach can continue as a nonprecision localizer approach. Accordingly, if the glide slope fails on an ILS approach, the pilot may switch to the localizer approach and descend to the localizer MDA. (minimum descent altitude).
explanations.C: because one should execute the missed approach procedure only after reaching the missed approach point.

questions.question: Apilot is making an ILS approach and is past the OM to a runway which has a VASI. What action should the pilot take if an electronic glide slope malfunction occurs and the pilot has the VASI in sight?

answers.A: The pilot should inform ATC of the malfunction and then descend immediately to the localizer DH and make a localizer approach.
answers.B: The pilot may continue the approach and use the VASI glide slope in place of the electronic glide slope.
answers.C: The pilot must request an LOC approach, and may descend below the VASI at the pilot's discretion.

explanations.A: because, once the pilot has the necessary visual references, the approach may be continued visually.
explanations.B: Once the necessary specified visual requirements, e.g., the VASI, are attained for the intended tunway, the pilot may continue the approach and use the VAS in place of the electronic glide slope.
explanations.C: because, once the pilot has the necessary visual references, the approach may be continued visually. Descent below the VASI glide path shall occur only when necessary for a safe landing.

questions.question: The rate of descent on the glide slope is dependent upon

answers.A: true airspeed.
answers.B: calibrated airspeed.
answers.C: ground speed.

explanations.A: because the rate of descent is based on ground speed, not true airspeed.
explanations.B: because the rate of descent is based on ground speed, not calibrated airspeed.
explanations.C: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope depends on the ground speed because the descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over the ground. Thus, the descent must be decreased if ground speed is decreased.

questions.question: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope

answers.A: must be increased if the ground speed is decreased.
answers.B: will remain constant if the indicated airspeed remains constant.
answers.C: must be decreased if the ground speed is decreased.

explanations.A: because, if ground speed decreases and descent increases, the airplane will go below the glide slope.
explanations.B: because ground speed rather than airspeed determines the rate of descent.
explanations.C: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope is dependent on the ground speed because the descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over the ground. Thus, the descent must be decreased if ground speed is decreased.

questions.question: To remain on the ILS glidepath, the rate of descent must be

answers.A: decreased if the airspeed is increased.
answers.B: decreased if the ground speed is increased.
answers.C: increased if the ground speed is increased.

explanations.A: because the rate of descent must be based upon ground speed, not airspeed, while on the glide slope.
explanations.B: because, if one decreases the rate of descent with ground speed increasing, the airplane will rise above the glide slope.
explanations.C: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope depends on the ground speed because the descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if ground speed is increased.

questions.question: When passing through an abrupt wind shear which involves a shift from a tailwind to a headwind, what power management would normally be required to maintain a constant indicated airspeed and ILS glide slope?

answers.A: Higher than normal power initially, followed by a further increase as the wind shear is encountered, then a decrease.
answers.B: Lower than normal power initially, followed by a further decrease as the wind shear is encountered, then an increase.
answers.C: Higher than normal power initially, followed by a decrease as the shear is encountered, then an increase.

explanations.A: because initially there is lower-than-normal, not higher-than-normal, power with a tailwind, and when the headwind is encountered, a decrease, not an increase, in power is required.
explanations.B: When an airplane is on the ILS glide slope and there is a change from a tailwind to a headwind, the groundspeed will decrease. During the tailwind, lower-than-normal power will be required. When the wind shear is encountered, even lower power will be required to decrease the spurt in airspeed. Once the wind shifts to a headwind, the airplane will require an increase in power to maintain the necessary groundspeed to stay on the ILS glide slope.
explanations.C: because initially there is lower-than-normal, not higher-than-normal, power with a tailwind.

questions.question: What effect will a change in wind direction have upon maintaining a 3° glide slope at a constant true airspeed?

answers.A: When ground speed decreases, rate of descent must increase.
answers.B: When ground speed increases, rate of descent must increase.
answers.C: Rate of descent must be constant to remain on the glide slope.

explanations.A: because, if you increase the rate of descent when the ground speed decreases, you will fly below the glide slope.
explanations.B: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope is dependent on the ground speed because the descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if ground speed is increased.
explanations.C: because the rate of descent must change with changes in ground speed.

questions.question: The glide slope and localizer are centered, but the airspeed is too fast. Which should be adjusted initially?

answers.A: Pitch and power.
answers.B: Power only.
answers.C: Pitch only.

explanations.A: because, although the pitch and power adjustments must be closely coordinated, the power is actually adjusted first.
explanations.B: If the glide slope and localizer are centered but the airspeed is too fast, you should reduce power initially. Aimost immediately, you will then have to make pitch adjustments to compensate for the power adjustment to maintain the glidepath.
explanations.C: because adjusting pitch initially would cause you to fly above the glide path.

questions.question: While being vectored, if crossing the ILS final approach course becomes imminent and an approach clearance has not been issued, what action should be taken by the pilot?

answers.A: Turn outbound on the final approach course, execute a procedure turn, and inform ATC.
answers.B: Turn inbound and execute the missed approach procedure at the outer marker if approach clearance has not been received.

questions.question: Thrust is managed to maintain IAS, and glide slope is being flown. What characteristics should be observed when a headwind shears to be a constant tailwind?

answers.A: PITCH ATTITUDE: Increases; REQUIRED THRUST: Increased, then reduced; VERTICAL SPEED: Increases; IAS: Increases, then decreases to approach speed.
answers.B: PITCH ATTITUDE: Decreases; REQUIRED THRUST: Increased, then reduced; VERTICAL SPEED: Increases; IAS: Decreases, then increases to approach speed.
answers.C: PITCH ATTITUDE: Increases; REQUIRED THRUST: Reduced, then increased; VERTICAL SPEED: Decreases; IAS: Decreases, then increases to approach speed.

explanations.A: because the airspeed decreases, not increases, initially as the headwind shears to a tailwind, causing the pitch to decrease, not increase.
explanations.B: When a headwind shears to a tailwind, the airplane's airspeed drops, its nose pitches down, and its vertical speed increases. The power must be increased initially to resume normal approach speed, then reduced as airspeed stabilizes to maintain the glide slope due to the increased groundspeed.
explanations.C: because the pitch attitude decreases, not increases, due to the decreased airspeed, causing the vertical speed to increase, not decrease. Initially, the thrust must be increased, not decreased, to maintain approach airspeed.

questions.question: While flying a 3° glide slope, a constant tailwind shears to a calm wind. Which conditions should the pilot expect?

answers.A: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.B: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.C: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go above glide slope.

explanations.A: because the airspeed and pitch increase, not decrease, and there is a tendency to go above, not below, the glide slope.
explanations.B: because the tendency is to go above, not below, the glide slope.
explanations.C: When a constant tailwind shears to a calm wind, the airplane's airspeed increases, its nose pitches up, and it has a tendency to go above the glide slope. The nose pitches up due to the increased lift from the increased airspeed.

questions.question: While flying a 3° glide slope, a headwind shears to a tailwind. Which conditions should the pilot expect on the glide slope?

answers.A: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to go below glide slope.
answers.B: Airspeed and pitch attitude increase and there is a tendency to go above glide slope.
answers.C: Airspeed and pitch attitude decrease and there is a tendency to remain on the glide slope.

explanations.A: When a headwind shears to a tailwind, the airplane's airspeed drops, its nose pitches down, and it begins to drop below the glide slope. The airplane will be both slow and power deficient.
explanations.B: because airspeed and pitch decrease, not increase, and there is a tendency to go below, not above, the glide slope.
explanations.C: because there is a tendency to go below, not remain on, the glide slope.

questions.question: During a precision radar or ILS approach, the rate of descent required to remain on the glide slope will

answers.A: remain the same regardless of groundspeed.
answers.B: increase as the groundspeed increases.
answers.C: decrease as the groundspeed increases.

explanations.A: because the descent rate varies with the groundspeed.
explanations.B: The rate of descent required to stay on the ILS glide slope is dependent on the groundspeed because the descent must be constant relative to the distance traveled over the ground. Thus, the descent must be increased if groundspeed is increased.
explanations.C: because the descent rate must increase, not decrease, as groundspeed increases.

questions.question: When tracking in bound on the localizer, which of the following is the proper procedure regarding drift corrections?

answers.A: Drift corrections should be accurately established before reaching the outer marker and completion of the approach should be accomplished with heading corrections no greater than 2°.
answers.B: Drift corrections should be made in 5° increments after passing the outer marker.
answers.C: Drift corrections should be made in 10° increments after passing the outer marker.

explanations.A: When you are tracking in bound on the localizer, your drift correction should be small and reduced proportionately as the course narrows. By the time you reach the outer marker, your drift correction should be established accurately enough to permit completion of the approach with heading corrections no greater than 2°.
explanations.B: because, after you pass the outer marker, your drift corrections should be no greater than 2°, not 5°.
explanations.C: because, after you pass the outer marker, your drift corrections should be no greater than 2°, not 10°.

questions.question: Which information, in addition to headings, does the radar controller provide without request during an ASR approach?

answers.A: The recommended altitude for each mile from the runway.
answers.B: When reaching the MDA.
answers.C: When to commence descent to MDA, the aircraft's position each mile on final from the runway, and arrival at the MAP.

explanations.A: because the recommended altitude for each mile from the runway is provided only upon request.
explanations.B: because the controller does not have precise altitude capability.
explanations.C: A surveillance approach (ASR) provides navigation guidance in azimuths (direction) only. The pilot is furnished headings to align the airplane with the extended centerline of the landing runway and will be advised when to commence descent to the MDA and the MAP. In addi tion, the pilot will be advised of the airplane's position each mile on the final approach from the runway or MAP as appropriate.

questions.question: How is ATC radar used for instrument approaches when the facility is approved for approach control service?

questions.question: When being radar vectored for an ILS approach, at what point may you start a descent from your last assigned altitude to a lower minimum altitude if cleared for the approach?

questions.question: (Refer to figure 126.) What landing minimums apply for a 14 CFR Part 91 operator at Dothan, AL using a category C aircraft during a circling LOC 31 approach at 120 knots? (DME available.)

explanations.B: because it describes the lost communication procedure.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 85.) What procedure should be followed if communications are lost before reaching 9,000 feet?

Cross FMG VORTAC at or above MCA, thence via assigned route or climb in holding pattern northeast on FMG
explanations.C: because there is no requirement to cross WAGGE INT at 9,000 ft.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 85.) What is the minimum rate climb per NM to 9,000 feet required for the WASH2 WAGGE Departure?

explanations.B: because 825 fpm is the rate of climb at approximately 125 kt., not 150 kt., that results in a climb of 400 ft. per NM.

questions.question: Under which condition does ATC issue a STAR?

answers.C: When ATC deems it appropriate, unless the pilot requests "No STAR."

explanations.B: because pilot request is necessary to avoid, not obtain, STARs.

questions.question: Whichis true regarding the use of an instrument departure procedure chart?

answers.A: The use of instrument departure procedures is mandatory.
answers.B: To use an instrument departure procedure, the pilot must possess at least the textual description of the approved procedure.
answers.C: To use an instrument departure procedure, the pilot must possess both the textual and graphic form of the approved procedure.

explanations.A: because use of a DP is never mandatory.
explanations.B: Use of an instrument departure procedure (DP) requires that the pilot have at least the textual description of the procedure.
explanations.C: because a pilot need only possess the textual form of the DP.

questions.question: Whichis true regarding STAR's?

answers.A: STAR's are used to separate IFR and VFR traffic.
answers.B: STAR's are established to simplify clearance delivery procedures.
answers.C: STAR's are used at certain airports to decrease traffic congestion.

explanations.B: A STAR's purpose is to simplify Clearance delivery procedures.
explanations.C: because STARs are used to decrease radio, not traffic, congestion.

questions.question: What action is recommended if a pilot does not wish to use an instrument departure procedure?

answers.A: Advise clearance delivery or ground control before departure.
answers.B: Advise departure control upon initial contact.
answers.C: Enter "No DP" inthe REMARKS section of the IFR flight plan.

explanations.A: because verbal requests are less desirable than entering "No DP" in the flight plan.
explanations.B: because verbal requests are less desirable than entering "No DP" in the flight plan.
explanations.C: A pilot who does not possess an instrument departure procedure (DP) chart or does not wish to use a DP should advise ATC by indicating "No DP" in the remarks section of the flight plan.

questions.question: A particular instrument departure procedure requires a minimum climb rate of 210 feet per NM to 8,000 feet. If you climb with a ground speed of 140 knots, what is the rate of climb required in feet per minute?

explanations.A: because 210 is the required ft. per NM, not fpm.
explanations.B: because the required climb rate is 490 fpm, not 450 fpm.
explanations.C: Use the Rate of Climb Table in Legend 16. Required climb rate (ft. per NM) is found on the left margin and ground speed (kt.) is found on the top. Since 210 ft. per NM is not on the chart, you must interpolate between 200 and 250 ft. per NM at 140 kt. At 200 ft. per NM the climb rate is 467 fpm, and at 250 ft. per NM it is 583 fpm. Interpolate for 210 ft. per NM to determine a rate of climb of 490 fpm.

questions.question: Which procedure applies to instrument departure procedures?

answers.A: Instrument departure clearances will not be issued unless requested by the pilot.
answers.B: The pilot in command must accept an instrument departure procedure when issued by ATC.
answers.C: If an instrument departure procedure is accepted, the pilot must possess at least a textual description.

explanations.A: because pilots operating from locations with DPs may expect ATC clearances containing a DP.
explanations.B: because you must reject a DP clearance if you do not have a text of the DP or if itis otherwise unacceptable.
explanations.C: Once an instrument departure procedure (DP) is accepted, the presumption by ATC is that the pilot possesses a textual description of the DP.

questions.question: Preferred IFR routes beginning with a fix, indicate that departing aircraft will normally be routed to the fix by

answers.A: the established airway(s) between the departure airport and the fix.
answers.B: an instrument departure procedure (DP), or radar vectors.
answers.C: direct route only.

explanations.A: because established airways may not exist between the airport and the fix, and other methods may be more efficient and effective.
explanations.B: Preferred IFR routes are correlated with DPs and STARs and may be defined by airways, jet routes, and direct routes between NAVAIDs. Thus, preferred routes beginning with a fix indicate that the departing traffic will normally be routed to the fix via a DP or radar vectors.
explanations.C: because a direct route may not be appropriate due to obstructions or traffic flows.

questions.question: What international Morse Code identifier is used to identify a specific interim standard microwave landing system?

answers.A: A two letter Morse Code identifier preceded by the Morse Code for the letters "IM".
answers.B: A three letter Morse Code identifier preceded by the Morse Code for the letter "M"
answers.C: A three letter Morse Code identifier preceded by the Morse Code for the letters "ML".

explanations.A: because the identifier letter is the single character "M," which is followed by three other letters.
explanations.B: MLS identification is a four-character alphabetic designation starting with the letter "M," transmitted in international Morse Code at least 6 times per minute.
explanations.C: because the identifier letter is the single character "M," which is followed by three other letters.

questions.question: If Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) is not available when setting up a GPS approach, the pilot should

answers.A: select another type of navigation and approach system.
answers.B: continue to the MAP and hold until the satellites are recaptured.
answers.C: continue the approach, expecting to recapture the satellites before reaching the FAF.

explanations.A: RAIM outages may occur due to an insufficient number of satellites or due to unsuitable satellite geometry, which causes the error in the position solution to become too large. If RAIM is not available when setting up a GPS approach, you must select another type of navigation and approach system.
explanations.B: because, if RAIM is not available when setting up a GPS approach, you should select another type of navigation and approach system. You should not fly to the MAP and hold. Additionally, there is no holding pattern at the MAP.
explanations.C: because, if RAIM is not available when setting up a GPS approach, you should select another type of navigation and approach system. If RAIM failure occurs while you are setting up the GPS approach or conducting a GPS approach, you must not continue the approach hoping that RAIM will become available before the FAF.

questions.question: When using GPS for navigation and instrument approaches, any required alternate airport must have

answers.A: an approved operational instrument approach procedure other than GPS.
answers.B: authorization to fly approaches under IFR using GPS avionics systems.
answers.C: a GPS approach that is anticipated to be operational and available at the ETA.

explanations.A: When you are using GPS for navigation and instrument approaches, any required alternate airport must have an approved instrument approach procedure, other than GPS, which is anticipated to be operational and available at the estimated time of arrival (ETA) and which the airplane is equipped to fly.
explanations.B: because authorization to fly approaches under IFR using GPS avionics systems requires that the GPS unit and installation meet FAA standards and receive FAA approval.
explanations.C: because any required alternate airport must have an approved instrument approach procedure other than GPS, not a GPS approach, that is anticipated to be operational and available at the ETA.

questions.question: Why is hypoxia particularly dangerous during flights with one pilot?

answers.A: Night vision may be so impaired that the pilot cannot see other aircraft.
answers.B: Symptoms of hypoxia may be difficult to recognize before the pilot's reactions are affected.
answers.C: The pilot may not be able to control the aircraft even if using oxygen.

explanations.A: because hypoxia, which is a lack of ‘sufficient oxygen, affects all mental and physical activity, not just night vision.
explanations.B: Hypoxia symptoms are gradual, and a pilot may not recognize the symptoms before his/her reactions are affected. Because the symptoms of hypoxia vary with the individual, having two pilots increases the chance of detection before pilot reactions are affected.
explanations.C: because hypoxia will not occur if supplemental oxygen is used properly.

questions.question: What action should be taken if hyperventilation is suspected?

answers.A: Breathe at a slower rate by taking very deep breaths.
answers.B: Consciously breathe at a slower rate than normal.
answers.C: Consciously force yourself to take deep breaths and breathe at a faster rate than normal.

explanations.A: because taking deep breaths will only aggravate hyperventilation.
explanations.B: Hyperventilation occurs when abnormally large amounts of air are breathed in and out of the lungs. Early ‘symptoms of hyperventilation and hypoxia are similar and include dizziness, drowsiness, tingling of the fingers and toes, and sensation of body heat. If hyperventilation is suspected, you should consciously breathe at a slower rate than normal.
explanations.C: because taking deep breaths and breathing at a faster rate than normal is the cause, not cure, of hyperventilation.

questions.question: Apilot is more subject to spatial disorientation if

answers.A: kinesthetic senses are ignored.
answers.B: eyes are moved often in the process of cross-checking the flight instruments.
answers.C: body signals are used to interpret flight attitude.

explanations.A: because spatial disorientation is prevented/overcome by ignoring the kinesthetic senses.
explanations.B: because spatial disorientation is prevented/overcome by using and trusting the flight instruments.
explanations.C: Spatial disorientation is a state of temporary confusion resulting from misleading information being sent to the brain by various sensory organs. Thus, the pilot should ignore sensations of muscles and inner ear and kinesthetic senses (those which sense motion).

questions.question: Which procedure is recommended to prevent or overcome spatial disorientation?

answers.A: Reduce head and eye movements to the extent possible.
answers.B: Rely on the kinesthetic sense.
answers.C: Rely on the indications of the flight instruments.

explanations.A: because, although rapid head movements should be avoided, eye movement is necessary for proper scanning of the flight instruments.
explanations.B: because the kinesthetic sense is creating the problem; it should be ignored.
explanations.C: To overcome the effect of spatial disorientation, pilots should rely entirely on the indications of the flight instruments.

questions.question: The sensations which lead to spatial disorientation during instrument flight conditions

answers.A: are frequently encountered by beginning instrument pilots, but never by pilots with moderate instrument experience.
answers.B: occur, in most instances, during the initial period of transition from visual to instrument flight.
answers.C: must be suppressed and complete reliance placed on the indications of the flight instruments.

explanations.A: because pilots with moderate and even heavy instrument experience can experience spatial disorientation.
explanations.B: because spatial disorientation can occur at any time outside visual references are lost. This can happen on
explanations.C: In instrument flight conditions, the only way to prevent spatial disorientation is by visual reference to and reliance on the flight instruments.

questions.question: How canan instrument pilot best overcome spatial disorientation?

answers.B: Use a very rapid cross-check.
answers.C: Read and interpret the flight instruments, and act accordingly.
answers.A: Rely on kinesthetic sense.

explanations.A: because the kinesthetic sense is what causes the problem; i.e., it should be ignored.
explanations.B: because the flight instruments should be read and understood in a deliberate manner, not in haste or panic.
explanations.C: To overcome spatial disorientation, the IFR pilot should read and interpret the flight instruments and ignore all the body senses.

questions.question: How canan instrument pilot best overcome spatial disorientation?

answers.A: Use a very rapid cross-check.
answers.B: Properly interpret the flight instruments and act accordingly.
answers.C: Avoid banking in excess of 30°.

explanations.A: because the flight instruments should be read and understood in a deliberate manner, not in haste or Panic.
explanations.B: To overcome spatial disorientation, the IFR pilot should read and interpret the flight instruments and ignore all the body senses.
explanations.C: because spatial disorientation can also occur in bank angles less than 30°.

questions.question: Without visual aid, a pilot often interprets centrifugal force as a sensation of

answers.A: rising or falling.
answers.B: turning.
answers.C: motion reversal.

explanations.A: Nerves in tendons and muscles, including shifting of abdominal muscles, often incorrectly interpret centrifugal force as vertical movement, i.e., rising or falling.
explanations.B: because centrifugal force is caused by turning but is often misinterpreted as rising or falling.
explanations.C: because centrifugal force is caused by turning, not motion reversal.

questions.question: Abrupt head movement during a prolonged constant rate turn in IMC or simulated instrument conditions can cause

answers.A: pilot disorientation.
answers.B: false horizon.
answers.C: elevator illusion.

explanations.A: An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system can create the ill ion of rotation or movement in an entirely different axis. This illusion is called the Coriolis illusion and can lead to spatial disorientation.
explanations.B: because a false horizon is an illusion caused by sloping cloud formations, an obscured horizon, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, or certain geometric patterns of ground light. This illusion creates the impression of not being aligned correctly with the actual horizon and can also lead to spatial disorientation.
explanations.C: because an elevator illusion is caused by an abrupt upward vertical acceleration, usually by an updraft. This illusion can also lead to spatial disorientation.

questions.question: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of

answers.A: tumbling backwards.
answers.B: a noseup attitude.
answers.C: a descent with the wings level.

explanations.A: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the illusion of tumbling backwards. The disoriented pilot will push the airplane abruptly into a nose-low attitude, possibly intensifying this illusion, which is called an inversion illusion.
explanations.B: because a rapid acceleration during takeoff can create an illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. This is called a somatogravic illusion.
explanations.C: because an observed loss of altitude during a coordinated constant-rate turn that has ceased ‘stimulating the motion sensing system (i.e., inner ear) can create the illusion of being in a descent with the wings level. This illusion is called a graveyard spiral

questions.question: Arapid acceleration during takeoff can create the illusion of

answers.A: spinning in the opposite direction.
answers.B: being in a noseup attitude.
answers.C: diving into the ground.

explanations.A: because a proper recovery from a spin that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system (i.e., inner ear) can create the illusion of spinning in the opposite direction. This is known as a graveyard spin.
explanations.B: A rapid acceleration during takeoff can create the illusion of being in a nose-up attitude. The disoriented pilot will push the airplane into a nose-low, or dive, attitude. This is called a somatogravic illusion.
explanations.C: because a rapid deceleration or an abrupt downward vertical acceleration (usually caused by a downdraft) can cause the illusion of a nose-down, or dive, attitude.

questions.question: Asloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, and a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars can create an illusion known as

answers.B: autokinesis.
answers.A: elevator illusions.
answers.C: _ false horizons.

explanations.A: because elevator illusions are caused by abrupt upward or downward vertical accelerations, usually by updrafts and downdrafts. These lead to illusions of being ina climb or descent.
explanations.B: because, at night, a static light will appear to move about when stared at for many seconds, creating an illusion known as autokinesis. C_ false horizons.
explanations.C: A sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, and certain geometric patterns of ground light can create an illusion known as false horizons. The disoriented pilot will place the airplane in a dangerous attitude.

questions.question: Which use of cockpit lighting is correct for night flight?

answers.A: Reducing the interior lighting intensity to a minimum level.
answers.B: The use of regular white light, such as a flashlight, will not impair night adaptation.
answers.C: Coloration shown on maps is least affected by the use of direct red lighting.

explanations.A: In darkness, vision becomes more sensitive to light, making it possible for the pilot to see distant objects. A pilot can achieve a moderate degree of this dark adaptation within 20 min. under dim red cockpit lighting. White cockpit lighting is required for map and instrument reading, especially when operating under IFR. To maintain some night vision, the interior lighting intensity is to be kept at a minimum level.
explanations.B: because, after a pilot's eyes have become adapted to darkness, the pilot must avoid exposing them to any bright white light, which would cause temporary night blindness and impair night adaptation.
explanations.C: because the colors on maps can be ‘severely distorted when using a red light.

questions.question: Which statement is correct regarding the use of cockpit lighting for night flight?

answers.A: Reducing the lighting intensity to a minimum level will eliminate blind spots.
answers.B: The use of regular white light, such as a flashlight, will impair night adaptation.
answers.C: Coloration shown on maps is least affected by the use of direct red lighting.

explanations.A: because the minimum level of cockpit lighting may be insufficient to read maps, gauges, etc.
explanations.B: After a pilot's eyes have become adapted to darkness, the pilot must avoid exposing them to any bright white light, which would cause temporary night blindness and impair night adaptation.
explanations.C: because the colors on maps can be severely distorted when using a red light.

questions.question: Which technique should a pilot use to scan for traffic to the right and left during ‘straight-and-level flight?

answers.A: Systematically focus on different segments of the sky for short intervals.
answers.B: Concentrate on relative movement detected in the peripheral vision area.
answers.C: Continuous sweeping of the windshield from right to left.

explanations.A: The most effective way to scan for other aircraft during daylight is to use a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into your central vision field. Only a very small center area of the eye has the ability to send clear, sharply focused messages to the brain. All other areas provide less detail.
explanations.B: because the peripheral areas do not send sharply focused messages to the brain. Peripheral vision is more effective at night.
explanations.C: because concentration for at least 1 second is needed for each 10° sector.

questions.question: What effect does haze have on the ability to see traffic or terrain features during flight?

answers.A: Haze causes the eyes to focus at infinity, making terrain features harder to see.
answers.B: The eyes tend to overwork in haze and do not detect relative movement easily.
answers.C: Haze creates the illusion of being a greater distance than actual from the runway, and causes pilots to fly a lower approach.

explanations.A: because haze may cause the condition known as empty-field myopia. This condition results when the pilot has nothing specific to focus on outside the airplane and the eyes relax and focus at a range of about 10 to 30 ft, not infinity.
explanations.B: because in haze the eyes tend to relax, not overwork, thus causing empty-field myopia, or looking without seeing.
explanations.C: Haze can create the illusion of being at a greater distance from the runway and often causes pilots to fly a lower approach.

questions.question: Due to visual illusion, when landing on a narrower-than-usual runway, the aircraft will appear to be

answers.A: higher than actual, leading to a lower-than-normal approach.
answers.B: lower than actual, leading to a higher-than-normal approach.
answers.C: higher than actual, leading to a higher-than-normal approach.

explanations.A: A narrower-than-usual runway may create the illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual, resulting ina lower-than-normal approach.
explanations.B: because wider, not narrower, runways give a lower-than-actual altitude illusion.
explanations.C: because a higher-than-actual altitude illusion results in a lower-than-usual, not higher-than-usual, approach.

questions.question: What visual illusion creates the same effect as a narrower-than-usual runway?

answers.A: An upsloping runway.
answers.B: A wider-than-usual runway.
answers.C: A downsloping runway.

explanations.A: Both narrower-than-usual runway and an upsloping runway may create the illusion that the airplane is at a higher altitude than it actually is. The pilot will fly a lower approach and risk striking obstructions or landing short.
explanations.B: because a wider-than-usual runway may create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it actually is, and the unknowing pilot may land hard or overshoot the runway.
explanations.C: because a downsloping runway may create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it actually is, and the unknowing pilot may land hard or overshoot the runway.

questions.question: The primary cause of all changes in the Earth's weather is

answers.A: variation of solar energy received by the Earth's regions.
answers.B: changes in air pressure over the Earth's surface.
answers.C: movement of the air masses.

explanations.A: Every physical process of weather is accompanied by, or is the result of, a heat exchange. Unequal solar heating of the Earth's surface causes differences in air pressure, which result in all changes in the Earth's weather.
explanations.B: because changes in air pressure are a result of varying temperatures.
explanations.C: because movement of air masses (wind) is a result of varying temperatures and pressures.

questions.question: Which force, in the Northern Hemisphere, acts at a right angle to the wind and deflects it to the right until parallel to the isobars?

answers.A: Centrifugal.
answers.B: Pressure gradient.
answers.C: Coriolis.

explanations.A: because centrifugal force is a force that acts outwardly on any object moving in a curved path.
explanations.B: because pressure gradient causes the wind to move perpendicular to the isobars. The wind is then deflected by Coriolis force.
explanations.C: Coriolis force is a result of the Earth's rotation. As the wind moves perpendicular to the isobars (from high to low pressure), it is apparently deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, until it is moving parallel to the isobars. This effect is most pronounced above 2,000 ft. AGL.

questions.question: What relationship exists between the winds at 2,000 feet above the surface and the surface winds?

answers.A: The winds at 2,000 feet and the surface winds flow in the same direction, but the surface winds are weaker due to friction.
answers.B: The winds at 2,000 feet tend to parallel the isobars while the surface winds cross the isobars at an angle toward lower pressure and are weaker.
answers.C: The surface winds tend to veer to the right of the winds at 2,000 feet and are usually weaker.

explanations.A: because the Coriolis force is less at the ‘surface, so surface winds flow in a direction different from those aloft.
explanations.B: Generally, winds near the surface are weaker than those aloft due to the friction between the Earth's surface and the wind. Also, because they are slower, winds near the surface are less affected by the Coriolis force. The pressure gradient forces are thus stronger near the surface, and the winds cross the isobars at an angle instead of flowing parallel to them.
explanations.C: because the winds aloft veer to the right of surface winds, not the opposite.

questions.question: Winds at 5,000 feet AGL on a particular flight are southwesterly while most of the surface winds are southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to

answers.A: a stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
answers.B: friction between the wind and the surface.
answers.C: stronger Coriolis force at the surface.

explanations.A: because the pressure differentials are approximately uniform through the altitudes.
explanations.B: Southerly winds at the surface will become southwesterly winds at 5,000 ft. because the Coriolis force deflects winds aloft to the right. This force has less effect on ‘surface winds which have been slowed by friction with the Earth's ‘surface.
explanations.C: because the Coriolis force at the surface is weaker with slower wind speed.

questions.question: What causes surface winds to flow across the isobars at an angle rather than parallel to the isobars?

answers.B: Surface friction.
answers.C: The greater density of the air at the surface.
answers.A: Coriolis force.

explanations.A: because the Coriolis force is directly Proportional to wind speed. At higher altitudes (above 2,000 to 3,000 ft. AGL), winds not slowed by surface friction are so deflected by the Coriolis force that they flow parallel to the isobars, not across them.
explanations.B: Generally, winds near the surface are weaker than those aloft due to the friction between the Earth's surface and the wind. Also, because they are slower, winds near the surface are less affected by the Coriolis force. The pressure gradient forces are thus stronger near the surface, and the winds cross the isobars at an angle instead of flowing parallel to them.
explanations.C: because the greater air density at the ‘surface has little effect on the relationship of winds to the isobars.

questions.question: Anair mass is a body of air that

answers.B: creates a wind shift as it moves across the Earth's surface.
answers.C: covers an extensive area and has fairly uniform properties of temperature and moisture.
answers.A: has similar cloud formations associated with it.

explanations.A: because an air mass may have cloud formations or it may be clear and dry.
explanations.B: because changes in wind, temperature, etc., indicate a frontal zone between two air masses.
explanations.C: An air mass is an extensive body of air within which the conditions of temperature and moisture in a horizontal plane are essentially uniformly distributed. Generally, an air mass takes on the properties of the large area it overlies.

questions.question: Acharacteristic of the stratosphere is

answers.A: an overall decrease of temperature with an increase in altitude.
answers.B: a relatively even base altitude of approximately 35,000 feet.
answers.C: relatively small changes in temperature with an increase in altitude.

explanations.A: because there is a slight increase, not decrease, in temperature with increase in altitude.
explanations.B: because the base of the stratosphere is considerably higher at the equator than at the poles.
explanations.C: The stratosphere is the atmospheric layer above the tropopause. It is the band of altitude from about 7 to 22 mi. It is characterized by a slight average increase in temperature from base to top and thus is very stable. It also has a low moisture content and an absence of clouds.

questions.question: Ajetstream is defined as wind of

answers.A: 30 knots or greater.
answers.B: 40 knots or greater.
answers.C: 50 knots or greater.

explanations.A: because a jet stream, by definition, is a wind of 50 kt, not 30 kt, or greater.
explanations.B: because a jet stream, by definition, is a wind of 50 kt., not 40 kt., or greater.
explanations.C: The jet stream is a roughly horizontal ‘stream of wind of 50 kt. or more (by definition) concentrated within a narrow band embedded in the westerly winds in the high troposphere. It occurs in an area of intensified pressure gradients. A second or even third jet stream may form at one time, and these may not be continuous.

questions.question: The average height of the troposphere in the middle latitudes is

explanations.A: because the average height of the troposphere is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the poles, not the mid-latitudes. B, 25,000 feet.
explanations.B: because the average height of the troposphere is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the poles, not the mid-latitudes.
explanations.C: In the mid-latitudes, the average height of the troposphere is about 37,000 ft. It is 25,000 to 30,000 ft. at the poles and 55,000 to 65,000 ft. at the equator. It is generally higher in summer than in winter.

questions.question: The strength and location of the jet stream is normally

answers.A: stronger and farther north in the winter.
answers.B: weaker and farther north in the summer.
answers.C: stronger and farther north in the summer.
