explanations.A: because the jet stream is usually farther south, not north, in winter.
explanations.B: In the mid-latitudes, the wind speed in the jet stream averages considerably less in the summer than in the winter. Also, the jet stream shifts farther north in summer than in winter.
explanations.C: because the jet stream is usually weaker, not stronger, in summer.

questions.question: Which feature is associated with the tropopause?

answers.B: Absolute upper limit of cloud formation.
answers.C: Abrupt change in temperature lapse rate.
answers.A: Absence of wind and turbulent conditions.

explanations.A: because there are usually very strong winds in the tropopause. These create narrow zones of wind shear, which may generate hazardous turbulence.
explanations.B: because clouds may form above the tropopause even though there is little moisture in the stratosphere.
explanations.C: The tropopause is the transition layer of atmosphere between the troposphere (surface to about 7 to 22 mi.) and the stratosphere. A characteristic of the tropopause is that there is an abrupt change in the temperature lapse rate, i.e., the rate at which temperature decreases with height.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon is always associated with the passage of a frontal system?

answers.A: Awind change.
answers.B: An abrupt decrease in pressure.
answers.C: Clouds, either ahead or behind the front.

explanations.A: Whenever a front passes, a wind shift will always occur. This discontinuity may be in direction, speed, or both.
explanations.B: because the pressure and/or temperature may not change significantly as a weak front passes.
explanations.C: because some fronts do not contain enough moisture to produce clouds. Therefore, clouds are not always associated with a frontal system.

questions.question: Whichis a characteristic of low-level wind shear as it relates to frontal activity?

answers.A: With a warm front, the most critical period is before the front passes the airport.
answers.B: With a cold front, the most critical period is just before the front passes the airport.
answers.C: Turbulence will always exist in wind-shear conditions.

explanations.A: Wind shear associated with a warm front occurs above an airport before the front passes the airport. A warm front is warmer air overtaking colder air.
explanations.B: because cold front wind shear occurs just as or just after the front passes rather than before it passes.
explanations.C: because wind shear can sometimes ‘occur with no forewarning from turbulence.

questions.question: Frontal waves normally form on

answers.A: slow moving cold fronts or stationary fronts.
answers.B: slow moving warm fronts and strong occluded fronts.
answers.C: rapidly moving cold fronts or warm fronts.

explanations.A: Frontal waves and cyclones (areas of low pressure) usually form in slow-moving cold fronts or in stationary fronts.
explanations.B: because frontal waves are usually not associated with warm fronts or occluded fronts.
explanations.C: because frontal waves usually form on slow-moving, not rapidly moving, cold fronts and not on warm fronts.

questions.question: Where do squall lines most often develop?

answers.B: Ina cold air mass.
answers.C: Ahead of a cold front.
answers.A: Inan occluded front.

explanations.A: because squall lines are usually associated with a fast-moving cold front.
explanations.B: because they occur ahead of the cold front, not behind the front in the cold air.
explanations.C: A squall line is a nonfrontal band of active thunderstorms that sometimes develops ahead of a cold front.

questions.question: Which are characteristics of an unstable cold air mass moving over a warm surface?

answers.A: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and poor visibility.
answers.B: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and good visibility.
answers.C: Stratiform clouds, smooth air, and poor visibility.

explanations.A: because unstable air lifts and blows haze away, resulting in good, not poor, visibility.
explanations.B: When a cold air mass moves over a warm surface, the warm air near the surface rises and creates an unstable situation. These convective currents give rise to cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and good visibility.
explanations.C: because unstable conditions produce cumuliform rather than stratiform clouds. Also, the air is turbulent, and visibility is good.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of stable air?

answers.A: Good visibility, steady precipitation, and stratus-type clouds.
answers.B: Poor visibility, intermittent precipitation, and cumulus-type clouds.
answers.C: Poor visibility, steady precipitation, and stratus-type clouds.

explanations.A: because the visibility is poor rather than good in stable air.
explanations.B: because the precipitation is steady and the clouds are stratiform.
explanations.C: Stable air is air which is still or moving horizontally but not vertically. As a result, the pollutants hang in the air and visibility is poor. Also, stable air forms stratus-type clouds since the air is moving in layers. Relatedly, precipitation spreads out over a wide area and is relatively steady.

questions.question: What type clouds can be expected when an unstable air mass is forced to ascend a mountain slope?

answers.A: Layered clouds with little vertical development.
answers.B: Stratified clouds with considerable associated turbulence.
answers.C: Clouds with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A: because layered clouds are associated with stable air.
explanations.B: because stratified clouds are associated with stable air and no turbulence.
explanations.C: Unstable air has a greater lapse rate. Because the air above is much colder than the air below, the lower (warmer) air tends to rise very easily. When an unstable air mass is forced to ascend up a mountain slope, it will probably continue to ascend beyond the mountain slope. Once the air expands and cools to the dew point, cumulus clouds will form with considerable vertical development. Any unstable air mass movement will usually result in turbulence as well.

questions.question: Whichis a characteristic of stable air?

answers.B: Stratiform clouds.
answers.C: Unlimited visibility.
answers.A: Fair weather cumulus clouds.

explanations.A: because cumulus clouds indicate unstable conditions.
explanations.B: Stratiform clouds, i.e., layer-type clouds, characteristically form in stable air. A stable atmosphere resists any upward or downward displacement, so clouds tend to lie horizontally instead of developing vertically.
explanations.C: because restricted, not unlimited, visibility near the ground is an indication of stable air.

questions.question: The general characteristics of unstable air are

answers.A: good visibility, showery precipitation, and cumuliform-type clouds.
answers.B: good visil , Steady precipitation, and stratiform-type clouds.
answers.C: poor visibility, intermittent precipitation, and cumuliform-type clouds.

explanations.A: Unstable air is moving vertically and usually produces cumulus clouds. The precipitation from cumulus clouds is showery. The lifting associated with unstable air generally clears smoke and other pollution away; thus vi: relatively good.
explanations.B: because unstable air generally has showery, not steady, precipitation and cumulus, not stratiform, clouds.
explanations.C: because unstable air generally has good, not poor, visibility.

questions.question: What type of clouds will be formed if very stable moist air is forced up slope?

answers.B: Vertical clouds with increasing height.
answers.C: Stratified clouds with little vertical development.
answers.A: First stratified clouds and then vertical clouds.

explanations.A: because there would be vertical clouds if the air were unstable rather than stable.
explanations.B: because there would be vertical clouds if the air were unstable rather than stable.
explanations.C: Even when being forced up slope, stable air forms stratus-type clouds. This is because the air resists any further upward movement.

questions.question: Steady precipitation, in contrast to showers, preceding a front is an indication of

answers.A: stratiform clouds with moderate turbulence.
answers.B: cumuliform clouds with little or no turbulence.
answers.C: stratiform clouds with little or no turbulence.

explanations.A: because stable air has little or no turbulence.
explanations.B: because stratiform rather than cumuliform clouds form in stable air.
explanations.C: Steady precipitation is a characteristic of stable air because of its lack of lifting action. Also characteristic are stratiform clouds with relatively little turbulence.

questions.question: What enhances the growth rate of precipitation?

answers.B: Upward currents.
answers.C: Cyclonic movement.
answers.A: Advective action.

explanations.A: because advective action usually refers to the horizontal transport of atmospheric properties by wind, such as warm advection (warm land air moving out over colder water).
explanations.B: The growth rate of precipitation is enhanced by upward currents, which carry moisture particles to cooler levels. The particles grow in size and weight (due to condensation) until the atmosphere can no longer hold them (saturation point) and they fall as precipitation.
explanations.C: because cyclonic movement refers to the counterclockwise movement around a low-pressure area.

questions.question: Which of the following combinations of weather producing variables would likely result in cumuliform-type clouds, good visibility, rain showers, and possible clear-type icing in clouds?

answers.A: Unstable, moist air, and no lifting mechanism.
answers.B: Stable, dry air, and orographic lifting.
answers.C: Unstable, moist air, and orographic lifting.

explanations.A: because, without a lifting mechanism, there would be no vertical development of clouds to result in showery rain and icing in clouds.
explanations.B: because stable conditions result in stratiform rather than cumuliform clouds, and dry air does not result in showery rain or icing even when lifted.
explanations.C: Cumuliform clouds, good visibility, and showery rain are produced as unstable, moist air is lifted into higher, cooler regions. When the lifting is the result of movement over terrain (e.g., up a mountain slope), it is called orographic lifting. Clear icing is formed from large drops such as those found in cumuliform clouds.

questions.question: What determines the structure or type of clouds which form as a result of air being forced to ascend?

answers.A: The method by which the air is lifted.
answers.B: The stability of the air before lifting occurs.
answers.C: The amount of condensation nuclei present after lifting occurs.

explanations.A: because the stability of the air, not the lifting mechanism, determines the type of cloud formations.
explanations.B: The structure of clouds is determined by the stability of the air before it is lifted. If unstable, the clouds will have vertical development. If stable, the clouds will be horizontal, ie., stratiform.
explanations.C: because condensation nuclei encourage the formation of rain droplets or ice but have no effect on the type of cloud formations.

questions.question: Stability can be determined from which measurement of the atmosphere?

answers.A: Low-level winds.
answers.B: Ambient lapse rate.
answers.C: Atmospheric pressure.

explanations.A: because stability refers to vertical air movement, not horizontal air movement.
explanations.B: The ambient lapse rate is the actual rate of decrease in temperature with height. A great decrease in temperature as altitude increases encourages warm air from below to rise and creates an unstable air mass. Lifting is inhibited by lesser or very small temperature decreases with altitude (i.e., a low lapse rate).
explanations.C: because atmospheric pressure is a measure of the weight or downward force of air and does not affect air stability.

questions.question: What are some characteristics of unstable air?

answers.A: Nimbostratus clouds and good surface visibility.
answers.B: Turbulence and poor surface visibility.
answers.C: Turbulence and good surface visibility.

explanations.A: because stratus clouds are characteristic of stable, not unstable, air.
explanations.B: because poor surface visibility is a characteristic of stable, not unstable, air.
explanations.C: The lifting tendency of unstable air creates turbulence and clears the surface air of clouds, dust, and other pollution.

questions.question: Unsaturated air flowing up slope will cool at the rate of approximately (dry adiabatic lapse rate)

answers.A: 3°C per 1,000 feet.
answers.B: 2°C per 1,000 feet.
answers.C: 2.5°C per 1,000 feet.

explanations.A: The dry adiabatic lapse rate signifies a prescribed rate of expansional cooling or compressional heating. The dry adiabatic rate is 3°C for each 1,000 ft. Note that this rate differs from the average normal lapse rate of 2°C for each 1,000 ft. of altitude. The average lapse rate does NOT occur in dry air, but rather in air with "average" humidity.
explanations.B: because 2°C per 1,000 ft. is the standard lapse rate in stable air.
explanations.C: because 2.5°C per 1,000 ft. is the rate at which the temperature and dew point converge in a convective current of unsaturated air.

questions.question: What feature is associated with a temperature inversion?

answers.A: Astable layer of air.
answers.B: An unstable layer of air.
answers.C: Air mass thunderstorms.

explanations.A: A temperature inversion is defined as an increase in temperature with height; i.e., the lapse rate is less than standard. The cooler air stays near the surface, and there is little or no vertical movement.
explanations.B: because instability occurs when the temperature decreases, not increases as in a temperature inversion, with an increase in height, and the warmer air continues to rise.
explanations.C: because air mass thunderstorms result from instability. They do not occur when there is a temperature inversion.

questions.question: Which weather conditions should be expected beneath a low-level temperature inversion layer when the relative humidity is high?

answers.A: Smooth air and poor visibility due to fog, haze, or low clouds.
answers.B: Light wind shear and poor visibility due to haze and light rain.
answers.C: Turbulent air and poor visibility due to fog, low stratus-type clouds, and showery precipitation.

explanations.A: A temperature inversion is an increase in temperature as altitude increases; normally temperature decreases with increases in altitude. In an inversion, warm air rises to its own temperature and forms a stable layer of air. A low-level inversion results in poor visibility by trapping fog, smoke, dust, etc., in low levels of the atmosphere.
explanations.B: because wind shear may be expected within, not beneath, a low-level temperature inversion.
explanations.C: because an inversion forms a stable layer of air, thus making it smooth, not turbulent, and causing steady, not showery, precipitation.

questions.question: A temperature inversion will normally form only

answers.B: in unstable air.
answers.C: when a stratiform layer merges with a cumuliform mass.
answers.A: instable air.

explanations.A: In a temperature inversion, warm air overlies colder air, i.e., the lapse rate is inverted. By definition, this is a stable condition since there is no lifting action.
explanations.B: because unstable air has colder air above warm air.
explanations.C: because a merger of stratus and cumulus Clouds is associated with an occluded front, not necessarily a temperature inversion.

questions.question: A common type of ground or surface based temperature inversion is that which is produced by

answers.A: warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
answers.B: the movement of colder air over warm air, or the movement of warm air under cold air.
answers.C: ground radiation on clear, cool nights when the wind is light.

explanations.A: because, when warm air is lifted, unstable, not stable, air is the result.
explanations.B: because a temperature inversion consists of warm air over colder air, not colder over warm.
explanations.C: A temperature inversion means the temperature becomes warmer rather than cooler with increases in altitude. A ground- or surface-based temperature inversion is produced when the air near the surface is cooled faster than the overlying air as a result of radiation of heat on a clear, still night. The air very close to the surface is thus cooler than the air a few hundred feet above.

questions.question: Which conditions are favorable for the formation of radiation fog?

answers.A: Moist air moving over colder ground or water.
answers.B: Cloudy sky and a light wind moving saturated warm air over a cool surface.
answers.C: Clear sky, little or no wind, small temperature/dew point spread, and over a land surface.

explanations.A: because advection fog, not radiation fog, forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. The sky may be cloudy over advection fog.
explanations.B: because advection fog, not radiation fog, forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. The sky may be cloudy over advection fog.
explanations.C: Conditions favorable for radiation fog are

questions.question: What situation is most conducive to the formation of radiation fog?

answers.A: Warm, moist air over low, flatiand areas on clear, calm nights.
answers.B: Moist, tropical air moving over cold, offshore water.
answers.C: The movement of cold air over much warmer water.

explanations.A: Conditions favorable for radiation fog are
explanations.B: because advection fog forms as a result of warm air moving over a colder surface.
explanations.C: because steam fog forms when cold air moves over a warmer surface.

questions.question: The most frequent type of ground- or surface-based temperature inversion is that produced by

answers.A: radiation on a clear, relatively still night.
answers.B: warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountainous terrain.
answers.C: the movement of colder air under warm air, or the movement of warm air over cold air.

explanations.A: An inversion often develops near the ground on clear, cool nights when the wind is light. The ground radiates heat and cools much faster than the overlying air. Air in contact with the ground becomes cold, while the temperature a few hundred feet above changes very little. Thus temperature increases with height.
explanations.B: because it describes orographic lifting.
explanations.C: because it describes a cold front anda warm front, respectively.

questions.question: What types of fog depend upon a wind in order to exist?

answers.A: Steam fog and down slope fog.
answers.B: Precipitation-induced fog and ground fog.
answers.C: Advection fog and up slope fog.

explanations.A: because down slope fog is a nonsense term.
explanations.B: because precipitation fog forms when warm rain or drizzle falls through cool air, and ground fog requires little or no wind.
explanations.C: Up slope fog forms as a result of moist, stable air being cooled as it moves up a sloping terrain. Advection fog forms when moist air is blown over a cold surface, decreasing the moist air's temperature to its dew point. Thus, both up slope fog and advection fog depend on air moving from one area to another; i.e., they depend on wind.

questions.question: In what localities is advection fog most likely to occur?

answers.A: Coastal areas.
answers.B: Mountain slopes.
answers.C: Level inland areas.

explanations.A: Advection fog forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. This type of fog is thus most common along coastal areas. During the winter, advection fog over the central and eastern United States results when moist air from the Gulf of Mexico spreads northward over cold ground.
explanations.B: because mountain slopes are required for upslope, not advection, fog.
explanations.C: because level inland areas will most likely produce radiation, not advection, fog.

questions.question: In which situation is advection fog most likely to form?

answers.A: Anair mass moving inland from the coast in winter.
answers.B: A light breeze blowing colder air out to sea.
answers.C: Warm, moist air settling over a warmer surface under no-wind conditions.

explanations.A: Advection fog forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. This type of fog is most likely to form when an air mass moves from the warmer water inland from the coast in winter. As the air moves over the cooler land, it cools to the dew point and forms advection fog.
explanations.B: because colder air blowing out to sea results in steam, not advection, fog.
explanations.C: because warm, moist air settling over a warmer surface would not cool, so fog would not form.

questions.question: Fog is usually prevalent in industrial areas because of

answers.A: atmospheric stabilization around cities.
answers.B: an abundance of condensation nuclei from combustion products.
answers.C: increased temperatures due to industrial heating.

explanations.A: because cities, per se, have no effect on air stability.
explanations.B: Fog often forms in industrial areas because the combustion products leave dust in the air on which water can condense. These particles are called condensation nuclei.
explanations.C: because the amount of heat that factories release into the air is not significant in the formation of fog.

questions.question: Which weather condition can be expected when moist air flows from a relatively warm surface to a colder surface?

answers.A: Increased visibility.
answers.B: Convective turbulence due to surface heating.
answers.C: Fog.

explanations.A: because fog forms, which decreases, not increases, visibility.
explanations.B: because the surface cools the air, resulting in stable air with little or no convective turbulence.
explanations.C: When moist air flows from a relatively warm surface to a colder surface, the warm, moist air is cooled to its dew point, and advection fog is produced.

questions.question: Under which condition does advection fog usually form?

answers.A: Moist air moving over colder ground or water.
answers.B: Warm, moist air settling over a cool surface under no-wind conditions.
answers.C: Aland breeze blowing a cold air mass over a warm water current.

explanations.A: Advection fog forms when moist air moves over colder ground or water. The moist air is cooled to the dew point, and fog forms.
explanations.B: because radiation fog, not advection fog, forms when warm, moist air settles over a cool surface under no-wind conditions.
explanations.C: because steam fog, not advection fog, forms when a land breeze blows a cold air mass over a warm water current.

questions.question: The amount of water vapor which air can hold largely depends on

answers.A: relative humidity.
answers.B: air temperature.
answers.C: stability of air.

explanations.A: because relative humidity is the ratio of the existing amount of water vapor in the air at a given temperature to the maximum amount that could be held at that temperature.
explanations.B: Air temperature largely determines how much water vapor can be held by the air. Warm air, which is less dense, can hold more water vapor than cold air.
explanations.C: because air stability is related to the temperature lapse rate, not moisture.

questions.question: Clouds, fog, or dew will always form when

answers.A: water vapor condenses.
answers.B: water vapor is present.
answers.C: the temperature and dew point are equal.

explanations.A: As water vapor condenses, it becomes visible as clouds, fog, or dew.
explanations.B: because some water vapor is usually present, but it does not necessarily form clouds, fog, or dew.
explanations.C: because, even at 100% humidity (when the dew point equals actual temperature), water vapor may not condense if sufficient condensation nuclei are not present.

questions.question: To which meteorological condition does the term "dew point" refer?

answers.A: The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated.
answers.B: The temperature at which condensation and evaporation are equal.
answers.C: The temperature at which dew will always form.

explanations.A: Dew point refers to the temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated by the water vapor in the air. Dew point, when related to air temperature in aviation weather reports, reveals how close the air is to saturation and possible cloud, fog, or precipitation formation.
explanations.B: because condensation (vapor to water) occurs at low temperatures, and evaporation (water to vapor) occurs at high temperatures.
explanations.C: because the formation of dew depends on relative humidity and the temperature of the collecting surface.

questions.question: Which conditions result in the formation of frost?

answers.A: The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below freezing and small droplets of moisture are falling.
answers.B: When dew forms and the temperature is below freezing.
answers.C: Temperature of the collecting surface is below the dewpoint of surrounding air and the dewpoint is colder than freezing.

explanations.A: because the dew point must also be below freezing and droplets of moisture are not necessary.
explanations.B: because the formation of dew is not required. The dew point of surrounding air must be below freezing, and the temperature of the collecting surface must be less than the dew point.
explanations.C: If the air temperature drops below the dew point, the air becomes more dense and can no longer hold the water vapor. The water vapor will condense to form visible moisture. Frost will form only if the temperature of the collecting surfaces is below the dew point of the surrounding air AND the dew point is below freezing.

questions.question: What are the four families of clouds?

answers.A: Stratus, cumulus, nimbus, and cirrus.
answers.B: Clouds formed by updrafts, fronts, cooling layers of air, and precipitation into warm air.
answers.C: High, middle, low, and those with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A: because it describes cloud formation and characteristic.
explanations.B: because it describes the way various clouds are formed.
explanations.C: For identification purposes, clouds are divided into four "families" based on their height range. The families are high clouds, middle clouds, low clouds, and clouds with extensive vertical development.

questions.question: Which family of clouds is least likely to contribute to structural icing on an aircraft?

answers.A: Low clouds.
answers.B: High clouds.
answers.C: Clouds with extensive vertical development.

explanations.A: because low clouds can contain supercooled water, which freezes on contact with the airplane.
explanations.B: High clouds are least likely to contribute to structural icing since they usually consist entirely of ice crystals. Since ice is already frozen, it will not freeze onto the structural surface of the airplane.
explanations.C: because clouds with extensive vertical development can contain supercooled water, which freezes on contact with the airplane.

questions.question: The presence of standing lenticular altocumulus clouds is a good indication of

answers.A: ajetstream.
answers.B: very strong turbulence.
answers.C: heavy icing conditions.

explanations.A: because the jet stream flows around the world at high altitudes and at varying latitudes.
explanations.B: When stable air crosses a mountain barrier, it tends to flow in layers. The barrier may set up waves in these layers, which remain stationary while the wind blows rapidly through them. Wave crests extend well above the highest mountain tops. Under each wave crestis a rotary circulation, which can create very violent turbulence. Crests of the standing waves may be marked by stationary lens-shaped clouds known as standing lenticular clouds.
explanations.C: because standing lenticular clouds occur at varying temperatures, not only below freezing.

questions.question: The suffix "nimbus", used in naming clouds, means a

answers.A: cloud with extensive vertical development.
answers.B: rain cloud.
answers.C: dark massive, towering cloud.

explanations.A: because "cumulo," not "nimbus," denotes
explanations.B: The prefix "nimbo" or the suffix "nimbus" means raincloud. For example, stratified clouds from which rain is falling are called nimbostratus clouds. A heavy, swelling, cumulus-type cloud which produces precipitation is called a cumulonimbus cloud.
explanations.C: because it specifies a cumulonimbus cloud, not any nimbus cloud.

questions.question: Standing lenticular clouds, in mountainous areas, indicate

answers.B: unstable air.
answers.C: turbulence.
answers.A: an inversion.

explanations.A: because stratus, not standing lenticular, Clouds indicate stable air which may be the result of a temperature inversion.
explanations.B: because cumulus, not standing lenticular, Clouds indicate unstable air.
explanations.C: The "waves" generated as wind flows across a mountain barrier may form standing lenticular clouds at the crest of each wave. Their presence indicates very strong turbulence, and they should be avoided.

questions.question: Which clouds have the greatest turbulence?

answers.A: Towering cumulus.
answers.B: Cumulonimbus.
answers.C: Altocumulus castellanus.

explanations.A: because towering cumulus clouds are only a preliminary stage of the cumulonimbus cloud.
explanations.B: Cumulonimbus clouds are thunderstorms and the ultimate manifestation of instability. They are huge vertically developed clouds with dense, billowy tops often crowned with thick veils of dense cirrus, called the "anvil." Nearly the entire spectrum of flying hazards is contained in these clouds, including violent turbulence.
explanations.C: because altocumulus castellanus is a middle-level convective cloud which indicates rough turbulence with some icing, but thunderstorms are far more turbulent.

questions.question: Ahigh cloud is composed mostly of

answers.B: condensation nuclei.
answers.C: ice crystals.
answers.A: ozone.

explanations.A: because ozone is an unstable form of oxygen. The heaviest concentrations are in the stratosphere, not in clouds.
explanations.B: because condensation nuclei are the small particles in the air onto which water vapor condenses or sublimates.
explanations.C: The high cloud family is cirriform. It includes cirrus, cirrocumulus, and cirrostratus clouds. They are composed almost entirely of ice crystals. Their bases range from 16,500 ft. to 45,000 ft.

questions.question: Fair weather cumulus clouds often indicate

answers.B: poor visibility.
answers.C: smooth flying conditions.
answers.A: turbulence at and below the cloud level.

explanations.A: Fair weather cumulus clouds form in convective currents and are characterized by relatively flat bases and dome-shaped tops. They indicate a shallow layer of instability, some turbulence, and no significant icing.
explanations.B: because the instability producing the cumulus clouds provides good, not poor, visibility.
explanations.C: because the instability producing the cumulus clouds creates some turbulence, not smooth conditions.

questions.question: What are the requirements for the formation of a thunderstorm?

answers.B: A cumulus cloud with sufficient moisture and an inverted lapse rate.
answers.C: Sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate, and a lifting action.
answers.A: Acumulus cloud with sufficient moisture.

explanations.A: because a lifting action is also required for formation of a thunderstorm.
explanations.B: because a lifting action and an unstable, not inverted, lapse rate are required for the formation of a thunderstorm.
explanations.C: For a thunderstorm to form, the air must have sufficient water vapor, an unstable lapse rate, and an initial upward lifting action to start the storm process in motion. Surface heating, converging winds, sloping terrain, a frontal surface, or any combination of these can provide the lift.

questions.question: What is an indication that downdrafts have developed and the thunderstorm cell has entered the mature stage?

answers.A: The anvil top has completed its development.
answers.B: Precipitation begins to fall from the cloud base.
answers.C: A gust front forms.

explanations.A: because an anvil top does not necessarily develop over every thunderstorm.
explanations.B: The mature stage of a thunderstorm is signaled when rain begins falling at the surface. This means that the downdrafts have developed sufficiently to carry water all the way through the thunderstorm.
explanations.C: because gust front is a nonsense term.

questions.question: Which procedure is recommended if a pilot should unintentionally penetrate embedded thunderstorm activity?

answers.A: Reverse aircraft heading or proceed toward an area of known VFR conditions.
answers.B: Reduce airspeed to maneuvering speed and maintain a constant altitude.
answers.C: Set power for recommended turbulence penetration airspeed and attempt to maintain a level flight attitude.

explanations.A: because a straight course will probably take you out of the storm most quickly. Also, turning maneuvers increase stresses on the aircraft.
explanations.B: because maintaining a constant airspeed (Va) in updrafts and downdrafts may be impossible. It is best to set power so you will operate at or below Va. Also, attempting to maintain constant altitude, not attitude, increases the stress on the airplane.
explanations.C: If a thunderstorm is penetrated, you should always attempt to maintain a constant attitude at or below the maneuvering or turbulence penetration speed recommended for the airplane. Note that the airspeed cannot always be kept constant, but the power can be set so that you will be operating generally at or below the maneuvering speed.

questions.question: Which thunderstorms generally produce the most severe conditions, such as heavy hail and destructive winds?

answers.A: Warm front.
answers.B: Squall line.
answers.C: Air mass.

explanations.A: because warm fronts indicate stable air, which does not usually produce thunderstorms.
explanations.B: A squall line is a nonfrontal narrow band of active thunderstorms. It often contains severe, steady-state thunderstorms and presents the single most intense weather hazard to airplanes.
explanations.C: because an air mass thunderstorm is the least severe type of thunderstorm.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon is always associated with a thunderstorm?

answers.A: Lightning.
answers.B: Heavy rain showers.
answers.C: Supercooled raindrops.

explanations.A: A thunderstorm, by definition, has lightning, because lightning causes the thunder. Lightning is the discharge of electricity generated by thunderstorms.
explanations.B: because hail may occur instead of heavy rain showers.
explanations.C: because supercooled raindrops may not occur if the lifting process does not extend above the freezing level.

questions.question: During the life cycle of a thunderstorm, which stage is characterized predominately by downdrafts?

answers.B: Dissipating.
answers.C: Mature.
answers.A: Cumulus.

explanations.A: because the cumulus stage is the building stage characterized by updrafts.
explanations.B: Thunderstorms have three stages in their life cycle: cumulus, mature, and dissipating. In the dissipating stage, the storm is characterized by downdrafts as the storm rains itself out.
explanations.C: because the mature stage has both updrafts and downdrafts, which create strong wind shears.

questions.question: If squalls are reported at your destination, what wind conditions should you anticipate?

answers.A: Sudden increases in wind speed of at least 16 knots rising to 22 knots or more, lasting for at least 1 minute.
answers.B: Peak gusts of at least 35 knots for a sustained period of 1 minute or longer.
answers.C: Rapid variation in wind direction of at least 20° and changes in speed of at least 10 knots between peaks and lulls.

explanations.A: A squall is a sudden increase in wind speed by at least 16 kt. rising to 22 kt. or more and lasting for at least 1 min. In contrast, a wind gust is a brief increase in wind with a variation between peaks and lulls of at least 10 kt. Note that these definitions involve variations in wind speed, not wind direction.
explanations.B: because a squall is a sudden increase in wind speed of at least 16 kt., rising to a peak of 22 kt. or more, not a peak gust of at least 35 kt. lasting for at least 1 min.
explanations.C: because squalls refer to changes in wind speed, not direction. Additionally, the wind is reported as gusty when there are changes in speed of at least 10 kt. between peaks and lulls.

questions.question: What is indicated by the term “embedded thunderstorms"?

answers.A: Severe thunderstorms are embedded within a squall line.
answers.B: Thunderstorms are predicted to develop in a stable air mass.
answers.C: Thunderstorms are obscured by massive cloud layers and cannot be seen.

explanations.A: because a squall line consists of severe thunderstorms which can usually be seen.
explanations.B: because thunderstorms do not usually occur in stable air masses.
explanations.C: The term "embedded thunderstorms" means that the storms are embedded in clouds or thick haze layers and cannot be seen.

questions.question: Which weather phenomenon signals the beginning of the mature stage of a thunderstorm?

answers.A: The start of rain at the surface.
answers.B: Growth rate of cloud is maximum.
answers.C: Strong turbulence in the cloud.

explanations.A: The mature stage of a thunderstorm is indicated when rain begins falling at the surface. This means that downdrafts have developed sufficiently to carry water all the way through the thunderstorm.
explanations.B: because maximum growth rate occurs in the first or cumulus stage.
explanations.C: because strong turbulence can occur in all stages.

questions.question: Which is true regarding the use of airborne weather-avoidance radar for the recognition of certain weather conditions?

answers.A: The radarscope provides no assurance of avoiding instrument weather conditions.
answers.B: The avoidance of hail is assured when flying between and just clear of the most intense echoes.
answers.C: The clear area between intense echoes indicates that visual sighting of storms can be maintained when flying between the echoes.

explanations.A: Weather-avoidance radar provides information on precipitation based on echo returns. Avoiding the heaviest areas of precipitation will often (not always) keep you out of the greatest turbulence. Radar does not show water vapor. Thus, clouds and fog, i.e., instrument weather conditions, are not indicated.
explanations.B: because intense thunderstorms can often hurl hail for miles.
explanations.C: because visual sighting of storms is not assured, because clouds and fog are not shown by radar.

questions.question: In which meteorological environment is aircraft structural icing most likely to have the highest rate of accumulation?

answers.A: Cumulonimbus clouds.
answers.B: High humidity and freezing temperature.
answers.C: Freezing rain.

explanations.A: because icing does not necessarily occur in thunderstorms due to the large variation in temperature in thunderstorms.
explanations.B: because visible moisture, not just high humidity, must be present for icing.
explanations.C: The condition most favorable for very hazardous icing is the presence of many large, supercooled water drops (i.e., freezing rain). The heaviest icing will usually be found at altitudes at or slightly above the freezing level where the temperature is never more than a few degrees below freezing.

questions.question: Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost having a thickness and roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can

answers.A: reduce lift by as much as 50 percent and increase drag by as much as 50 percent.
answers.B: increase drag and reduce lift by as much as 25 percent.
answers.C: reduce lift by as much as 30 percent and increase drag by 40 percent.

explanations.A: because ice, snow, or frost having a thickness or roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can reduce lift by as much as 30%, not 50%, and increase drag by 40%, not 50%.
explanations.B: because ice, snow, or frost having a thickness or roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can reduce lift by as much as 30%, not 25%, and increase drag by 40%, 25%.
explanations.C: Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost formations having a thickness and surface roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of an airfoil can reduce lift by as much as 30% and increase drag by 40%. These changes in lift and drag significantly increase stall speed, reduce controllability, and alter aircraft flight characteristics.

questions.question: Which precipitation type normally indicates freezing rain at higher altitudes?

answers.B: Hail.
answers.C: Ice pellets.
answers.A: Snow.

explanations.A: because snow indicates that the temperature of the air above you is well below freezing.
explanations.B: because hail indicates instability of the air aloft where supercooled droplets above the freezing level begin to freeze. Once a drop has frozen, other drops latch onto it, and the hailstone grows.
explanations.C: Ice pellets normally indicate that rain droplets are freezing at a higher altitude. Warmer air above exists from which rain is falling and freezing on the way down, as it enters cooler air (i.¢., freezing rain exists above).

questions.question: What is an operational consideration if you fly into rain which freezes on impact?

answers.B: Temperatures are above freezing at some higher altitude.
answers.C: You have flown through a cold front.
answers.A: You have flown into an area of thunderstorms.

explanations.A: because freezing rain does not necessarily indicate the presence of thunderstorms.
explanations.B: Rain which freezes on impact is called freezing rain. If rain falls through freezing air, it will usually form supercooled water droplets, i.e., freezing rain. It indicates that temperatures somewhere above the airplane are above freezing.
explanations.C: because freezing rain does not necessarily indicate the presence of cold fronts.

questions.question: What temperature condition is indicated if wet snow is encountered at your flight altitude?

answers.A: The temperature is above freezing at your altitude.
answers.B: The temperature is below freezing at your altitude.
answers.C: You are flying from a warm air mass into a cold air mass.

explanations.A: If snow is wet at your altitude, you are in above-freezing temperatures because the snow has started to melt.
explanations.B: because the wet snow indicates the temperature is above freezing, not below freezing, at your altitude.
explanations.C: because the temperature is lower above you, but not necessarily in front of you.

questions.question: The presence of ice pellets at the surface is evidence that

answers.B: a cold front has passed.
answers.C: there is freezing rain at a higher altitude.
answers.A: there are thunderstorms in the area.

explanations.A: because thunderstorms do not necessarily cause ice pellets.
explanations.B: because cold fronts do not necessarily cause ice pellets.
explanations.C: Ice pellets form as a result of rain freezing at a higher altitude. Rain droplets cool as they fall from a warmer layer through air with a temperature below freezing.

questions.question: Why is frost considered hazardous to flight operation?

answers.A: Frost changes the basic aerodynamic shape of the airfoil.
answers.B: Frost decreases control effectiveness.
answers.C: Frost causes early airflow separation resulting in a loss of lift.

explanations.A: because frost is very thin. It does not change the airfoil shape as structural icing does.
explanations.B: because frost has no bearing on control effectiveness, only airfoil lift.
explanations.C: Frost spoils the smooth flow of air, thus Causing a slowing of the airflow. This causes early airflow separation over the affected airfoil, resulting in a loss of lift. A heavy coat of hard frost will cause a 5 to 10% increase in stall speed. Even a small amount of frost on airfoils may prevent an aircraft from becoming airborne at normal takeoff speed.

questions.question: If the air temperature is +8 °C at an elevation of 1,350 feet and a standard (average) temperature lapse rate exists, what will be the approximate freezing level?

answers.A: 3,350 feet MSL.
answers.B: 5,350 feet MSL.
answers.C: 9,350 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because it represents a standard lapse rate of 4° per 1,000 ft.
explanations.B: The decrease of temperature with altitude is defined as the lapse rate. The standard lapse rate is 2°C per 1,000 ft. To reach the freezing level, you must have a drop of 8°C. Thus the freezing level is 4,000 ft. (8/2 x 1,000 ft.) up, or 5,350 ft. MSL (1,350 + 4,000).
explanations.C: because it represents a standard lapse rate of 1° per 1,000 ft.

questions.question: What is an important characteristic of wind shear?

answers.B: The Coriolis phenomenon in both high- and low-level air masses is the principal generating force.
answers.C: Itis an atmospheric condition that may be associated with a low-level temperature inversion, a jet stream, or a frontal zone.
answers.A: ltis an atmospheric condition that is associated exclusively with Zones of convergence.

explanations.A: because zones of convergence are low-pressure areas. Wind shear can occur in highs as well as lows.
explanations.B: because the Coriolis force is the deflective force of the Earth's rotation which affects all wind flows, not just wind shear.
explanations.C: Wind shear can occur at any level where winds are blowing in different directions or at different speeds. It is an atmospheric condition associated with low-level temperature inversions, the jet stream, or a frontal zone.

questions.question: A pilot reporting turbulence that momentarily causes slight, erratic changes in altitude and/or attitude should report it as

answers.A: light turbulence.
answers.B: moderate turbulence.
answers.C: light chop.

explanations.A: Light turbulence is defined as a disturbed air flow that momentarily causes slight erratic changes in altitude and/or attitude.
explanations.B: because moderate turbulence is more intense. It is sufficient to cause changes in altitude, but the pilot maintains control throughout.
explanations.C: because light chop means slight or moderate, rapid, and somewhat rhythmic bumpiness without appreciable changes in altitude or attitude.

questions.question: What is an important characteristic of wind shear?

answers.B: It usually exists only in the vicinity of thunderstorms, but may be found near a strong temperature inversion.
answers.C: It may be associated with either a wind shift or a wind speed gradient at any level in the atmosphere.
answers.A: tis primarily associated with the lateral vortices generated by thunderstorms.

explanations.A: because wind shear is found in Conditions other than thunderstorm turbulence, e.g., mountain waves, fronts, etc.
explanations.B: because wind shear is found in conditions other than thunderstorm turbulence, e.g., mountain waves, fronts, etc.
explanations.C: Wind shear can occur at any level where winds are blowing in different directions or at different speeds.

questions.question: Where can wind shear associated with a thunderstorm be found? Choose the most complete answer.

answers.A: In front of the thunderstorm cell (anvil side) and on the right side of the cell.
answers.B: In front of the thunderstorm cell and directly under the cell.
answers.C: On all sides of the thunderstorm cell and directly under the cell.

explanations.A: because wind shear may be found on all sides and beneath the thunderstorm cell.
explanations.B: because wind shear may be found on all sides and beneath the thunderstorm cell.
explanations.C: Wind shear associated with thunderstorms may be found on all sides of the thunderstorm cell, including directly beneath it and as much as 20 mii. laterally.

questions.question: Where does wind shear occur?

answers.A: Exclusively in thunderstorms.
answers.B: Wherever there is an abrupt decrease in pressure and/or temperature.
answers.C: With either a wind shift or a wind speed gradient at any level in the atmosphere.

explanations.A: because wind shear is also caused by barriers to wind flow, occurs behind and below airplanes generating lift, etc.
explanations.B: because wind shear is the result of wind change, not a change in temperature or pressure, per se.
explanations.C: Wind shear can occur at any level where winds are blowing in different directions (wind shift) or at different speeds (a wind speed gradient).

questions.question: Hazardous wind shear is commonly encountered near the ground

answers.A: during periods when the wind velocity is stronger than 35 knots.
answers.B: during periods when the wind velocity is stronger than 35 knots and near mountain valleys.
answers.C: during periods of strong temperature inversion and near thunderstorms.

explanations.A: because any wind, not only wind shear, is hazardous when in excess of 35 kt.
explanations.B: because wind shear usually occurs on the leeward side of mountains, not in valleys.
explanations.C: Thunderstorms produce hazardous wind shear near the ground. Wind shear during temperature inversions is also hazardous when at low levels as it affects aircraft approaching and departing airports.

questions.question: An aircraft that encounters a headwind of 45 knots, within a microburst, may expect a total shear across the microburst of

answers.A: 40 knots.
answers.B: 80 knots.
answers.C: 90 knots.

explanations.A: because the total wind shear expected across a microburst is twice the initial headwind, e.g., 45 kt. x 2 = 90 kt., not 40 kt.
explanations.B: because the total wind shear expected across a microburst is twice the initial headwind, e.g., 45 kt. x 2 = 90 kt., not 80 kt.
explanations.C: If a headwind in a microburst is 45 kt., the wind will be going in the opposite direction on the other side of the microburst at presumably the same 45 kt., resulting in a wind shear between the headwind and tailwind of 90 kt.

questions.question: Maximum downdrafts in a microburst encounter may be as strong as

answers.A: 8,000 feet per minute.
answers.B: 7,000 feet per minute.
answers.C: 6,000 feet per minute.

explanations.A: because maximum downdrafts are usually 6,000 FPM, not 8,000 FPM.
explanations.B: because maximum downdrafts are usually 6,000 FPM, not 7,000 FPM.
explanations.C: Downdrafts in a microburst can be as strong as 6,000 FPM. Horizontal winds near the surface can be as strong as 45 Kt., resulting in a 90-kt. wind shear. The strong horizontal winds occur within a few hundred feet of the ground.

questions.question: What is the expected duration of an individual microburst?

answers.A: Two minutes with maximum winds lasting approximately 1 minute.
answers.B: One microburst may continue for as long as 2 to 4 hours.
answers.C: Seldom longer than 15 minutes from the time the burst strikes the ground until dissipation.

explanations.A: because microbursts last 15, not 2 min., and maximum winds last 2 to 4 min., not 1 min.
explanations.B: because the maximum winds last 2 to 4 min., not 2 to 4 hr., and the microburst is usually limited to about 15 min.
explanations.C: An individual microburst will seldom last longer than 15 min. from the time it strikes ground until dissipation. The horizontal winds continue to increase during the first 5 min. with maximum-intensity winds lasting approximately 2 to 4 min.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 13.) When penetrating a microburst, which aircraft will experience an increase in performance without a change in pitch or power?

explanations.A: because at point 3 the airplane is experiencing a strong downdraft.
explanations.B: because at point 2 the airplane is experiencing a decreasing headwind component.
explanations.C: Refer to Fig. 13 and note that, as the airplane at point 1 approaches the microburst, it will experience an increasing headwind and increasing performance.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 13.) The aircraft in position 3 will experience which effect ina microburst encounter?

answers.A: Decreasing headwind.
answers.B: Increasing tailwind.
answers.C: Strong downdraft.

explanations.A: because at point 2, not 3, the airplane encounters decreasing headwind.
explanations.B: because at point 5 the airplane encounters an increasing tailwind that may result in an extreme situation as pictured, i.e., just before impact.
explanations.C: At point 3 in Fig. 13, the airplane is experiencing a strong downdraft as it is approaching the center of the microburst.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 13.) What effect will a microburst encounter have upon the aircraft in position 4?

answers.A: Strong tailwind.
answers.B: Strong updraft.
answers.C: Significant performance increase.

explanations.A: At point 4 in Fig. 13, the airplane is encountering a strong tailwind in addition to a strong downdraft.
explanations.B: because there are no updrafts in microbursts, only downdrafts.
explanations.C: because the significance in performance increase occurs at point 1, not 4, where there is an increase in headwind.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 13.) How will the aircraft in position 4 be affected by a microburst encounter?

answers.A: Performance increasing with a tailwind and updraft.
answers.B: Performance decreasing with a tailwind and downdraft.
answers.C: Performance decreasing with a headwind and downdraft.

explanations.A: because performance decreases at point 4 due to the tailwind and a downdraft, not an updraft.
explanations.B: In Fig. 13, point 4 represents decreased performance as a result of both the windshear shift from a headwind to a tailwind and a strong downdraft.
explanations.C: because the performance decreases as

questions.question: (Refer to figure 13.) If involved in a microburst encounter, in which aircraft positions will the most severe downdraft occur?

answers.B: 2 and 3.
answers.A: 4 and 5.
answers.C: 3 and 4.

explanations.A: because point 5 has significantly less downdraft even though it has considerably more tailwind.
explanations.B: because point 2 has not so significant a downdraft as 3 and 4, but it contains significant headwind even though it is decreasing.
explanations.C: In Fig. 13, the most severe downdrafts occur at the center of the microburst, which are indicated by points 3 and 4.

questions.question: AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis every

answers.A: 15 minutes after the hour only.
answers.B: 15 minutes until the AIRMET is canceled.
answers.C: six hours.

explanations.A: because AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis every 6 hr., not every 15 min. past the hour.
explanations.B: because AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis every 6 hr., not every 15 min. until the AIRMET is canceled.
explanations.C: AIRMETs are issued on a scheduled basis every 6 hr., with unscheduled amendments issued as required.

questions.question: What is the maximum forecast period for AIRMET's?

answers.A: Two hours.
answers.B: Four hours.
answers.C: Six hours.

explanations.A: because convective SIGMETs, not AIRMETs, are valid for up to 2 hr.
explanations.B: because SIGMETs, not AIRMETs, are valid for up to 4 hr.
explanations.C: The maximum forecast period for AIRMETs is 6 hr. If conditions persist beyond 6 hr., the AIRMET must be updated and reissued.

questions.question: SIGMETs are issued as a warning of weather conditions potentially hazardous

answers.A: particularly to light aircraft.
answers.B: to all aircraft.
answers.C: only to light aircraft operations.

explanations.A: because SIGMETs apply to all aircraft.
explanations.B: SIGMETs warn of weather considered potentially hazardous to all categories of aircraft. SIGMETs are forecasts of tornadoes, lines of thunderstorms, embedded thunderstorms, large hail, severe and extreme turbulence, severe icing, and widespread sandstorms and snowstorms.
explanations.C: because AIRMETs, not SIGMETs, apply to light aircraft.

questions.question: Which meteorological condition is issued in the form of a SIGMET (WS)?

answers.A: Widespread sand or dust storms lowering visibility to less than 3 miles.
answers.B: Moderate icing.
answers.C: Sustained winds of 30 knots or greater at the surface.

explanations.A: SIGMETs are issued for severe and extreme turbulence; severe icing; and widespread dust storms, sandstorms, or volcanic ash lowering visibility below 3 mi.
explanations.B: because moderate icing is issued in the form of an AIRMET, not a SIGMET.
explanations.C: because sustained winds of 30 kt. or greater at the surface are issued in the form of an AIRMET, not a SIGMET.

questions.question: Pilots of IFR flights seeking ATC in-flight weather avoidance assistance should keep in mind that

answers.A: ATC radar limitations and, frequency congestion may limit the controllers capability to provide this service.
answers.B: circumnavigating severe weather can only be accommodated in the en route areas away from terminals because of congestion.
answers.C: ATC Narrow Band Radar does not provide the controller with weather intensity capability.

explanations.A: The controllers’ primary function is to provide safe separation between aircraft. Any additional service, such as weather avoidance, can be provided only to the extent it does not interfere with the primary function. Unfortunately, the separation workload is usually greater when weather disrupts the normal flow of traffic.
explanations.B: because controllers can provide weather circumnavigation in terminal areas when workload permits.
explanations.C: because ATC narrowband radar is replacing digitized radar weather displays in ARTCC facilities to provide even better measurement of precipitation density.

questions.question: The Hazardous Inflight Weather Advisory Service (HIWAS) is a continuous broadcast over selected VORs of

answers.A: SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Severe Weather Forecast Alerts (AWW), and Center Weather Advisories.
answers.B: SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Wind Shear Advisories, and Severe Weather Forecast Alerts (AWW).
answers.C: Wind Shear Advisories, Radar Weather Reports, SIGMETs, CONVECTIVE SIGMETs, AIRMETs, and Center Weather Advisories (CWA).

explanations.A: The Hazardous Inflight Weather Advisory Service (HIWAS) is a continuous broadcast service over selected VORs of in-flight weather advisories, i.e., SIGMETs, convective SIGMETs, AIRMETs, severe weather forecast alerts (AWW), and center weather advisories (CWA).
explanations.B: because a runway wind shear advisory would be given to arriving and departing aircraft by a tower controller, not the HIWAS.
explanations.C: because radar weather reports would be available from the En Route Flight Advisory Service (EFAS), not the HIWAS.

questions.question: What is meant by the entry in the remarks section of METAR surface report for KBNA? METAR KBNA 211250Z 33018KT 290V260 1/2SM R31/2700FT +SN BLSNFG VV008 00/M03 A2991 RMK RAE42SNB42

answers.A: The wind is variable from 290° to 360°.
answers.B: Heavy blowing snow and fog on runway 31.
answers.C: Rain ended 42 past the hour, snow began 42 past the hour.

explanations.A: because the remarks section indicates that rain ended 42 min. past the hour and snow began 42 min. past the hour, not that the wind is variable from 290° to 360°.
explanations.B: because the remarks section indicates that rain ended 42 min. past the hour and snow began 42 min. past the hour, not that there is heavy blowing snow and fog on Rwy 31.
explanations.C: The contraction RMK follows the altimeter in the body and precedes remarks. RMK RAE42SNB42 means remarks follow, rain ended 42 min. past the hour (RAE42), and ‘snow began 42 min. past the hour (SNB42).

questions.question: Aceiling is defined as the height of the

answers.A: highest layer of clouds or obscuring phenomena aloft that covers over 6/10 of the sky.
answers.B: lowest layer of clouds that contributed to the overall overcast.
answers.C: lowest layer of clouds or obscuring phenomena aloft that is reported as broken or overcast.

explanations.A: because the ceiling is the base of the lowest, not highest, broken or overcast layer.
explanations.B: because the lowest layer of clouds must be broken or overcast, not simply a contributor to the overall overcast.
explanations.C: For aviation purposes, the ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility into an obscuration.

questions.question: The reporting station originating this Aviation Routine Weather Report has a field elevation of 620 feet. If the reported sky cover is one continuous layer, what is its thickness (tops of OVC are reported at 6,500 feet)? METAR KMDW 121856Z AUTO 32005KT 1 1/2SM +RA BR OVC007 17/16 A2980

answers.B: 5,800 feet.
answers.C: 5,880 feet.
answers.A: 5,180 feet.

explanations.A: The sky cover for KMDW is reported as a ceiling of 700 ft. AGL, overcast (OVC007). The field elevation is 620 ft. MSL; thus, the base of the overcast layer is 1,320 ft. MSL (700+620). The tops of the overcast are reported at 6,500 ft.; thus, the thickness of the overcast layer is 5,180 ft. (6,500-1,320).
explanations.B: because 5,800 ft. would be the thickness. of the sky cover if the field elevation were 0 ft., not 620 ft.
explanations.C: because 5,880 ft. is the height above ground of the tops of the overcast layer, not the thickness of the overcast layer.

questions.question: The station originating the following weather report has a field elevation of 1,300 feet MSL. From the bottom of the overcast cloud layer, what is its thickness (tops of OVC are reported at 3,800 feet)? SPECI KOKC 22282 28024G36KT 3/4SM BKNO08 OVC020 28/23 A3000

answers.B: 1,700 feet.
answers.C: 2,500 feet.
answers.A: 500 feet.

explanations.A: The question is to determine the thickness of the overcast layer at KOKC. The SPECI reported the base of the overcast cloud layer at 2,000 ft. AGL (OVC020). The field elevation is 1,300 ft. MSL; thus, the base of the overcast layer is 3,300 ft. MSL (2,000+1,300). The tops of the overcast layer are reported at 3,800 ft. MSL; thus, the thickness of the overcast cloud layer is 500 ft. (3,800-3,300).
explanations.B: because 1,700 ft. is the distance from the base of the broken (BKN), not overcast (OVC), cloud layer to the top of the overcast.
explanations.C: because 2,500 ft. is the height above the ground of the tops of the overcast, not the thickness of the overcast layer.

questions.question: What significant sky condition is reported in this METAR observation? METAR KBNA 1250Z 33018KT 290V360 1/2SM R31/2700FT +SN BLSNFG VV008 00/M03 A2991 RMK RERAE42SNB42

answers.A: Runway 31 ceiling is 2,700 feet.
answers.B: Sky is obscured with vertical visibility of 800 feet.
answers.C: Measured ceiling is 300 feet overcast.

explanations.A: because runway 31 RVR, not ceiling, is 2,700 ft.
explanations.B: The sky condition follows the weather element. At KBNA, the sky cover is reported as VV008, which means the sky is obscured (indefinite ceiling) with a vertical visibility of 800 feet.
explanations.C: because 00/M03 means the temperature is 0°C and the dew point is -3°C, not that there is a measured ceiling of 300 ft. overcast.

questions.question: Interpret this PIREP. MRB UA/OV MRB/TM 1430/FL 060/TP C182/SK BKN BL WX RAITB MDT.

answers.A: Ceiling 6,000 feet intermittently below moderate thundershowers; turbulence increasing westward.
answers.B: FL 60,000, intermittently below clouds; moderate rain, turbulence increasing with the wind.
answers.C: At 6,000 feet; between layers; moderate turbulence; moderate rain.

explanations.A: because the flight level, not the ceiling, is 6,000 ft., and TB MDT means moderate turbulence, not thundershowers.
explanations.B: because the flight level is 6,000 ft., not 60,000 ft., and BL means between layers, not below clouds.
explanations.C: The PIREP decodes as follows: pilot report, over Martinsburg, WV at 1430 UTC, flight level is 6,000 ft., type of aircraft is a Cessna 182, and sky condition is broken with the pilot reporting between layers in moderate rain and moderate turbulence.

questions.question: Which response most closely interprets the following PIREP? UA/OV OKC 063064/TM 1522/FLO80/TP C172/TA - 04 IWV245040/TB LGT/RM IN CLR.

answers.A: 64 nautical miles on the 63 degree radial from Oklahoma City VOR at 1522 UTC, flight level 8,000 ft. Type of aircraft is a Cessna 172.
answers.B: Reported by a Cessna 172, turbulence and light rime icing in climb to 8,000 ft.
answers.C: 63 nautical miles on the 64 degree radial from Oklahoma City, thunderstorm and light rain at 1522 UTC.

explanations.A: The PIREP decodes as follows: pilot report, 64 NM on the 063° radial from Oklahoma City VOR at 1522 UTC, flight level is 8,000 ft., type of aircraft is a Cessna 172, outside air temperature is -4°C, wind is from 245° at 40 kt. with light turbulence, remarks are that the pilot is in clear skies.
explanations.B: because TB LGT RM IN CLR means light turbulence (remark) in clear, not turbulence and rime icing in climb.
explanations.C: because OKC 063064 means the aircraft was located 64 NM, not 63 NM, on the 063° radial, not the 064° radial. Additionally, there is no report of thunderstorm and rain.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 4.) The Weather Depiction Chart in the area of northwestern Wyoming indicates

answers.B: 1,000-foot ceilings and visibility 3 miles or more.
answers.C: 500-foot ceilings and continuous rain, less than 3 miles visibility.
answers.A: overcast with scattered rain showers.

explanations.A: because the chart provides data only from observation stations. Rain showers would be reported as intermittent, not scattered. Intermittent showers (moderate intensity at time of observation) would be shown as two vertical, not horizontal, dots.
explanations.B: because the station in Wyoming is reporting a ceiling of 500 ft., not 1,000 ft., and since visibility is not shown, it is interpreted to mean greater than 6 SM, not 3 SM or more.
explanations.C: The station circle in northwestern Wyoming indicates an overcast sky (darkened circle), 500-ft. ceiling ("5" under the circle), and continuous rain (two dots over circle). The station circle is in a shaded area, which indicates IFR with ceiling less than 1,000 ft. and/or visibility less than 3 SM.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 4.) The Weather Depiction Chart indicates the heaviest precipitation is occurring in

answers.B: north central Minnesota.
answers.C: central South Dakota.
answers.A: north central Florida.

explanations.A: because no precipitation is reported for north central Florida.
explanations.B: The heaviest precipitation is occurring in north central Minnesota. The station near the southern edge of the shaded area has four dots in a diamond shape above the circle, which means continuous rain (not freezing), heavy at the time of observation.
explanations.C: because no precipitation is reported for central South Dakota.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 4.) What is the meaning of a bracket ( ] ) plotted to the right of the station circle on a weather depiction chart?

answers.A: The station represents the en route conditions within a 50 mile radius.
answers.B: The station is an automated observation location.
answers.C: The station gives local overview of flying conditions for a six-hour period.

explanations.A: because a bracket to the right of the station circle means the station is an automated site. The chart does not provide en route conditions between stations.
explanations.B: Data for the weather depiction chart come from the observations reported by both manual and automated observation locations. The automated stations are denoted by a bracket (] ) plotted to the right of the station circle.
explanations.C: because a bracket to the right of the station circle means that the station is an automated site, not that the station gives a local overview of flying conditions for a 6-hr. period.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow A on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Moderate to strong echoes; echo tops 30,000 feet MSL; line movement toward the northwest.
answers.B: Weak to moderate echoes; average echo bases 30,000 feet MSL; cell movement toward the southeast; rain showers with thunder.
answers.C: Strong to very strong echoes; echo tops 30,000 feet MSL; thunderstorms and rain showers.

explanations.A: because an area contained within two circles has strong to very strong echoes, not moderate echoes.
explanations.B: because 30,000 ft. refers to echo tops, not echo bases and an area within two circles has strong to very strong, not weak to moderate, echoes.
explanations.C: On Fig. 8, find arrow A. Note that it points to a dot indicating the highest top in hundreds of feet, which is 30,000 ft. It lies within the second ring in a circuit, which makes it level 3 to 4, meaning strong to very strong. The entire area is TRW-RW, which indicates an area of thunderstorms and rainshowers. bile

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow B on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Weak echoes, heavy rain showers, area movement toward the southeast.
answers.B: Weak to moderate echoes, rain showers increasing in intensity.
answers.C: Strong echoes, moderate rain showers, no cell movement.

explanations.A: because the echoes are weak to moderate with the area movement to the northeast, not southeast.
explanations.B: Arrow B on Fig. 8 points to the first level of contours, which are weak to moderate echoes with rainshowers increasing in intensity as indicated by RW+.
explanations.C: because the echoes are weak to moderate (first contour), not strong.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow C on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Average echo bases 2,800 feet MSL, thundershowers, and intense to extreme echo intensity.
answers.B: Cell movement toward the northwest at 20 knots, intense echoes, and echo bases 28,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: Area movement toward the northeast, strong to very strong echoes, and echo tops 28,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A: because 280 indicates tops of 28,000 MSL, not bases of 2,800 MSL and the second level of contours indicates strong to very strong, not intense, echoes.
explanations.B: because area, not cell, movement is to the northeast, not northwest and echo tops, not bases, are 28,000 feet MSL.
explanations.C: The point of arrow C on Fig. 8 is in the second level of contours, which indicates strong to very strong echo intensity. The 280 indicates 28,000 ft. MSL tops. The arrow with two feathers indicates northeast movement at 20 kt.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow

answers.A: Echo tops 4,100 feet MSL, strong to very strong echoes within the smallest contour, and area movement toward the northeast at 50 knots.
answers.B: Intense to extreme echoes within the smallest contour, echo tops 29,000 feet MSL, and cell movement toward the northeast at 50 knots.
answers.C: Strong to very strong echoes within the smallest contour, echo bases 29,000 feet MSL, and cell in northeast Nebraska moving northeast at 50 knots.

explanations.A: because the 410 is for another area of echoes to the northeast of arrow D, with tops of 41,000 ft. MSL, not 4,100 ft MSL.
explanations.B: Arrow D in Fig. 8 is in the third contour, which means that the echo intensity is intense to extreme. The 290 indicates tops of 29,000 ft. MSL. The arrow with the 50 at its point indicates movement to the northeast at 50 kt.
explanations.C: because the tops, not bases, are 29,000 ft. MSL and the echoes are intense to extreme, not strong to very strong. bile

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow E on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.B: Echo bases 29,000 to 30,000 feet MSL, strong echoes, rain showers increasing in intensity, and area movement toward northwest at 15 knots.
answers.C: Thundershowers decreasing in intensity, area movement toward northwest at 15 knots; echo bases 30,000 feet MSL.
answers.A: Highest echo tops 30,000 feet MSL, weak to moderate echoes, thunderstorms and rain showers, and cell movement toward northwest at 15 knots.

explanations.A: The point of arrow E in Fig. 8 is in the first contour. Accordingly, the echoes are weak to moderate. The 300 indicates tops of 30,000 ft. MSL. The TRW indicates thunderstorms and rain showers. The arrow to the northwest with
explanations.B: because the tops, not the bases, are 29,000 ft. MSL and the echoes are weak to moderate, not strong.
explanations.C: because the tops, not the bases, are 30,000 ft. MSL. Also, if thundershowers were decreasing in intensity, the TRW would have a minus (-) after it. bile

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow F onthe Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Line of echoes; thunderstorms; highest echo tops 45,000 feet MSL; no line movement indicated.
answers.B: Echo bases vary from 15,000 feet to 46,000 feet MSL; thunderstorms increasing in intensity; line of echoes moving rapidly toward the north.
answers.C: Line of severe thunderstorms moving from south to north; echo bases vary from 4,400 feet to 4,600 feet MSL; extreme echoes.

explanations.A: The solid line to which arrow F in Fig. 8 is pointing is a line of echoes. They are thunderstorms as indicated by TRW. The highest echo tops are 45,000 ft. MSL, which appears as 450. No movement of the line itself is indicated.
explanations.B: because the tops, not the bases, are approximately 46,000 ft. MSL. No movement or change in intensity is indicated.
explanations.C: because the tops are 44,000 to approximately 46,000 ft. MSL, not 4,400 to 4,600. No movement of the line is indicated.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 8.) What weather conditions are depicted in the area indicated by arrow G on the Radar Summary Chart?

answers.A: Echo bases 10,000 feet MSL; cell movement toward northeast at 15 knots; weak to moderate echoes; rain.
answers.B: Area movement toward northeast at 15 knots; rain decreasing in intensity; echo bases 1,000 feet MSL; strong echoes.
answers.C: Strong to very strong echoes; area movement toward northeast at 15 knots; echo tops 10,000 feet MSL; light rain.

explanations.A: Arrow G in Fig. 8 points to an area of echoes with bases of 10,000 ft. MSL moving to the northeast at 15 kt. Since the echoes are in the first level of contours, they are weak to moderate. The R indicates rain.
explanations.B: because the bases are 10,000 ft. MSL, not 1,000 ft. MSL. Also, decreasing intensity would be indicated by a minus sign after the R.
explanations.C: because there is only one contour level, signifying weak to moderate intensity, not strong to very strong.

questions.question: What important information is provided by the Radar Summary Chart that is not shown on other weather charts?

answers.B: Types of precipitation.
answers.C: Areas of cloud cover and icing levels within the clouds.
answers.A: Lines and cells of hazardous thunderstorms.

explanations.A: A radar summary chart shows lines of thunderstorms and hazardous cells that are not shown on other weather charts.
explanations.B: because other weather charts show types of precipitation.
explanations.C: because icing conditions cannot be detected by radar.

questions.question: For the most effective use of the Radar Summary Chart during preflight planning, a pilot should

answers.B: compare it with the charts, reports, and forecasts of a three-dimensional picture of clouds and precipitation.
answers.C: utilize the chart as the only source of information regarding storms and hazardous conditions existing between reporting stations.
answers.A: consult the chart to determine more accurate measurements of freezing levels, cloud cover, and wind conditions between reporting stations.

explanations.A: because a radar summary chart does not show freezing levels, cloud cover, or wind conditions.
explanations.B: A radar summary chart graphically indicates a collection of radar reports, i.e., reports of echoes from thunderstorms and heavy precipitation. In conjunction with the weather depiction chart, which is a composite of METAR reports, a radar summary chart provides a more three-dimensional picture of clouds and precipitation.
explanations.C: because a radar summary chart must be used in conjunction with other reports and forecasts for an accurate picture of weather conditions.

questions.question: From which primary source should you obtain information regarding the weather expected to exist at your destination at your estimated time of arrival?

answers.A: Weather Depiction Chart.
answers.B: Radar Summary and Weather Depiction Chart.
answers.C: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast.

explanations.A: because a weather depiction chart is a national weather map of observed, not forecast, weather at the time specified on the chart. It is useful for flight planning to get a broad overview of the observed conditions.
explanations.B: because radar summary and weather depiction charts are national weather maps of observed, not forecast, weather at a specific time. They are useful for flight planning but do not provide specific information about a particular destination.
explanations.C: A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) is a concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions at an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). Thus, a TAF contains information regarding the expected weather at the destination airport at the ETA.

questions.question: What is the wind shear forecast in the following TAF? TAF KCVG 231051Z 231212 12012KT 4SM -RA BR OVC008 WS005/27050KT TEMPO 1719 1/2SM -RA FG FM1930 09012KT 1SM -DZ BR VV003 BECMG 2021 5SM HZ=

answers.A: 5 feet AGL from 270° at 50 KT.
answers.B: 50 feet AGL from 270° at 50 KT.
answers.C: 500 feet AGL from 270° at 50 KT.

explanations.A: because the height of the wind shear (WS005) is 500 ft. AGL, not 5 ft. AGL.
explanations.B: because the height of the wind shear (WS005) is 500 ft. AGL, not 50 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: Wind shear in a TAF is a forecast of nonconvective low-level wind shear (up to 2,000 ft. AGL) andis entered after the sky condition when wind shear is expected.
