questions.question: Which primary source should be used to obtain forecast weather information at your destination for the planned ETA?

answers.B: Radar Summary and Weather Depiction Charts.
answers.C: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF).
answers.A: Area Forecast.

explanations.A: because an area forecast (FA) is a forecast of general weather conditions over an area the size of several states, not for a specific airport. The FA is used if the destination airport does not have a TAF.
explanations.B: because radar summary and weather depiction charts are national weather maps of observed weather at a specific time. They are useful for flight planning but do not provide specific information about a particular destination airport.
explanations.C: A terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) is a concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions at an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). Thus, a TAF contains information regarding the expected weather at the destination airport at the ETA.

questions.question: The body of a Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) covers a geographical proximity within a

answers.A: 5 nautical mile radius of the center of an airport.
answers.B: 5 statute mile radius from the center of an airport runway complex.
answers.C: 5 to 10 statute mile radius from the center of an airport runway complex.

explanations.A: because the TAF covers a geographic area within a 5-SM radius of the airport's center, not a 5-NM Tadius.
explanations.B: The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) is a concise statement of the expected meteorological conditions at an airport during a specified period (usually 24 hr.). The TAF covers a geographic area within a 5 SM radius of the airport's center.
explanations.C: because the TAF covers a geographic area within a 5 SM radius of the airport's center, not 5 to 10 statute miles. The letters VC in the TAF describe conditions that will occur within the vicinity of the airport (5 to 10 SM), not at the airport, and will be used only with FG (fog), SH (showers), or TS (thunderstorms).

questions.question: Area forecasts generally include a forecast period of 18 hours and cover a

answers.C: area the size of several states.

explanations.B: because an FA forecast covers an area greater than, not less than, 3,000 sq. mi. and gives a general description of clouds and weather which are significant to VFR operations.
explanations.C: Area forecasts (FA) generally include a total forecast period of 18 hr. and cover a geographical area the size of several states.

questions.question: Astation is forecasting wind and temperature aloft at FL 390 to be 300° at 200 knots; temperature -54°C. How would this data be encoded in the FD?

explanations.A: because it indicates winds from 300° at 0 kt. However, when forecast speed is less than 5 kt., the code is 9900 for wind direction and speed.
explanations.B: At FL 390, a 300° wind at 200 Kt. is encoded as 809954. Note that the first two digits are the direction. The second two digits are velocity. 200 kt. or greater wind speeds are coded as 99 for the speed, and 50 is added to the two-digit direction code. Here, the direction is 80 for 300°. The temperature is the last two digits, and minus signs are omitted above 24,000 ft. MSL.
explanations.C: because it indicates a 99-kt. wind speed from 300°.

questions.question: How much colder than standard temperature is the forecast temperature at 9,000 feet, as indicated in the following excerpt from the Winds and Temperature Aloft Forecast? FT 6000 9000 0737-04 1043-10

explanations.A: because standard temperature at 9,000 ft. is -3°C, not -7°C.
explanations.B: because standard temperature at 9,000 ft is -3°C, not 0°C.
explanations.C: At 9,000 ft., the forecast temperature is -10°C. Standard temperature is 15°C at sea level with a lapse tate of 2°C per 1,000 ft., which would bring the standard temperature to -3°C at 9,000 ft. (15° - 18°). Therefore, the forecast temperature of -10°C is 7° colder than the standard temperature of -3°C.

questions.question: What wind direction and speed is represented by the entry 9900+00 for 9,000 feet, on a Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)?

answers.A: Light and variable; less than 5 knots.
answers.B: Vortex winds exceeding 200 knots.
answers.C: Light and variable; less than 10 knots.

explanations.A: The entry 9900 in a winds and temperatures aloft forecast indicates light and variable winds. +00 is the air temperature on the Celsius scale.
explanations.B: because an example of the code for winds over 200 kt. would be 7099, for 200° at 199 kt. or greater.
explanations.C: because light and variable means less than 5 kt, not 10 kt.

questions.question: When is the wind-group at one of the forecast altitudes omitted at a specific location or station in the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)? When the wind

answers.A: is less than 5 knots.
answers.B: is less than 10 knots.
answers.C: at the altitude is within 1,500 feet of the station elevation.

explanations.A: because, when forecast wind speed is less than 5 kt., the code 9900 is used for direction and velocity.
explanations.B: because, when forecast wind speed is less than 5 kt., not 10 kt., the code 9900 is used for direction and velocity.
explanations.C: No winds are forecast within 1,500 ft. of the station elevation. No temperatures are forecast for the 3,000-ft. MSL or for a level within 2,500 ft. of station elevation.

questions.question: When is the temperature at one of the forecast altitudes omitted at a specific location or station in the Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast (FD)?

answers.A: When the temperature is standard for that altitude.
answers.B: For the 3,000-foot altitude (level) or when the level is within 2,500 feet of station elevation.
answers.C: Only when the winds are omitted for that altitude (level).

explanations.A: because temperatures are reported whether standard or not.
explanations.B: No temperatures are forecast for the 3,000-ft. level or for a level within 2,500 ft. of station elevation. No winds are forecast within 1,500 ft. of the station elevation.
explanations.C: because the winds are omitted within 1,500 ft. of the ground and temperatures are omitted within 2,500 ft. of the ground.

questions.question: Decode the excerpt from the Winds and Temperature Aloft Forecast (FD) for OKC at 39,000 feet. FT 3000 6000 39000 OKC 830558,

answers.B: Wind 330° at 105 knots, temperature -58°C.
answers.C: Wind 330° at 205 knots, temperature -58°C.

explanations.B: At OKC at 39,000 ft., the 83 for wind direction means that 100 kt. have been deducted from the wind speed and 50 added to the wind direction. Thus, the wind speed is 105 kt. Also, subtract 50 from the first two-digit code for direction to get 330°. Above 24,000 ft., the temperatures are always negative.

questions.question: Which values are used for winds aloft forecasts?

answers.A: Magnetic direction and knots.
answers.B: Magnetic direction and MPH.
answers.C: True direction and knots.

explanations.A: because true, not magnetic, direction is used.
explanations.B: because true, not magnetic, direction and knots, not MPH, are used.
explanations.C: Winds aloft are forecast in true direction and knots.

questions.question: A prognostic chart depicts the conditions

answers.A: existing at the surface during the past 6 hours.
answers.B: which presently exist from the 1,000-millibar through the 700-millibar level.
answers.C: forecast to exist at a specific time in the future.

explanations.A: because prognostic charts relate to the future, not the past.
explanations.B: because prognostic charts relate to the future, not the present.
explanations.C: Prognostic charts show conditions as they are forecast to be at the valid time (UTC or Zulu) for the chart. The charts are issued four times daily.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 5.) What is the meaning of the symbol depicted as used on the U.S. Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart?

explanations.C: because thunderstorms are indicated by an R with an arrow on the leg.

questions.question: Which meteorological conditions are depicted by a prognostic chart?

answers.A: Conditions existing at the time of the observation.

answers.C: Conditions forecast to exist at a specific time shown on the chart.

explanations.A: because prognostic charts relate to the future, not the present.
explanations.B: because prognostic charts relate to the future, not the present.
explanations.C: Prognostic charts show conditions as they are forecast to be at the valid time for the chart. The charts are issued four times daily.

questions.question: The Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart depicts weather conditions

explanations.C: because prognostic charts look to the future; they do not report the past.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 18 SFC-400MB.) The 24-Hour Low Level Significant Weather Prog at 12Z indicates that southwestern West Virginia will likely experience

questions.question: (Refer to figure 18, SFC-PROG.) A planned low altitude flight from northern Florida to southern Florida at 00Z is likely to encounter

questions.question: (Refer to figure 9.) The Severe Weather Outlook Chart, which is used primarily for advance planning, provides what information?

answers.C: A 24-hour severe weather outlook for possible thunderstorm activity.

explanations.B: because the severe weather outlook chart is a 48-hr., not 12-hr., outlook for possible general thunderstorm activity as well as severe thunderstorms, not convective turbulence.
explanations.C: A severe weather outlook chart is presented in two panels. The left panel covers the first 24-hr. period beginning at 1200Z and depicts areas of possible thunderstorm activity. The right panel covers the following day beginning at 1200Z and contains the same information as the left

answers.B: General.

explanations.C: because areas where thunderstorm activity is forecast are shown to the right of the lines ona Convective Outlook chart when facing in the direction of the arrow. Montana is not situated to the right of any lines ont he Day 1 Convective Outlook panel, meaning that no thunderstorm activity is forecast.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 9.) The Severe Weather Outlook Chart depicts

answers.A: areas of probable severe thunderstorms by the use of single hatched areas on the chart.
answers.B: areas of forecast, severe or extreme turbulence, and areas of severe icing for the next 24 hours.
answers.C: areas of general thunderstorm activity (excluding severe) by the use of hatching on the chart.

explanations.A: The severe weather outlook chart is a 48-hr. outlook for thunderstorm activity, presented in two panels. The hatched area indicates possible severe thunderstorms. NOTE: This question refers to an old version of the severe weather outlook chart. The current chart does not use hatched areas to indicate severe thunderstorms. Expect the FAA to revise this question in the future. NOTE: This question refers to an old version of the severe weather outlook chart. The current chart does not use hatched
explanations.B: because areas of forecast severe or extreme turbulence for the next 24 hr. can be found on the significant weather panel of the significant weather prog, not the severe weather outlook chart.
explanations.C: because an area of possible general thunderstorm activity is shown to the right of a line with an arrowhead (when facing in the direction of the arrow), not a hatched area.

questions.question: Apilot planning to depart at 1100Z on an IFR flight is particularly concerned about the hazard of icing. What sources reflect the most accurate information onicing conditions (current and forecast) at the time of departure?

answers.A: Low-Level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart, and the Area Forecast.
answers.B: The Area Forecast, and the Freezing Level Chart.
answers.C: Pilot weather reports (PIREPs), AIRMETs, and SIGMETs.

explanations.A: because low-level sig weather prog charts do not forecast icing conditions but do forecast freezing levels, and an area forecast does not provide any information on icing conditions.
explanations.B: because a freezing-level chart cannot be used to determine current or forecast icing conditions, and an area forecast does not provide any information on icing conditions.
explanations.C: Pilot reports (PIREPs) can reflect the most current icing conditions for a specific area, including type and intensity. AIRMET Zulu is for icing and freezing levels for a specified time and normally an outlook. A SIGMET is issued for areas of severe icing.

questions.question: What flight planning information can a pilot derive from constant pressure charts?

answers.A: Clear air turbulence and icing conditions.
answers.B: Levels of widespread cloud coverage.
answers.C: Winds and temperatures aloft.

explanations.A: because clear air turbulence is shown on the low-level prog chart.
explanations.B: because areas and levels of widespread Cloud coverage are shown on the weather depiction and surface analysis charts.
explanations.C: Constant pressure charts provide information about the observed temperature, wind, and temperature-dew point spread along your proposed route.

questions.question: What conclusion(s) can be drawn from a 500-milli-bar Constant Pressure Chart for a planned flight at FL 180?

answers.A: Winds aloft at FL 180 generally flow across the height contours.
answers.B: Observed temperature, wind, and temperature/dew point spread along the proposed route can be approximated.
answers.C: Upper highs, lows, troughs, and ridges will be depicted by the use of lines of equal pressure.

explanations.A: because the winds usually flow parallel to, not across, the height contours.
explanations.B: From a constant pressure analysis chart, you can approximate the observed temperature, wind, and temperature-dew point spread along a proposed route.
explanations.C: because heights of the specified pressure for each station are depicted via solid lines called contours to give a height pattern. The contours depict high height centers and low height centers, not highs and lows.

questions.question: Which weather forecast describes prospects for an area coverage of both severe and general thunderstorms during the following 24 hours?

answers.B: Convective outlook.
answers.C: Radar Summary Chart.
answers.A: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast.

explanations.A: because a terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) is a statement of expected conditions around an airport, not a forecast of thunderstorms only.
explanations.B: The convective outlook (AC) describes the prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following 24 hr. Areas with a high, moderate, or slight risk of severe thunderstorms are included, as well as areas where thunderstorms may approach severe limits.
explanations.C: because a radar summary chart depicts observed radar returns, which show precipitation intensity, at the time shown on the chart. It provides an indication of observed, not forecast, severe and general thunderstorms.

questions.question: The Surface Analysis Chart depicts

answers.A: actual pressure systems, frontal locations, cloud tops, and precipitation at the time shown on the chart.
answers.B: frontal locations and expected movement, pressure centers, cloud coverage, and obstructions to vision at the time of chart transmission.
answers.C: actual frontal positions, pressure patterns, temperature, dew point, wind, weather, and obstructions to vision at the valid time of the chart.

explanations.A: because the surface analysis chart does not depict cloud tops.
explanations.B: because expected movement of weather systems is not depicted. This chart depicts current conditions at the time of issuance.
explanations.C: The surface analysis chart provides the locations of pressure systems, dew points, wind, and obstructions to vision at the valid time of the chart.

questions.question: What information is provided by a Convective Outlook (AC)?

answers.A: It describes areas of probable severe icing and severe or extreme turbulence during the next 24 hours.
answers.B: It provides prospects of both general and severe thunderstorm activity during the following 24 hours.
answers.C: Itindicates areas of probable convective turbulence and the extent of instability in the upper atmosphere (above 500 MB).

explanations.A: because areas of severe or extreme turbulence are forecast in the significant weather prog charts, not in anAC. Additionally, icing is not specifically forecast but is implied in clouds and precipitation above the freezing level.
explanations.B: The convective outlook describes the prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following 24 hr. Areas with a high, moderate, or slight risk of severe thunderstorms are included, as well as areas where thunderstorms may approach severe limits.
explanations.C: because areas of probable convective turbulence and with the extent of instability above 500 mb/hPa (18,000 ft. MSL) are depicted by the contraction "CB" ina high-level significant weather prog, not an AC.

questions.question: What does a Convective Outlook (AC) describe for a following 24-hr. period?

answers.A: General thunderstorm activity.
answers.B: A severe weather watch bulletin.
answers.C: When forecast conditions are expected to continue beyond the valid period.

explanations.A: A convective outlook (AC) describes the prospects for general thunderstorm activity during the following 24 hr.
explanations.B: because a severe weather watch bulletin is a separate product. An AC forecasts general thunderstorm activity for the following 24 hr., while a severe weather watch bulletin is issued as necessary to define areas of possible severe thunderstorms or tornado activity.
explanations.C: because an AC is a forecast of thunderstorm activity for the following 24-hr. period, not a statement of forecast conditions that are expected to continue beyond the valid period.

questions.question: When are severe weather watch bulletins (WW) issued?

answers.A: Every 12 hours as required.
answers.B: Every 24 hours as required.
answers.C: Unscheduled and issued as required.

explanations.A: because severe weather watch bulletins are unscheduled and are issued as required, not every 12 hr. as required.

questions.question: Whatis the definition of MEA?

answers.A: The lowest published altitude which meets obstacle clearance requirements and assures acceptable navigational signal coverage.
answers.B: The lowest published altitude which meets obstacle requirements, assures acceptable navigational signal coverage, two-way radio communications, and provides adequate radar coverage.
answers.C: An altitude which meets obstacle clearance requirements, assures acceptable navigation signal coverage, two-way radio communications, adequate radar coverage, and accurate DME mileage.

explanations.A: The minimum en route altitude (MEA) is the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets the obstacle clearance requirements between those fixes.
explanations.B: because, by definition, the MEA does not assure either two-way radio communications or adequate radar coverage.
explanations.C: because, by definition, the MEA is the lowest published, not any, altitude that meets obstacle clearance requirements and assures acceptable navigation signal ‘coverage. It does not provide for either two-way radio communications or adequate radar coverage.

questions.question: Reception of signals from an off-airway radio facility may be inadequate to identify the fix at the designated MEA. In this case, which altitude is designated for the fix?

answers.A: MRA.
answers.B: MCA.
answers.C: MOCA.

explanations.A: MRA (minimum reception altitude) is the lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined. It is the altitude assigned for a fix when the MEA will not provide adequate reception of an off-airway radio facility (NAVAID) identifying the fix.
explanations.B: because MCA (minimum crossing altitude) is the lowest altitude at a fix at which an aircraft must cross when proceeding in the direction of a higher MEA.
explanations.C: because the MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route segment and which assures acceptable navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.

questions.question: Reception of signals from a radio facility, located off the airway being flown, may be inadequate at the designated MEA to identify the fix. In this case, which altitude is designated for the fix?

answers.A: MOCA.
answers.B: MRA.
answers.C: MCA.

explanations.A: because the MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route segment and which assures acceptable navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B: MRA (minimum reception altitude) is the lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined. It is the altitude assigned for a fix when the MEA will not provide adequate reception of an off-airway radio facility (NAVAID) identifying the fix.
explanations.C: because MCA (minimum crossing altitude) is the lowest altitude at a fix at which an aircraft must cross when proceeding in the direction of a higher MEA.

questions.question: ATC may assign the MOCA when certain special conditions exist, and when within

answers.A: 22 NM ofa VOR.
answers.B: 25 NM ofa VOR.
answers.C: 30 NM ofa VOR.

explanations.A: MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route segment and which assures acceptable navigational signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR. Thus, ATC may assign the MOCA as an assigned altitude, but only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B: because the MOCA provides acceptable navigational signal coverage only within 25 SM, not 25 NM, of a VOR.
explanations.C: because ATC may assign the MOCA as an assigned altitude only within 22 NM, not 30 NM.

questions.question: Acceptable navigational signal coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of only

answers.B: 22 NM.
answers.C: 25 NM.

explanations.A: because acceptable navigational signal coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of 22 NM, not 12 NM.
explanations.B: MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) is the lowest published altitude in effect between radio fixes on VOR airways, off-airway routes, or route segments which meets obstacle clearance requirements for the entire route ‘segment and which assures acceptable navigational signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR. Thus, ATC may assign the MOCA as an assigned altitude, but only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.C: because acceptable navigational signal coverage at the MOCA is assured for a distance from the VOR of 22 NM, not 25 NM.

questions.question: Which aeronautical chart depicts Military Training Routes (MTR) above 1,500 feet?

answers.A: FR Planning Chart.
answers.B: IFR Low Altitude En Route Chart.
answers.C: IFR High Altitude En Route Chart.

explanations.A: because the U.S. IFR/VFR Planning Chart does not depict MTRs. The DOD Area Planning Chart depicts all MTRs, not only those above 1,500 ft. AGL.
explanations.B: IFR En Route Low-Altitude Charts depict all IFR and VFR MTRs (IR and VR routes) that accommodate operations above 1,500 ft. AGL.
explanations.C: because IFR En Route High-Altitude Charts cover altitudes at and above 18,000 ft. MSL; generally, MTRs are established below 10,000 ft. MSL.

questions.question: The altitude that provides acceptable navigational signal coverage for the route, and meets obstacle clearance requirements is the minimum:

answers.A: obstacle clearance altitude.
answers.B: reception altitude.
answers.C: enroute altitude.

explanations.A: because the MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) only guarantees acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance requirements when within 22 NM of a NAVAID, not along an entire route that takes the aircraft more than 22 NM froma NAVAID.
explanations.B: because the MRA (minimum reception altitude) is the lowest altitude at which an intersection can be identified. It is usually higher than the MEA.
explanations.C: The MEA (minimum en route altitude) is the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance requirements between those fixes.

questions.question: Which condition is guaranteed for all of the following altitude limits: MAA, MCA, MRA, MOCA, and MEA? (Non-mountainous area.)

answers.A: Adequate navigation signals.
answers.B: Adequate communications.
answers.C: 1,000-foot obstacle clearance.

explanations.A: because the MOCA assures acceptable navigational signals only within 22 NM of a VOR.
explanations.B: because the minimum IFR altitudes do not guarantee adequate communications coverage.
explanations.C: The MAA, MCA, MRA, MOCA, and MEA meet the minimum obstacle clearance requirements. In non-mountainous areas, 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle is guaranteed within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown.

questions.question: Ifno MCA is specified, what is the lowest altitude for crossing a radio fix, beyond which a higher minimum applies?

answers.A: The MEA at which the fix is approached.
answers.B: The MRA at which the fix is approached.
answers.C: The MOCA for the route segment beyond the fix.

explanations.A: If no MCA (minimum crossing altitude) is specified, the lowest altitude for crossing a radio fix beyond which a higher minimum IFR altitude exists is the MEA at which the fix is approached. A climb must be initiated to a higher minimum immediately after passing the point beyond which that minimum altitude applies.
explanations.B: because, if a higher minimum altitude exists after the fix and a higher altitude is needed to identify a fix, usually an MCA, not an MRA, is established at that fix.
explanations.C: because, if there is no MCA, the higher minimum altitude does not apply until immediately after passing the fix.

questions.question: Inthe case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of

answers.A: 3 SM from the course flown.
answers.B: 4 SM from the course flown.
answers.C: 4.NM from the course flown.

explanations.A: because the horizontal distance is 4 NM, not 3 SM, from the course flown.
explanations.B: because the horizontal distance is 4 NM, not SM, from the course flown.
explanations.C: In the case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown.

questions.question: Inthe case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below an altitude of

answers.A: 500 feet above the highest obstacle.
answers.B: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle.
answers.C: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle.

explanations.A: because no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below an altitude of 2,000 ft., not 500 ft., above the highest obstacle in a mountainous area.
explanations.B: because no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below an altitude of 1,000 ft. above the highest obstacle in a nonmountainous, not mountainous, area.
explanations.C: In the case of operations over an area designated as a mountainous area where no other minimum altitude is prescribed, no person may operate an aircraft under IFR below 2,000 ft. above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 NM from the course to be flown.

questions.question: MEA is an altitude which assures

answers.A: obstacle clearance, accurate navigational signals from more than one VORTAC, and accurate DME mileage.
answers.B: a 1,000-foot obstacle clearance within 2 miles of an airway and assures accurate DME mileage.
answers.C: acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets obstruction clearance requirements.

explanations.A: because only one VORTAC is needed at
explanations.B: because the clearance is within 4 NM, not 2 mi., and there is no assurance of DME coverage.
explanations.C: The minimum en route altitude (MEA) is the lowest published altitude between radio fixes which assures acceptable navigational signal coverage and meets the obstacle clearance requirements between those fixes.

questions.question: Unless otherwise specified on the chart, the minimum en route altitude along a jet route is

answers.A: 18,000 feet MSL.
answers.B: 24,000 feet MSL.
answers.C: 10,000 feet MSL.

explanations.A: Each designated jet route consists of a direct course for navigating from 18,000 ft. MSL up to and including FL 450 between the navigational aids and intersections specified for that route. Thus, the MEA along a jet route is 18,000 ft MSL.
explanations.B: because 24,000 ft. MSL (FL 240) is the minimum altitude at which DME is required when navigating by VOR, not the MEA for a jet route.
explanations.C: because 10,000 ft. MSL is the minimum altitude at which aircraft are required to operate the transponder on Mode C, not the MEA for a jet route.

questions.question: Under which of the following circumstances will ATC issue a VFR restriction to an |FR flight?

answers.A: Whenever the pilot reports the loss of any navigational aid.
answers.B: When it is necessary to provide separation between IFR and special VFR traffic.
answers.C: When the pilot requests it.

explanations.A: because a pilot would report only a malfunction of navigation equipment, not a loss of any navigational aid, to ATC.
explanations.B: because special VFR traffic would be found near an airport in Class B, C, or D airspace or Class E airspace designated for an airport that is currently experiencing IMC. Thus, ATC would not issue a VFR restriction to an IFR flight.
explanations.C: VFR-on-top is an ATC authorization for an IFR aircraft to operate in VFR conditions at any appropriate VFR altitude. ATC may not authorize VFR-on-top operations unless the pilot requests the clearance to operate in VFR conditions.

questions.question: What altitude may a pilot select upon receiving a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.B: Any appropriate VFR altitude at or above the MEA in VFR weather conditions.
answers.C: Any VFR altitude appropriate for the direction of flight at least 1,000 feet above the meteorological condition.
answers.A: Any altitude at least 1,000 feet above the meteorological condition.

explanations.A: because, after receiving a VFR-on-top clearance, the pilot may select any appropriate VFR altitude at or above the minimum IFR altitude in VMC, not only 1,000 ft. above the meteorological condition. This may be above, below, between layers, or in areas where there is no meteorological obscuration.
explanations.B: When operating in VMC with an ATC authorization to “maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions," pilots on IFR flight plans are required to 1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude; 2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds criteria; and 3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the flight, i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.
explanations.C: because, after receiving a VFR-on-top clearance, the pilot may select any appropriate VFR altitude at or above the minimum IFR altitude in VMC, not only 1,000 ft. above the meteorological condition. This may be above, below, between layers, or in areas where there is no meteorological obscuration.

questions.question: Which rules apply to the pilot in command when operating on a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.A: VER only.
answers.B: VFR and IFR.
answers.C: VFR when “in the clear" and IFR when "in the clouds."

explanations.A: because an ATC clearance to operate VFR-on-top does not imply cancellation of the IFR flight plan.
explanations.B: When operating in VMC with an ATC authorization to “maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions," pilots on IFR flight plans are required to 1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude; 2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds criteria; and 3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the flight, i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.
explanations.C: because a VFR-on-top clearance is issued when the pilot is in VMC and must remain in VMC unless the VFR-on-top clearance is canceled. It does not allow a pilot to fly in IMC.

questions.question: Which ATC clearance should instrument-rated pilots request in order to climb through a cloud layer or an area of reduced visibility and then continue the flight VFR?

answers.B: Special VFR to VFR Over-the-Top.
answers.C: VFR Over-the-Top.
answers.A: To VFR on Top.

explanations.A: Pilots desiring to climb through a cloud, haze, smoke, or other meteorological formation and then either cancel their IFR flight plan or operate VFR-on-top may request an ATC clearance to climb to VFR-on-top.
explanations.B: because a special VFR clearance is issued only in Class B, C, or D airspace or Class E airspace designated for an airport, and the pilot must remain clear of clouds, not climb through them.
explanations.C: because it is VFR-on-top, not VFR-over-the-top.

questions.question: When can a VFR-on-Top clearance be assigned by ATC?

answers.A: Only upon request of the pilot when conditions are indicated to be suitable.
answers.B: Any time suitable conditions exist and ATC wishes to expedite traffic flow.
answers.C: When VFR conditions exist, but there is a layer of clouds below the MEA.

explanations.A: ATC may assign a VFR-on-top clearance only when the pilot requests such a clearance, and the flight must be conducted in VFR weather conditions.
explanations.B: because ATC can issue a VFR-on-top clearance only upon a pilot's, not ATC’s, request.
explanations.C: because ATC can issue a VFR-on-top clearance only upon a pilot's request; clearance is not based only on the meteorological conditions.

questions.question: When ona VFR-on-Top clearance, the cruising altitude is based on

answers.B: magnetic course.
answers.C: magnetic heading.
answers.A: true course.

explanations.A: because VFR cruising altitudes are based on magnetic, not true, course.
explanations.B: While operating under a VFR-on-top clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR altitude, which is based on magnetic course.
explanations.C: because VFR cruising altitudes are based on magnetic course, not heading.

questions.question: When must a pilot fly at a cardinal altitude plus 500 feet on an IFR flight plan?

answers.A: When flying above 18,000 feet in VFR conditions.
answers.B: When flying in VFR conditions above clouds.
answers.C: When assigned a VFR-on-Top clearance.

explanations.A: because VFR-on-top is not permitted in Class A airspace, which is from 18,000 ft. MSL to and including FL 600.
explanations.B: because a pilot on an IFR flight plan uses VFR altitudes only when assigned a VFR-on-top clearance.
explanations.C: VFR-on-top clearances are flown at VFR altitudes, which are even or odd thousand-foot intervals plus 500 ft. This is in contrast to IFR altitudes that are at even or odd thousand-foot intervals. Cardinal altitude means 1,000-ft. intervals, e.g., 3,000, 4,000, etc.

questions.question: Where are VFR-on-Top operations prohibited?

answers.A: In Class A airspace.
answers.B: During off-airways direct flights.
answers.C: When flying through Class B airspace.

explanations.A: ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top operations in Class A airspace.
explanations.B: because VFR-on-top operations during off-airway direct flights are not prohibited.
explanations.C: because VFR-on-top operations within Class B airspace are permitted.

questions.question: You have filed an IFR flight plan with a VFR-on-Top clearance in lieu of an assigned altitude. If you receive this clearance and fly a course of 180°, at what altitude should you fly? (Assume VFR conditions.)

answers.A: Any IFR altitude which will enable you to remain in VFR conditions.
answers.B: An odd thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 feet.
answers.C: An even thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 feet.

explanations.A: because, on VFR-on-top, one uses VFR, not IFR, altitudes.
explanations.B: because odd thousand-foot altitudes plus 500 ft. are for a magnetic course of 0° through 179°, not 180°.
explanations.C: When operating in VMC with a VFR-on-top clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR cruising altitude. On a magnetic course of 180° through 359°, an even thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 ft. must be flown.

questions.question: What minimums must be considered in selecting an altitude when operating with a VFR-on-Top clearance?

answers.B: At least 1,000 feet above the lowest MEA, appropriate MOCA, or existing meteorological condition.
answers.C: Minimum IFR altitude, minimum distance from clouds, and visibility appropriate to altitude selected.
answers.A: Atleast 500 feet above the lowest MEA, or appropriate MOCA, and at least 1,000 feet above the existing meteorological condition.

explanations.A: because you must be at or above, not a specified distance from, the minimum IFR altitude, and while ona VFR-on-top clearance, you may operate above, below, or between layers of, not only above, the existing meteorological condition.
explanations.B: because you must be at or above, not a specified distance from, the minimum IFR altitude, and while on a VFR-on-top clearance, you may operate above, below, or between layers of, not only above, the existing meteorological condition.
explanations.C: When operating in VMC with an ATC authorization to "maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions,” pilots on IFR flight plans are required to 1. Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude; 2. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from clouds criteria; and 3. Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to the flight, ie., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, course to be flown, adherence to ATC clearances, etc.

questions.question: If, while in Class E airspace, a clearance is received to "maintain VFR conditions on top," the pilot should maintain a VFR cruising altitude based on the direction of the

answers.A: true course.
answers.B: magnetic heading.
answers.C: magnetic course.

explanations.A: because VFR cruising altitudes are based on magnetic, not true, course.
explanations.B: because VFR cruising altitudes are based on magnetic course, not heading.
explanations.C: While operating under a VFR-on-top clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR cruising altitude, which is based on magnetic course.

questions.question: In which airspace is VFR-on-Top operation prohibited?

answers.A: Class B airspace.
answers.B: Class E airspace.
answers.C: Class A airspace.

explanations.A: because VFR-on-top operations are permitted, not prohibited, in Class B airspace.
explanations.B: because VFR-on-top operations are permitted, not prohibited, in Class E airspace.
explanations.C: ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top operations in Class A airspace.

questions.question: What cruising altitude is appropriate for VFR on Top on a westbound flight below 18,000 feet?

answers.B: Even thousand-foot levels plus 500 feet, but not below MEA.
answers.C: Odd thousand-foot levels plus 500 feet, but not below MEA.

explanations.B: When operating in VMC with a VFR-on-top clearance, you must fly at the appropriate VFR cruising altitude but not below the minimum IFR altitude (e.g., MEA). Ona magnetic course of 180° through 359° (i.e., westbound), an even thousand-foot MSL altitude plus 500 ft. must be flown.
explanations.C: because an odd thousand-foot level plus 500 ft. is for eastbound, not westbound, flight or a magnetic course from 0° to 179°.

questions.question: What reports are required of a flight operating on an IFR clearance specifying VER on Top in a nonradar environment?

answers.A: The same reports that are required for any IFR flight.
answers.B: All normal IFR reports except vacating altitudes.
answers.C: Only the reporting of any unforecast weather.

explanations.B: because all normal IFR reports are required when operating on a VFR-on-top clearance. You should advise ATC prior to any altitude change to ensure the exchange of accurate traffic information.
explanations.C: because all IFR reports, not only unforecast weather, must be made while operating on a VFR-on-top clearance.

questions.question: When operating under IFR with a VFR-On-Top clearance, what altitude should be maintained?

answers.A: An FR cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown.
answers.B: A VFR cruising altitude appropriate to the magnetic course being flown and as restricted by ATC.
answers.C: The last IFR altitude assigned by ATC.

questions.question: inthe event of two-way radio communications failure while operating on an IFR clearance in VFR conditions, the pilot should continue

explanations.B: If two-way radio communications fail while operating in VFR conditions, or if VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, each pilot shall continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable.

questions.question: (Refer to figure 65.) Which point would be the appropriate VOR COP on V552 from the LFT to the TBD VORTACs?

answers.B: HATCH intersection.
answers.C: 34 DME from the LFT VORTAC.

explanations.B: because HATCH INT is 5 NM before the COP at 34 NM (i.e., midway point between the LFT and TBD VORTACs).
explanations.C: The changeover point (COP) is located midway between the navigation facilities for straight route segments, unless the COP symbol (n ) is depicted on the route, in which case the indicated location is the COP. Since no COP symbol appears on V552 from LFT VORTAC (middle left) to TBD VORTAC (lower right), in Fig. 65, the COP is at the midway point. questions.question: (Refer to figures 65 and 66.) What is your position relative to GRICE intersection?

answers.A: Right of V552 and approaching GRICE intersection.
answers.B: Right of V552 and past GRICE intersection.
answers.C: Left of V552 and approaching GRICE intersection.

explanations.A: GRICE INT is located at the lower middle portion of Fig. 65 along V552; it is the intersection of V552 and the localizer course to Harry P. Williams Mem. Airport. Your No. 1 VOR (Fig. 66) is tuned to the TBD VORTAC with an OBS setting of 116E TO the station. If you are flying toward TBD VORTAC on 552 (R-296), a left CDI deflection indicates that you are to the right of V552. Your No. 2 VOR is tuned to the LPTN localizer course. If you are flying inbound on the localizer, a left CDI needle deflection indicates that you are to the right of the localizer i course. Thus, you are right of V552 and approaching GRICE INT.
explanations.B: because, if you were past GRICE INT, you would be to the left of the localizer; thus, the CDI needle would have a right, not left, deflection.
explanations.C: because, if you were to the left of V552, the CDI needle would have a right, not left, deflection.

questions.question: (Refer to figures 65 and 67.) What is the significance of the symbol at GRICE intersection?

answers.A: It signifies a localizer-only approach is available at Harry P. Williams Memorial.
answers.B: The localizer has an additional navigation function.
answers.C: GRICE intersection also serves as the FAF for the ILS approach procedure to Harry P. Williams Memorial.

explanations.A: because the localizer symbol indicates the availability of an ILS, not an LOC only, approach.
explanations.B: The large localizer symbol from Harry P. Williams Memorial to GRICE INT (Fig. 65) indicates that the localizer has a navigation function in addition to course guidance. In this case, the localizer's navigational function is to identify GRICE INT.
explanations.C: because GRICE INT is identified by the localizer course. The FAF on an ILS is the interception of the glide slope, not an intersection.
